順天府鄉試錄序

皇上明天子臨御大寶十有九年於茲，奉天法祖，進賢圖治。自壬午迄庚子，有司大比凡七，蓋云久矣。時順天府臣循例請事。事，上命左庶子臣承叙、左中允臣學詩往主考試，蓋云專矣。同考則進士臣若林、教授臣榕、教諭臣輔、臣雲臺、臣埴、臣成立、臣仁、臣性、臣儒，凡九人。監試則御史臣鋐、臣學，凡二人，罔不矢心而戮力也。提調則府尹臣淦、府丞臣魯
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

His Majesty, the enlightened Son of Heaven, has now occupied the imperial throne for nineteen years. Revering Heaven and emulating his ancestors, he advances worthy men and strives for good government. From the renwu year to the gengzi year, the responsible authorities have held seven triennial examinations: this has indeed continued for a considerable time. On this occasion, the officials of Shuntian Prefecture petitioned, according to precedent, to conduct the examination. [The transcription repeats 事 here; its sense is doubtful.] His Majesty ordered his servants Chengxu, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction, and Xueshi, Left Rectifier, to go and preside as Examiners: responsibility was thus specifically entrusted to them.

The Associate Examiners were nine in all: his servant Ruolin, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi); his servant Rong, a Prefectural School Instructor; and his servants Fu, Yuntai, Zhi, Chengli, Ren, Xing, and Ru, County School Instructors. The officials overseeing the examination were two Censors, his servants Hong and Xue. All pledged themselves wholeheartedly and joined their efforts.

The Proctors were his servant Gan, Prefect, and his servant Lu, Vice Prefect …

矣及期提學御史臣黃綬曁諸
曹六館所選士咸集京師凡三
千人有竒蓋云盛矣三試之拔
其雋凡百三十有五人錄其文
凡二十篇以
獻
===

神化昭孚徵諸人職事靖共徵諸嚴
文治敷同徵諸盛俊乂明揚徵
諸精廼若其專則臣二人之首
責而懼其溷且蔽焉者也粹是
五者而為錄將不可程矣乎臣
承敘竊聞之取士以科取文以

夫神化昭孚，徵諸人；職事靖共，徵諸嚴；文治敷同，徵諸盛；俊乂明揚，徵諸精。廼若其專，則臣二人之首責，而懼其溷且蔽焉者也。粹是五者而為錄，將不可程矣乎？臣承敘竊聞之：取士以科，取文以
translation_en:
…two in all, likewise without exception taking precautions well in advance: the arrangements could indeed be called rigorous. At the appointed time, the scholars selected by your servant Huang Shou, the Investigating Censor for Education, and by the various offices and the six colleges all assembled in the capital. They numbered more than three thousand: the gathering could indeed be called flourishing. They were examined in three sessions, and the outstanding among them were selected, numbering 135 in all. Twenty of their compositions were recorded for presentation to the throne, as prescribed: the selection could indeed be called refined.
The manifest and trusted efficacy of your divine transforming influence is attested by these men; reverent discharge of official duties is attested by this rigor; the widespread diffusion of civil cultivation is attested by this flourishing gathering; and the recognition and advancement of outstanding talent is attested by this refined selection. As for the exclusive charge entrusted to us, this is the foremost responsibility of us two servants, and we fear that our judgment may be confused or obscured. If the essence of these five things is gathered into a record, could it not serve as a model? Your servant Chengxu has humbly heard it said: selecting men through examinations, and selecting compositions by …

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
程皆非古也自關雎麟趾之詩
廢周官之法度弛焉所由來非
一朝夕之積使選舉猶至今存
則其弊奚啻科目而已故為之
科以樹風聲也為之程以尚體
要也蓋約選舉之意而變通之
自漢以來未之有改矣然文之
===
可程獨科目乎哉是故彌綸兩
儀品裁六度叶和三靈敷宣五
彝暉麗萬類莫非其用也而聖
人體之為德措之為業載之為
經咸取衷焉後世建國君民立
綱陳紀於文之道欲須臾舍不
可得矣文之時義大矣哉我

彝暉麗萬類莫非其用也而聖
人體之爲德措之爲業載之爲

punctuated: 程，皆非古也。自《關雎》《麟趾》之詩廢，周官之法度弛焉，所由來非一朝夕之積。使選舉猶至今存，則其弊奚啻科目而已？故為之科以樹風聲也，為之程以尚體要也。蓋約選舉之意而變通之，自漢以來未之有改矣。然文之可程，獨科目乎哉？是故彌綸兩儀，品裁六度，叶和三靈，敷宣五彝，暉麗萬類，莫非其用也。而聖人體之為德，措之為業，載之為經，咸取衷焉。後世建國君民，立綱陳紀，於文之道欲須臾舍，不可得矣。文之時義大矣哉！我
translation_en:
…by prescribed standards: neither practice is ancient. Since the poems “The Ospreys” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hoof” (Linzhi) fell into disuse and the institutions of the Offices of Zhou grew lax, the conditions that brought this about have accumulated over far more than a single day or night. Had the old system of selection and recommendation survived to the present, would its abuses have been confined to those of the examination system? Thus examination categories were established to foster exemplary influence, and model standards were established to esteem substance and essentials. This adapted the intent of selection and recommendation to changing circumstances; since the Han, this principle has remained unchanged. Yet is the capacity of writing and cultural pattern (wen) to serve as a standard confined to examinations alone?

Thus, encompassing Heaven and Earth, ordering and regulating the six measures [?], harmonizing the three celestial powers, setting forth the five enduring human relationships, and illuminating the myriad kinds of beings—all are its functions. The sages embody it as virtue, put it into practice as achievement, and record it as the Classics, in all cases drawing their proper standard from it. In later ages, those who establish states and rule the people, set up guiding principles and lay out regulations, cannot dispense with the Way of wen even for a moment. Great indeed is the significance of wen in its time! Our…

No Way was put into practice unless it was that of the sage emperors and kings; no words were recorded unless they were those of sages and worthies. title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
元良
至仁達孝鴻儀鉅典翔洽輝映是又
文之經緯天地綱維宇宙者也
夫王畿首善聲名文物爲四方
極士生其中融液鼓鑄既已乆
矣茲復仰
休光侈偉觀鼓舞振迅天下尤莫先
焉非其幸歟故臣等日校其文
雲蒸波涌珠駢綺錯其見拔者
又皆敦厖而閎衍淵懿而宣鬯
可以見帝王之謨焉可以見聖
賢之訓焉可以見
祖宗之澤焉亦盛且精矣是皆思皇
譽髦之質而奮庸熈載之具也

矣茲復仰
===
休光侈偉觀鼓舞振迅天下尤莫先
焉非其幸歟故臣等曰校其文
雲蒸波涌珠駢綺錯其見拔者
又皆敦龐而閎衍淵懿而宣卷
可以見帝王之謨焉可以見聖
賢之訓焉可以見
祖宗之澤焉亦盛且精矣是皆思皇
髦之質而奮庸熙載之具也
punctuated:
元良。至仁達孝，鴻儀鉅典，翔洽輝映，是又文之經緯天地、綱維宇宙者也。

夫王畿首善，聲名文物爲四方極。士生其中，融液鼓鑄，既已乆矣。茲復仰休光，侈偉觀，鼓舞振迅，天下尤莫先焉，非其幸歟？故臣等日校其文，雲蒸波涌，珠駢綺錯。其見拔者，又皆敦厖而閎衍，淵懿而宣鬯，可以見帝王之謨焉，可以見聖賢之訓焉，可以見祖宗之澤焉，亦盛且精矣。是皆思皇譽髦之質，而奮庸熈載之具也。
translation_en:
…the heir apparent. Such consummate benevolence and fully realized filial piety, such grand ceremonies and great rites, spread harmoniously and shine upon one another. These, too, are manifestations of civil culture that give order to Heaven and Earth and hold the universe together.

Now the royal metropolitan region leads in goodness, and its renown, cultural accomplishments, and institutions set the standard for all quarters. Scholars born here have long been steeped in these influences and molded by them. Now, moreover, they look up to the imperial radiance and behold this magnificent spectacle; nowhere else in the realm surpasses them in inspiration and vigorous endeavor. Is this not their good fortune? Thus, as we, your servants, assessed their writings each day, they rose like clouds and surged like waves, like pearls strung together and patterned silks interwoven. Those selected were, moreover, substantial and broad-ranging, profound and admirable, lucid and fluent. In them may be seen the plans of emperors and kings, the teachings of sages and worthies, and the beneficent legacy of the imperial ancestors. They are both abundant and refined indeed. All these men possess the qualities of splendid, renowned talents and the capacities to apply themselves vigorously to service and bring the affairs of government to fruition.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
錄而傳之謂不足以程也可乎
抑臣聞之記曰可言也不可行
君子不言也可行也不可言君
子不行也故言則有物行則有
恒夫民受中天地所謂性也聖
人因所固有而裁之故其行也
亦至乎不踰矩而止矩也者中
===
也二三子既以言進矣其務以
行前言反躬實踐窮理盡性舉
民物而甄陶之以上翊
聖人範圍曲成之能視今日先資之
言不至如弁髦焉則夫文之程
也不亦大且遠矣乎矧幽都黃
帝所宅寔人文肇開地而習俗

也不亦大且遠矣乎矧幽都黃
帝所宅寔人文肇開地而習俗
punctuated:
錄而傳之，謂不足以程也，可乎？
抑臣聞之，《記》曰：「可言也，不可行，君子不言也；可行也，不可言，君子不行也。故言則有物，行則有恒。」夫民受中天地，所謂性也。聖人因所固有而裁之，故其行也，亦至乎不踰矩而止。矩也者，中也。二三子既以言進矣，其務以行前言，反躬實踐，窮理盡性，舉民物而甄陶之，以上翊聖人範圍曲成之能。視今日先資之言，不至如弁髦焉，則夫文之程也，不亦大且遠矣乎？矧幽都，黃帝所宅，寔人文肇開地，而習俗
translation_en:
…Having recorded and transmitted these writings, could one say that they are inadequate to serve as models?
Moreover, your servant has heard this saying in the Record of Rites: “What can be spoken but cannot be put into practice, the gentleman does not say; what can be done but cannot be spoken of, the gentleman does not do. Thus his words have substance, and his conduct has constancy.” The people receive the mean from Heaven and Earth; this is what is called their nature. The sage shapes what they inherently possess, and thus his conduct reaches the point of never overstepping the rules. These rules are the mean. You gentlemen have now advanced through your words. Strive, then, to put your earlier words into practice, examine yourselves and act upon them, investigate principles and fully realize your nature. Take all people and things under your formative care, thereby assisting the sage ruler above in his capacity to encompass all things and bring each to fulfillment. If the words upon which you have initially relied today [?] do not come to be treated like a discarded ceremonial cap and childhood forelocks, will not the exemplary influence of these writings be great and far-reaching indeed? Moreover, Youdu, where the Yellow Emperor dwelt, is truly a place where human culture first arose, and its customs…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
忱慨多長材偉略器藝之美二
三子蓋已兼之其為科目重有
足徵者臣等專且嚴之責庶幾
逭矣臣不佞往貳太學與聞教
養茲復竊文柄職掄選則以人
事君臣尤有深懼焉故於其始
進以程之說申告而胥飭之
===
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼翰
林院侍講童承敘謹序

奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼翰
林院侍講童承敘謹序
punctuated:
忱慨，多長材偉略、器藝之美，二三子蓋已兼之。其為科目重，有足徵者。臣等專且嚴之責，庶幾逭矣。臣不佞，往貳太學，與聞教養；茲復竊文柄，職掄選，則以人事君，臣尤有深懼焉。故於其始進，以程之說申告而胥飭之。
奉議大夫、左春坊左庶子兼翰林院侍講童承敘謹序。
translation_en:
…earnest and impassioned [?], with many outstanding gifts, great strategic abilities, and excellent capacities and skills. You gentlemen presumably already possess these together. There is sufficient evidence that you will bring distinction to the examination system. We, your servants, may thus hope to have discharged our responsibility to exercise undivided attention and strict judgment. Unworthy though I am, I formerly served as deputy at the Imperial University and participated in its work of instruction and nurture. Now I have again been entrusted, beyond my deserts, with authority over literary assessment and the duty of selecting talent. Since this means serving my sovereign by providing him with men, I feel especially profound apprehension. Thus, as these gentlemen begin their advancement, I have reiterated this explanation of standards and models to admonish them all.
Preface respectfully composed by Tong Chengxu, Grand Master for Consultative Advice, Left Secretariat Supervisor in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Expositor-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試
提調官
嘉議大夫順天府府尹蔣淦〔汝潔廣西全州人辛未進士〕
順天府府丞尤魯〔懋宗直隸無錫縣人壬辰進士〕
考試官
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼翰林院侍講童承叙〔士疇湖廣沔陽州人辛巳進士〕
左春坊左中允兼翰林院修撰李學詩〔正夫山東平度州人丙戌進士〕
同考試官

translation_en:
Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, the nineteenth year of Jiajing (1540)

Proctors

Jiang Gan, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian, had the courtesy name Rujie and was a native of Quanzhou, Guangxi. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinwei year.

You Lu, Vice Prefect of Shuntian, had the courtesy name Maozong and was a native of Wuxi County, Zhili. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renchen year.

Examiners

Tong Chengxu, Grand Master for Court Discussion, Left Mentor in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Expositor in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Shichou and was a native of Mianyang Subprefecture, Huguang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year.

Li Xueshi, Left Rectifier in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Zhengfu and was a native of Pingdu Subprefecture, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Associate Examiners

Sheng Ruolin, a metropolitan graduate assigned to administrative duties in the Bureau of Personnel Appointments of the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Zicai and was a native of Haiyang County, Guangdong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year.

Huang Zhen, Director of the Confucian School of Luzhou Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Zhongcai and was a native of Nanchang County, Jiangxi. He became a tribute student (gongshi) in the renwu year.

Tang Fu, Instructor in the Confucian School of Xin'an County, Henan Prefecture, Henan, had the courtesy name Zhiyi. He was registered with Longjiang Left Guard in Zhili and was a native of Huangyan County, Zhejiang. He became a tribute student in the xinmao year.

Wu Wangtai, Instructor in the Confucian School of Ningyang County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, had the courtesy name Wenxiang and was a native of Putian County, Fujian. He became a tribute student in the xinmao year.

Yuan Zhi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Songyang County, Chuzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, had the courtesy name Bangqi and was a native of Fengcheng County, Jiangxi. He became a tribute student in the renwu year.

Lin Chengli, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jiyang County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, had the courtesy name Zhongli and was a native of Putian County, Fujian. He became a tribute student in the jiawu year.

Hou Ren, Instructor in the Confucian School of Dingtao County, Caozhou Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, had the courtesy name Yuanqing and was a native of Fuliang County, Jiangxi. He became a tribute student in the xinmao year.

Dong Xing, Instructor in the Confucian School of Shanyang County, Huai'an Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Yuanshan and was a native of Macheng County, Huguang. He became a tribute student in the dingyou year.

Hong Ru, Instructor in the Confucian School of Yicheng County, Xiangyang Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Mengchun. He was registered with Yunnan Front Guard and was a native of Qiantang County, Zhejiang. He became a tribute student in the xinmao year.

Examination Inspectors

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Ji Kangzi asked, “Could Zhong You be entrusted with government?” The Master said, “You is decisive; what difficulty would he have in governing?” He asked, “Could Ci be entrusted with government?” The Master said, “Ci has sound understanding; what difficulty would he have in governing?” He asked, “Could Qiu be entrusted with government?” The Master said, “Qiu is accomplished; what difficulty would he have in governing?”

Thus, one of great virtue is certain to obtain the position, emoluments, renown, and longevity due to him.

When a sage governs All under Heaven, he makes beans and grain as plentiful as water and fire. When beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire, how could any of the people fail to be humane?

Book of Changes (Yi)

The former kings accordingly made music to exalt virtue, offering it in abundance to the Lord on High, with their ancestors associated in the sacrifice.

Nine in the fifth place: Sweet moderation. Auspicious. To go forward brings esteem.

They speak of the most intricate things under Heaven, yet cannot be disliked; they speak of the greatest movements under Heaven, yet cannot be thrown into disorder. Compare before speaking; deliberate before acting. Through comparison and deliberation, they accomplish their changes and transformations.

All under Heaven reaches the same destination by different paths, and arrives at one outcome through a hundred deliberations.

Book of Documents (Shu)

translation_en:
Every three years, achievements were assessed; after three assessments, officials were dismissed or promoted [two characters illegible]. All undertakings prospered, and the Sanmiao were separated and banished.
Assist the worthy and support the virtuous; distinguish the loyal and advance the good.
The enlightened king attended carefully to virtue, and the peoples of the four quarters all submitted. Far and near alike, they presented the products of their lands: clothing, food, implements, and utensils. The king then distributed what his manifest virtue had brought him to states ruled by other surnames, so that they would not neglect their service. He distributed precious jade to the states of his paternal uncles, thereby displaying affection for his kin. He did not slight people and prize objects; virtue alone was what he prized.
The common people reverently complied, and the myriad states all enjoyed peace and well-being.

Book of Odes
The spring days grow warm; the orioles sing. The girls carry fine baskets and follow the narrow paths, seeking tender mulberry leaves. The spring days are long; in throngs they gather white southernwood.
The gleaming white colt is in that empty valley. A bundle of fresh-cut fodder is there; its owner is like jade.
Rise early and retire late; sprinkle and sweep within the courtyard, serving as a model for the people. Put your chariots and horses in order, along with bows, arrows, and weapons of war, to prepare against the outbreak of warfare and to drive back the peoples of the distant regions.
Grant me long life, and aid me with abundant blessings. Having honored my illustrious deceased father with offerings, I also honor my accomplished mother.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In the sixth month, the Marquis of Qi came to present spoils from his victory over the Rong. Thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang.
Luan Shu of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. Sixth year of Duke Cheng. In summer, in the fifth month, on the jiawu day…

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Question: Heaven brings forth the people and establishes rulers and teachers for them in order to uphold Heaven’s constant norms and invigorate the guiding principles of human relations. The Two Emperors and Three Kings succeeded one another, sage following sage; none could surpass them. In later ages, however, there arose the notions of the succession of legitimate rulership and the transmission of the Way. Where, in fact, did these originate? From middle antiquity onward, who were those whose reform of government and establishment of instruction qualified them to transmit the succession of rulership and the Way? May we hear about them? Now, no work sets forth the succession of legitimate rulership more authoritatively than the Spring and Autumn Annals; as for the Way…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
統莫正於書綱目序統系進蜀漢而黜
曹魏果春秋尊王之義歟或者於秦晉
隋之相承也不能無議焉亦有見歟宋
史傳道學取康節南軒而舍象山果尚
書傳心之法歟或者於胡康侯呂伯恭
蔡季通眞希元魏華父之未錄也不能
無疑焉亦有說歟我
皇祖驅胡元闢函夏以復帝王之舊治道之統
無論漢唐宋其視湯武果孰優歟今
===
聖人在上纘承儀式君師之道既明且行然而
同符往聖紹休
皇祖者亦可得而窺測其萬一否歟夫輔理承
化從政敷教二三子與有責也願質之
以究所學
問
儲副之建國本攸屬故選左右蚤諭教最急
虞夏殷周有三公四輔之官而記但言
師保而不及傅言疑丞而不及輔弼何

問
儲副之建國本攸屬故選左右蚤諭教最急
虞夏殷周有三公四輔之官而記但言
師保而不及傳言疑丞而不及輔爾何
punctuated:
統莫正於《書》。《綱目》序統系，進蜀漢而黜曹魏，果《春秋》尊王之義歟？或者於秦、晉、隋之相承也，不能無議焉，亦有見歟？《宋史》傳道學，取康節、南軒而舍象山，果《尚書》傳心之法歟？或者於胡康侯、呂伯恭、蔡季通、眞希元、魏華父之未錄也，不能無疑焉，亦有說歟？我皇祖驅胡元，闢函夏，以復帝王之舊，治道之統，無論漢、唐、宋，其視湯、武，果孰優歟？今聖人在上，纘承儀式，君師之道既明且行。然而同符往聖、紹休皇祖者，亦可得而窺測其萬一否歟？夫輔理承化，從政敷教，二三子與有責也，願質之以究所學。

問：儲副之建，國本攸屬，故選左右、蚤諭教最急。虞、夏、殷、周有三公四輔之官，而《記》但言師、保而不及傅，言疑、丞而不及輔、弼，何
translation_en:
…the succession of the Way is nowhere more authoritatively established than in the Book of Documents. In setting out the line of legitimate succession, the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian gangmu) elevates Shu Han and excludes Cao Wei. Does this truly accord with the Spring and Autumn Annals’ principle of honoring the rightful king? Some cannot refrain from questioning its treatment of the succession through Qin, Jin, and Sui. Do they, too, have grounds for their view? In its biographies of scholars of the Learning of the Way, the History of the Song includes Kangjie and Nanxuan but omits Xiangshan. Does this truly accord with the Book of Documents’ method of transmitting the teachings of the mind? Some cannot refrain from expressing doubts about the omission of Hu Kanghou, Lü Bogong, Cai Jitong, Zhen Xiyuan, and Wei Huafu. Do they, too, have reasons for their position? Our imperial ancestor expelled the non-Chinese Yuan and opened up the Chinese realm, restoring the ancient order of the sage emperors and kings. In the succession of governance and the Way, leaving aside Han, Tang, and Song, how does he compare with Tang and Wu: who truly excels? Now the sage occupies the throne, carrying forward the inherited models; the Way of ruler and teacher is both clearly understood and put into practice. Yet can we glimpse even one ten-thousandth of how he accords with the sages of the past and continues the glorious achievements of our imperial ancestor? You candidates, too, bear responsibility for assisting in government and carrying forward moral transformation, serving in office and spreading instruction. We wish to put these questions to you to probe the extent of your learning.

Question: Establishing the heir apparent concerns the very foundation of the state. Thus the most urgent matters are choosing his attendants and instructing him from an early age. Under Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou there were the offices of the Three Dukes and Four Assistants. Yet the Record of Rites mentions only the Grand Preceptor and Grand Guardian, without mentioning the Grand Mentor; it mentions the Adviser and Aide, without mentioning the Supporter and Corrector. Why…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
耶傅儲之久莫如周公設官之備亦莫
如周典然東僚獨缺如記所言自三師
三少之外無聞焉何耶將所設者止此
耶抑其所以為教者不同耶自齒胄之
禮廢官屬寖建漢宋猶略而唐之六典
獨詳可得聞其職守耶成王之賢所輔
者周公數人而足何後世設官分職而
其功反不古若耶周公而下由漢訖宋
擅承華之望而揚翊贊之休者亦不可
===
謂無人也可得而歷舉耶我
皇祖建官
東朝之制增損六典而近臣參攝尤革前代
之弊比者
皇上豫建
儲宮簡置僚屬誠億萬載根本之福也諸士
欣戴快睹之餘其於職守人品必究心
矣夫職守正則章程具而業可大人品
別則儀法著而德可久是固今日所欲

別則儀法著而德可久是固今日所欲
punctuated: 耶？傅儲之久，莫如周公；設官之備，亦莫如周典。然東僚獨缺，如記所言，自三師三少之外無聞焉，何耶？將所設者止此耶？抑其所以為教者不同耶？自齒胄之禮廢，官屬寖建，漢宋猶略，而唐之六典獨詳，可得聞其職守耶？成王之賢，所輔者周公數人而足，何後世設官分職，而其功反不古若耶？周公而下，由漢訖宋，擅承華之望而揚翊贊之休者，亦不可謂無人也，可得而歷舉耶？我皇祖建官東朝之制，增損六典，而近臣參攝，尤革前代之弊。比者皇上豫建儲宮，簡置僚屬，誠億萬載根本之福也。諸士欣戴快睹之餘，其於職守人品必究心矣。夫職守正，則章程具而業可大；人品別，則儀法著而德可久。是固今日所欲
translation_en:
…why is this so? No one served longer as tutor to the heir apparent than the Duke of Zhou, and no provisions for establishing offices were more comprehensive than those in the Institutions of Zhou. Yet the offices of the Eastern Palace alone are lacking: as the Record of Rites states, nothing is heard of beyond the Three Preceptors and Three Junior Preceptors. Why is this? Were these the only offices established, or were their methods of instruction different? After the rite by which the heir apparent took his place at school according to age fell into disuse, subordinate offices gradually multiplied. Their organization under the Han and Song was still relatively simple, whereas the Tang Six Statutes alone gives detailed provisions. May we hear what their official duties were? For the worthy King Cheng, the assistance of the Duke of Zhou and a few others sufficed. Why did later generations establish offices and divide responsibilities, yet achieve less than the ancients? From the Duke of Zhou onward, through the Han down to the Song, there were certainly men who enjoyed distinction in the heir apparent’s palace and won acclaim for their assistance and counsel. Can you enumerate them in turn?

When Our Imperial Ancestor established the offices of the Eastern Court, he made additions to and reductions from the Six Statutes; in particular, having close ministers concurrently undertake these duties remedied the defects of previous dynasties. Recently His Majesty designated the heir apparent in good time and selected and appointed his staff. This is truly a blessing for the foundations of the dynasty for countless ages. You gentlemen, besides joyfully supporting and gladly witnessing this event, must surely have devoted thought to these officials’ duties and personal qualities. When official duties are properly ordered, regulations are complete and great accomplishments become possible; when personal qualities are discerningly assessed, standards of conduct are made manifest and virtue can endure. This, indeed, is what we wish today to…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聞也幸明以告我
問古者右史記言而因革之法存焉左史
記動而理亂之事存焉自史職寢廢孔
子嘅文獻之不足廼取六經而刪述之
帝王之道於是會通故六經萬世之文
獻也其後司馬遷作史記於坑焚之餘
有八書以著其法有紀傳以載其事盖
自附於文獻之續也班固漢書悉準遷
例稍增損焉然或者亦互有評隲二書
===
果相異同否耶固以下斷代爲史會通
之道始分至梁吳均作通史盖其事也
宋司馬光復總十六史而作通鑑然於
法之因革又略而不載何耶唐杜佑作
通典盖其法也元馬端臨復廣二十四
目而作通考然於事之理亂又缺而不
著何耶若夫鄭樵所撰通志盖合二者
而並錄之爲紀爲略爲年譜爲世家爲
傳爲載記凡二百卷亦足以言會通否

果相異同否耶固以下斷代爲史會通
之道始分至梁吳均作通史蓋其事也
宋司馬光復總十六史而作通鑑然於
法之因革又略而不載何耶唐杜佑作
通典蓋其法也元馬端臨復廣二十四
目而作通考然於事之理亂又缺而不
著何耶若夫鄭樵所撰通志蓋合二者
而並錄之爲紀爲略爲年譜爲世家爲
傳爲載記凡二百卷亦足以言會通否
punctuated:
聞也，幸明以告我。

問：古者右史記言，而因革之法存焉；左史記動，而理亂之事存焉。自史職寢廢，孔子嘅文獻之不足，廼取六經而刪述之，帝王之道於是會通，故六經萬世之文獻也。其後司馬遷作《史記》於坑焚之餘，有八書以著其法，有紀傳以載其事，盖自附於文獻之續也。班固《漢書》悉準遷例，稍增損焉。然或者亦互有評隲，二書果相異同否耶？固以下，斷代爲史，會通之道始分。至梁吳均作《通史》，盖其事也。宋司馬光復總十六史而作《通鑑》，然於法之因革，又略而不載，何耶？唐杜佑作《通典》，盖其法也。元馬端臨復廣二十四目而作《通考》，然於事之理亂，又缺而不著，何耶？若夫鄭樵所撰《通志》，盖合二者而並錄之，爲紀，爲略，爲年譜，爲世家，爲傳，爲載記，凡二百卷，亦足以言會通否
translation_en:
…to hear. Kindly explain it clearly to me.

Question: In antiquity, the Historiographer of the Right recorded words, thereby preserving the institutions that were retained or changed; the Historiographer of the Left recorded actions, thereby preserving the events that brought order or disorder. As the historiographers’ office gradually fell into disuse, Confucius lamented the insufficiency of documentary and learned testimony. He therefore took the Six Classics and edited and expounded them, bringing together into a coherent whole the Way of the emperors and kings. Thus the Six Classics provide documentary and learned testimony for all ages. Later, Sima Qian composed the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) in the aftermath of the burying of scholars and burning of books. Its eight treatises set forth institutions, and its annals and biographies recorded events: he evidently regarded his work as a continuation of that documentary and learned tradition. Ban Gu’s History of the Han (Hanshu) followed Qian’s conventions throughout, with some additions and omissions. Yet some critics have offered contrasting assessments of the two works. In what respects are they actually alike or different?

From Gu onward, histories were confined to individual dynasties, and the approach of comprehensive synthesis began to fragment. Under the Liang, Wu Jun composed the Comprehensive History (Tongshi), concerned principally with events. Under the Song, Sima Guang then brought together the sixteen histories to compose the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian), yet he treated the retention and alteration of institutions cursorily and left them unrecorded. Why was this? Under the Tang, Du You composed the Comprehensive Institutions (Tongdian), concerned principally with institutions. Under the Yuan, Ma Duanlin further expanded the scope to twenty-four categories and composed the Comprehensive Examination (Tongkao), yet his treatment of events bringing order or disorder was incomplete and left them unexpounded. Why was this?

As for the Comprehensive Treatises (Tongzhi) compiled by Zheng Qiao, it brought the two together and recorded both, comprising annals, monographs, chronological tables, hereditary houses, biographies, and records of rulers, in two hundred juan altogether. Is this, too, sufficient to qualify as comprehensive synthesis…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
耶其視通鑑通考又何如也夫損益倣
乎法勸戒徵乎事此經世之具通儒之
業也治道所關非特藝焉而已願相與
訂之
問知人之道自古爲難三代以後惟漢世
人物猶爲近古試即史氏所紀及世儒
所論不能無疑者相與評之善藏其用
者有儒者氣象也而或訾其術宗黃老
事多陰謀有王佐之才者伊呂之儔也
===
而或病其專事申韓學不純正不知其
何所指歟尾大不掉之說切中其幾矣
顧見疎于明主或曰年少紛亂諸事建
削七國之策卒如所料矣迺賈禍於東
市或曰擅權多所紛更不知其何所見
歟踞厠而見者本騎奴之流顧兩辭招
賢斬將之請持論不根者畜以俳優之
賤迺數犯喜功好大之君二子人品信
如其所云乎有恬于勢利好古樂道者

何所指歟尾大不掉之說切中其幾矣
顧見疎于明主或曰年少紛亂諸事建

歟踞厠而見者本騎奴之流顧兩辭招
賢斬將之請持論不根者畜以俳優之
賤適數犯喜功好大之君二子人品信
如其所云乎有恬于勢利爽古樂道者
punctuated:
耶？其視通鑑、通考又何如也？夫損益倣乎法，勸戒徵乎事，此經世之具、通儒之業也。治道所關，非特藝焉而已，願相與訂之。
問：知人之道，自古爲難。三代以後，惟漢世人物猶爲近古。試即史氏所紀及世儒所論不能無疑者，相與評之。善藏其用者，有儒者氣象也，而或訾其術宗黃老，事多陰謀；有王佐之才者，伊呂之儔也，而或病其專事申韓，學不純正。不知其何所指歟？尾大不掉之說，切中其幾矣，顧見疎于明主，或曰年少紛亂諸事；建削七國之策，卒如所料矣，迺賈禍於東市，或曰擅權多所紛更。不知其何所見歟？踞厠而見者，本騎奴之流，顧兩辭招賢斬將之請；持論不根者，畜以俳優之賤，迺數犯喜功好大之君。二子人品，信如其所云乎？有恬于勢利、好古樂道者
translation_en:
…? And how does it compare with the Comprehensive Mirror and the Comprehensive Examination? Institutions provide models for what should be discarded or added; events furnish evidence for encouragement and admonition. These are the instruments of ordering the world and the work of broadly learned scholars. They concern the way of government, rather than merely literary skill. We hope you will examine these matters together.
Question: Knowing people has been difficult since antiquity. After the Three Dynasties, only the figures of the Han still approached the ancients. Let us assess together those matters in historians’ records and scholars’ judgments that cannot be free from doubt. One who excelled at concealing his abilities had the bearing of a Confucian scholar, yet some criticized his methods as grounded in the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi and his actions as frequently involving secret plots. Another, endowed with the talent to assist a king, was a peer of Yi Yin and Lü Shang, yet some faulted him for devoting himself exclusively to Shen Buhai and Han Fei and for learning that was not pure and orthodox. What, we ask, were these criticisms directed at? The argument about a tail too large to wag struck precisely at the incipient danger, yet its author was estranged from an enlightened ruler; some said that, being young, he threw affairs into confusion. Another proposed reducing the territories of the seven kingdoms, and events ultimately unfolded as he had predicted, yet he brought upon himself execution in the eastern marketplace; some said that he arrogated power and made numerous disruptive changes. What, we ask, was the basis for these judgments? One whom the ruler received while squatting at the privy originally belonged to the ranks of mounted slaves, yet on two occasions he declined requests to recruit worthy men and to execute a general. Another, whose arguments lacked foundation, was kept in the lowly position of an entertainer, yet repeatedly challenged a ruler who delighted in achievements and grand undertakings. Were these two men’s characters truly as described? There was one who was indifferent to power and profit, cherished antiquity, and delighted in the Way…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
或病其劇秦美新有才似子房道似伯
夷者或短其邀名漢代二子心術果如
其所論乎爾諸士居則曰古之人古之
人也亦嘗以身體之而察其心否乎夫
尚論折衷學者之事幸言之毋委曰不
暇
問名與實常相須也然有名者不必有實
有實者不必有名是以賢主察焉孔子
爲政必也正名名固聖人之所重也及
荅子貢之問廼謂無信不立實固有重
於名歟後之論者曰先實後名曰循名
責實或又以練名實爲言其於治體亦
有識乎否也漢唐宋以來綜核剛明勵
精之主率見欺罔雖中興創業守文之
英辟君子不能無責實之論焉其故何
歟今
皇明御極化理弘洽每
詔司必以略虛文崇實政爲訓凡厥有位罔

荅子貢之問乃謂無信不立實固有重
於名歟後之論者曰先實後名曰循名
責實或又以綜名實爲言其於治體亦
有識乎否也漢唐宋以來綜核剛明勵
精之主率見欺罔雖中興創業守文之
英辟君子不能無責實之論焉其故何
歟今
皇明御極化理弘洽每
詔有司必以略虛文崇實效爲訓凡厥有位罔
punctuated:
或病其劇秦美新；有才似子房、道似伯夷者，或短其邀名。漢代二子心術果如其所論乎？爾諸士居則曰：「古之人，古之人也！」亦嘗以身體之而察其心否乎？夫尚論折衷，學者之事，幸言之，毋委曰不暇。

問：名與實常相須也，然有名者不必有實，有實者不必有名，是以賢主察焉。孔子爲政，必也正名，名固聖人之所重也；及荅子貢之問，廼謂無信不立，實固有重於名歟？後之論者曰先實後名，曰循名責實，或又以練名實爲言，其於治體亦有識乎否也？漢唐宋以來，綜核剛明、勵精之主率見欺罔，雖中興、創業、守文之英辟，君子不能無責實之論焉，其故何歟？今皇明御極，化理弘洽，每詔司，必以略虛文、崇實政爲訓。凡厥有位罔
translation_en:
… some fault him for his Criticizing Qin and Praising Xin; of the man whose talent resembled Zifang’s and whose adherence to the Way resembled Boyi’s, some disparage him for courting fame. Were the inner motives of these two men of the Han really as their critics claim? You candidates habitually exclaim, “The men of antiquity! The men of antiquity!” But have you ever sought to embody their conduct yourselves and thereby examine their hearts? Evaluating the ancients and arriving at a balanced judgment are the scholar’s business. Please explain your views; do not evade the task by saying that you have no time.

Question: Name and substance ordinarily depend upon one another. Yet those who possess a name do not necessarily possess the substance, and those who possess the substance do not necessarily possess a name. Thus worthy rulers scrutinize them. Confucius said that, in governing, he would certainly begin by rectifying names: names were assuredly something the sage valued. Yet when answering Zigong’s question, he said that without trust there could be no standing firm. Is substance, then, more important than name? Later commentators spoke of putting substance before name, or of following names and demanding the corresponding substance; some also spoke of examining name and substance. Did they understand the essentials of government or not? Since the Han, Tang, and Song, rulers who scrutinized affairs comprehensively, who were resolute and discerning, and who devoted themselves earnestly to government have commonly been deceived. Even outstanding sovereigns who restored a dynasty, founded one, or maintained its established institutions could not escape the gentleman’s criticism that they should demand substantive results. Why was this? Now our august Ming occupies the imperial throne, and its transforming influence and good government extend widely. Whenever it issues edicts to the authorities, it invariably instructs them to dispense with empty formalities and promote substantive government. Among all those holding office, there are none who …

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不祓除以效精白誠盛會也然試求之
吏皆廉平而無矯飾歟士皆醇謹而無
翾躁歟民皆樸茂而無狡詐歟政皆簡
乂而無煩辟歟俗皆忠厚而無澆薄歟
夫上有願治之
君而下無咸熙之績内有承式之臣而外無允
釐之效必有任其咎者兹欲反之其道
何繇二三子具以實對
alt_text:
不祓除以效精白誠感會也然試求之
吏皆康平而無矯飾歟士皆醇謹而無
翾躁歟民皆樸茂而無狡詐歟政皆簡
乂而無煩辟歟俗皆忠厚而無澆薄歟
夫上有願治之
君而下無咸熙之續內有承式之臣而外無允
釐之效必有任其咎者茲欲反之其道
何繇二三子具以實對
punctuated: 不祓除以效精白，誠盛會也。然試求之：吏皆廉平而無矯飾歟？士皆醇謹而無翾躁歟？民皆樸茂而無狡詐歟？政皆簡乂而無煩辟歟？俗皆忠厚而無澆薄歟？夫上有願治之君，而下無咸熙之績；内有承式之臣，而外無允釐之效，必有任其咎者。兹欲反之，其道何繇？二三子具以實對。
translation_en: …none fails to cleanse himself of faults and demonstrate purity of purpose. Truly, this is a flourishing age. Yet let us examine it: are all officials incorruptible and impartial, without affectation? Are all scholars sincere and circumspect, without frivolity or impetuosity? Are all common people honest and sound in character, without cunning or deceit? Is all administration simple and orderly, without burdensome laws? Are all customs loyal and generous, without shallowness or meanness? When above there is a ruler who desires good government, yet below there are no achievements of universal prosperity; when at court there are ministers who observe the established standards, yet beyond the court there are no results of truly effective governance—there must be those who bear responsibility. If we now wish to reverse this state of affairs, what path should we follow? You candidates should each reply fully, grounding your answers in actual circumstances.

第壹場

四書

季康子問：「仲由可使從政也與？」子曰：「由也果，於從政乎何有？」曰：「賜也可使從政也與？」曰：「賜也達，於從政乎何有？」曰：「求也可使從政也與？」曰：「求也藝，於從政乎何有？」

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Ji Kangzi asked, “Could Zhong You be entrusted with conducting government?” The Master said, “You is decisive. What difficulty would he have in conducting government?” He asked, “Could Ci be entrusted with conducting government?” The Master said, “Ci has understanding. What difficulty would he have in conducting government?” He asked, “Could Qiu be entrusted with conducting government?” The Master said, “Qiu has many abilities. What difficulty would he have in conducting government?”

Zhang Zhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: “This composition captures the sage’s words: direct yet tactful, substantial yet dignified. It may indeed be called a worthy composition.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Instructor: “In treating the three words ‘decisive,’ ‘understanding,’ and ‘abilities,’ writers are generally verbose and vague. Only this essay is clear, pertinent, precise, and apt.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Professor: “Concise and clear, well ordered and fluent, it brings out the meaning of the Master’s reply to Kangzi. The concluding thought is especially nuanced and praiseworthy. It should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion of the Heir Apparent: “Closely pertinent.”

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Secretariat Supervisor: “Clear and fluent.”

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
問曰及門之士如由也者嘗聞其人矣使之爲
大夫而從政也可乎孔子曰政之立也由於果
然而柔者屈之矣由也忠信之質見之決而能
斷剛毅之氣執之固而不撓是其果也施於有
政可以定紛譁焉可以决嫌疑焉殆確然而無
乎不立也夫何難曰如賜也者嘗聞其人矣使
之從政也可乎曰政之行也由於達然而蔽者
塞之矣賜也練習而鬯而人情之周知明悟而
穎而物理之旁燭是其達也施於有政可以測
===
機微焉可以識體要焉殆沛然而無乎不行也
夫何難曰如求也者嘗聞其人矣使之從政也
可乎曰政之修也由於藝而拘於隘陋者有矣
求也思慮精研而多經畫之方智識流通而廣
應酬之略是其藝也以政授之繁劇可得而理
焉纖悉可得而舉焉殆飾然而未有不修者也
又何難哉由是觀之政不患於乏才才每限於
失遇無不用之才斯無不舉之政矣抑三子所
長合而觀之不過聖人之一體魯之君臣有孔

punctuated: 問曰：「及門之士，如由也者，嘗聞其人矣。使之爲大夫而從政也，可乎？」孔子曰：「政之立也，由於果，然而柔者屈之矣。由也，忠信之質，見之決而能斷；剛毅之氣，執之固而不撓。是其果也，施於有政，可以定紛譁焉，可以决嫌疑焉，殆確然而無乎不立也。夫何難？」曰：「如賜也者，嘗聞其人矣。使之從政也，可乎？」曰：「政之行也，由於達，然而蔽者塞之矣。賜也，練習而鬯，而人情之周知；明悟而穎，而物理之旁燭。是其達也，施於有政，可以測機微焉，可以識體要焉，殆沛然而無乎不行也。夫何難？」曰：「如求也者，嘗聞其人矣。使之從政也，可乎？」曰：「政之修也，由於藝，而拘於隘陋者有矣。求也，思慮精研，而多經畫之方；智識流通，而廣應酬之略。是其藝也，以政授之，繁劇可得而理焉，纖悉可得而舉焉，殆飾然而未有不修者也。又何難哉？」由是觀之，政不患於乏才，才每限於失遇。無不用之才，斯無不舉之政矣。抑三子所長，合而觀之，不過聖人之一體。魯之君臣有孔
translation_en:
…he asked: “Among those who have studied under you, I have heard of You. Would he be capable of serving as a grand master and taking part in government?” Kongzi replied: “The establishment of government depends on decisiveness, yet the weak allow it to falter. You’s loyal and trustworthy character manifests itself in his ability to decide and act; his firm and resolute spirit holds fast without yielding. Such is his decisiveness. Applied to government, it could settle turmoil and resolve doubts, establishing affairs so firmly that nothing would remain unsettled. What difficulty would he have?” He asked: “I have heard of Ci. Would he be capable of taking part in government?” Kongzi replied: “The conduct of government depends on understanding, yet those of obscured judgment obstruct it. Ci is practiced and proficient, comprehensively acquainted with human feelings; perceptive and acute, he broadly illuminates the principles of things. Such is his understanding. Applied to government, it could discern the subtlest workings of affairs and recognize their essentials, allowing everything to proceed freely and abundantly. What difficulty would he have?” He asked: “I have heard of Qiu. Would he be capable of taking part in government?” Kongzi replied: “The ordering of government depends on accomplishments, yet some are constrained by narrowness and ignorance. Qiu’s deliberations are precise and searching, and he possesses many methods of planning; his knowledge and judgment are versatile, and he has a wide range of strategies for responding to affairs. Such are his accomplishments. Entrust government to him, and even its most complex and demanding affairs could be managed, while its smallest details could be attended to. Everything would be brought into proper order, with nothing left uncultivated. What difficulty, then, would he have?”

If no talent were left unused, no governmental undertaking would remain unaccomplished. text:
子而不能用顧拳拳於由與求之問無亦仲尼
豈賢於子之見乎將所用者止於具臣而所謂
以道事君者非其所得用乎此魯之所以爲魯
也或又以康子此問意尤在求夫以求之才文
以禮樂幾於成人一附益之卒爲聚斂之臣蓋
又具臣之不若也噫人之用才與才之自用可
鑒也夫
故大德必得其位必得其祿必得其名必
得其壽

作辭理兼到出人意表是用心於理學者
考試官左中允李批詞意俱足

translation_en:
…Confucius, yet they could not employ him; instead, they persisted in asking about You and Qiu. Was this perhaps the outlook expressed in the words, “How could Zhongni be worthier than you?” Or could they employ only ministers who merely filled their posts, while those who served their ruler according to the Way were beyond their capacity to employ? This is what made Lu the state it was. Some further hold that Kangzi’s question was directed particularly at Qiu. With Qiu’s talents, refined through ritual and music, he would have approached the fully accomplished person. Yet once he helped increase his master’s wealth, he ultimately became a minister devoted to extracting revenue, inferior even to one who merely filled his post. Alas! Here is a warning both about how people employ talent and how talented people employ themselves!

“Therefore, one of great virtue is certain to attain his proper position, his proper emolument, his proper renown, and his proper longevity.”

This composition alone develops the underlying principle. It is closely pertinent and leaves much to ponder; it deserves selection and inclusion in the record.”

Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor, comments: “The meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean is exceptionally difficult to expound with precision and refinement. This composition succeeds in both expression and reasoning, surpassing expectations. Its author is someone who has devoted himself to the Learning of Principle.”

Examiner Li, Left Secretariat Aide, comments: “Both expression and meaning are fully adequate.”

Examiner Tong, Left Secretariat Supervisor, comments: “Pure and sound.”

The Doctrine of the Mean reasons from the person whose virtue has reached perfection and affirms the completeness of his blessings. For blessings are the manifestation of virtue. How much more, then, for one whose virtue has reached perfection: could the blessings he receives be anything less than complete?

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
子思引孔子言舜之事以明費隱及此蓋謂舜
以聖人之德而垂光裕之休皆理之常也理之
所以可必者亦德而已矣是故性由仁義之常
而至純至粹足以建極於當時道備人倫之至
而盡善盡美足以垂範於後世是其德也大矣
德之大者眷之隆也吾知雖不與位期而位至
焉天與之也主神器于九五人歸之也膺大寶
于離明殆有推之而不能去者矣雖不與祿期
而祿至焉任土而貢畢受方物之供則壤而賦
===
安享玉食之奉殆有辭之而不能免者矣名係
於人者也聖人何求焉而聲華所被洋溢于中
國也昭格于上下也曰聖曰神理所必致者耳
壽定於天者也聖人何與焉而天和所萃眉壽
其綏也享國其永也或耄或期理所必有者耳
由是觀之動天者德也舜非求于天也眷德者
天也天非私于舜也其所以克受天命而備享
天福者夫豈偶然之故哉雖然豈惟舜哉自堯
而下禹湯文武福德相符者皆常理也至於仲

translation_en:
Zisi quotes Confucius’s account of Shun to illuminate the Way’s pervasive workings and hidden subtlety, and his discussion reaches this point. His meaning is that Shun, possessing the virtue of a sage, bequeathed the blessings of glorious and abundant beneficence: all this accords with the constant operation of principle. What makes the effects of principle certain is simply virtue. Thus, his nature followed the constant norms of benevolence and righteousness and was utterly pure and refined, sufficient to establish the highest standard for his own age. His Way embodied the utmost perfection of human relationships and was wholly good and beautiful, sufficient to leave a model for later generations. Great indeed was his virtue! The greater the virtue, the more abundant Heaven’s favor.

I know that although he did not look for high position, high position came to him. Heaven bestowed it upon him, and he presided over the sacred vessel of sovereignty in the ruler’s place, symbolized by the nine in the fifth position. The people gave him their allegiance, and he assumed the supreme throne in sovereign radiance, symbolized by the trigram Li. Indeed, even had he sought to push it away, he could not have rid himself of it! Although he did not look for emoluments, emoluments came to him. Tribute was levied according to the land’s productive capacity, and he received offerings of local products in full; taxes were assessed according to the soil, and he peacefully enjoyed provisions of exquisite food. Indeed, even had he declined them, he could not have escaped receiving them!

Reputation depends upon others: what did the sage seek from it? Yet the splendor of his fame spread throughout the central lands and reached brightly above and below. That he should be called a sage and called divine was simply what principle necessarily brought about. Longevity is determined by Heaven: what part could the sage take in it? Yet Heaven’s harmonious vital forces gathered in him, securing him venerable longevity and a lasting reign. Whether he lived to eighty or ninety, or to a hundred, this was simply what principle necessarily entailed.

Viewed in this light, it is virtue that moves Heaven; Shun did not solicit Heaven. It is Heaven that cherishes virtue; Heaven showed no partiality toward Shun. Could his ability to receive Heaven’s mandate and enjoy Heaven’s blessings in full possibly have been accidental? Yet why speak only of Shun? From Yao onward, in the cases of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, the correspondence between blessings and virtue always exemplified this constant principle. As for Zhongni [Confucius]…

translation_en:
…Zhongni did not possess All-under-Heaven; some therefore consider Heaven’s disposition not yet settled. Yet the sage’s mind dares not rest complacently in what is constant and neglect what may change. Consider Shun’s vigilance and diligence: he took no pleasure in his position and transmitted it to a worthy man, not daring to favor his own son. Zhongni revered Heaven’s mandate and grieved over human distress; throughout his life he was anxiously engaged, yet harbored neither resentment nor blame. Both knew well how to serve Heaven. Master Shao said, “Zhongni took the myriad generations as his domain.” Master Zhou said, “His teaching and transforming influence are inexhaustible.” In this he and Shun followed the same standard. Can one say that Heaven’s disposition was not yet settled?
“When a sage governs All-under-Heaven, he ensures that beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire. With beans and grain as plentiful as water and fire, how could any among the people fail to be benevolent?”

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
富民者以其足以成化也聖人之治天下重農
而薄斂既有以開其端謹制而節用又有以導
其末使天下之民其耕而穫也莫不有菽之可
啜焉有粟之可食焉其穫而多也莫不如水之
不竭焉如火之不熄焉俯仰之給取諸其倉者
無異取諸其井焉者也朝夕之供取諸其廋者
無異取諸其竈焉者也夫天下之民性之皆善
不啻如水火之足也心之欲仁不啻如菽粟之
切也然而無所興者無所賴焉爾今也菽粟如
===
水火吾知衣食之計裕則秉彛之念生而其從
善也輕凍餒之患無則貪戾之非泯而其歸德
也厚強不至於陵焉衆不至於暴焉廉耻勵而
風俗於是乎興矣禮可得而脩焉義可得而正
焉行誼篤而治化於是乎舉矣若夫放僻邪侈
而患不仁者焉有是理乎由此觀之仁民者教
也富民者養也非養無以施教非恭儉又何足
以爲養哉考之戰國之時封殖者衆田賦之制
壞已久矣故孟子於齊梁之君每以農桑爲言

punctuated: 富民者，以其足以成化也。聖人之治天下，重農而薄斂，既有以開其端；謹制而節用，又有以導其末。使天下之民，其耕而穫也，莫不有菽之可啜焉，有粟之可食焉；其穫而多也，莫不如水之不竭焉，如火之不熄焉。俯仰之給，取諸其倉者，無異取諸其井焉者也；朝夕之供，取諸其廋者，無異取諸其竈焉者也。夫天下之民，性之皆善，不啻如水火之足也；心之欲仁，不啻如菽粟之切也。然而無所興者，無所賴焉爾。今也菽粟如水火，吾知衣食之計裕，則秉彛之念生，而其從善也輕；凍餒之患無，則貪戾之非泯，而其歸德也厚。強不至於陵焉，衆不至於暴焉，廉耻勵而風俗於是乎興矣；禮可得而脩焉，義可得而正焉，行誼篤而治化於是乎舉矣。若夫放僻邪侈而患不仁者，焉有是理乎？由此觀之，仁民者，教也；富民者，養也。非養無以施教，非恭儉又何足以爲養哉？考之戰國之時，封殖者衆，田賦之制壞已久矣。故孟子於齊梁之君，每以農桑爲言
translation_en:
…enriching the people, because this is sufficient to bring about their moral transformation. In governing the world, the sage honors agriculture and levies light taxes, thereby providing a sound beginning; he carefully regulates institutions and restrains expenditure, thereby guiding matters through to their completion. Thus, when the people cultivate and reap, all have beans to consume and grain to eat; when their harvests are abundant, their supplies are as inexhaustible as water and as unceasing as fire. For the necessities of supporting parents above and children below, drawing from their granaries is no different from drawing from their wells; for their morning and evening provisions, drawing from their stores [?] is no different from drawing from their hearths.

The goodness inherent in all the people’s natures is no less ample than these supplies of water and fire; their hearts’ desire for benevolence is no less pressing than their need for beans and grain. Yet if they fail to rise to goodness, it is simply because they lack the means of support. Now, with beans and grain as plentiful as water and fire, I know that when provision for clothing and food is ample, awareness of their innate moral constants arises, and they readily follow goodness. When the danger of cold and hunger disappears, the wrongs of greed and viciousness vanish, and their allegiance to virtue deepens. The strong do not go so far as to oppress others, nor do the many resort to violence. Integrity and a sense of shame are encouraged, and social customs thereby flourish. Ritual propriety can be cultivated and righteousness set aright; moral conduct becomes steadfast, and orderly government and moral transformation are thereby achieved. As for people indulging in depravity, perversity, wickedness, and extravagance, and suffering from a lack of benevolence—how could such a thing occur?

Viewed in this light, making the people benevolent is a matter of teaching; enriching the people is a matter of nourishing them. Without nourishing them, there is no means of imparting instruction; and without reverence and frugality, how could one adequately nourish them? Looking back to the Warring States period, many sought to build up their own wealth and power, and the system of land taxation had long been in disarray. Thus, when addressing the rulers of Qi and Liang, Mengzi invariably spoke of farming and sericulture…

為生矣夫先王之政不可見也然則使民之自
為生也不可乎
易

…As for the regulations governing field boundaries, even to a state as small as Teng he invariably explained them. 者奮至德之光者也故其和順之懿自著乎音

故取諸其奮，則契聲氣之元，而笙鏞也、管籥也、綴兆也，於是乎作焉；取諸其豫，則昭天地之和，而清濁也、高下也、俯仰也，於是乎作焉。然樂也者，奮至德之光者也，故其和順之懿，自著乎音律之精，盖盡美也，而又盡善矣；勳華之盛，式昭乎器數之備，盖有文也，而又有本矣。先王之作樂如此，而豈徒哉？彼祀天於郊而配以祖，所以報本也，則殷薦於泰壇之上，以致尊尊之仁焉；祭帝於屋而配以考，所以報生成也，則合作於明堂之中，以致親親之孝焉。九德之歌，九功之間，情文具備，天神其可得而禮乎？九韶之舞，九奏之協，聲容兼盡，人鬼其可得而享乎？由是觀之，崇德則盡樂之體，而管乎人情矣；殷薦則盡樂之用，而通乎天下矣。聖人體豫之意至矣哉！

… Thus, by drawing upon its stirring force, they accorded with the primal source of sound and vital energy: mouth organs and great bells, pipes and flutes, and the marked positions of the dancers were accordingly established. By drawing upon its joyful ease, they manifested the harmony of Heaven and Earth: clear and deep tones, high and low pitches, and movements of bowing and rising were accordingly brought forth. Music, however, gives stirring expression to the radiance of consummate virtue. Thus the excellence of its harmony and concord naturally appears in the refinement of its tones and tuning: it is entirely beautiful and also entirely good. The magnificence of Yao and Shun shines forth in the completeness of the instruments and their prescribed arrangements: it possesses both outward refinement and an underlying foundation. Such was the music made by the former kings. Could it have been without purpose?

When they sacrificed to Heaven in the suburban rite and associated their founding ancestor with it, they were repaying their origins. They therefore made a grand musical offering upon the great altar, fully expressing the benevolence of honoring those worthy of honor. When they sacrificed to the Lord on High within a building and associated their deceased father with him, they were repaying the gift of life and nurture. They therefore performed the music together within the Hall of Enlightenment, fully expressing the filial devotion of loving one’s kin. With songs of the nine virtues and alternating songs of the nine achievements, both feeling and ceremonial form were fully present: could the celestial spirits then be duly honored? With the dances of the Nine Shao and the harmony of nine musical performances, both sound and bodily movement were fully realized: could the ancestral spirits then be presented with offerings? Viewed in this light, exalting virtue fully realizes the substance of music and brings human feelings under its direction; making grand musical offerings fully realizes the function of music and extends its influence throughout the world. How consummate was the sages’ intent in embodying the joyful ease of Yu!

Nevertheless, in the former kings’ governance of the realm, a foundation gave rise to order, and order gave rise to harmony. Thus their profound stillness in laying the foundation of the mandate constituted music without sound. Ritual comes first and music afterward: Confucian scholars have repeatedly discussed this. If heavenly virtue is not pure and the people’s dispositions are not settled, yet one seeks to create music to display the age’s flourishing condition, one will inevitably indulge desires and encourage extravagance, leaving the former kings’ intent neglected. In responding to stimuli, the gentleman likewise does no more than run principle through it all. What need, then, is there for deliberation? text:
乎往來則有塗理之所由以行者也盖吾以一
身立乎酬酢之中因其所感而應之則事物不
同形變化不同迹當然之則有不容於約其趨
者矣趨之異此塗之所以分而殊也何也體無
定用不能强而同之而亦未嘗不同也自夫有
所究而極者之謂致所以極者理而已理也者
心之全德也萬事萬物之裁於是乎極焉是其
致也一矣然其一者心之體不能不措者事之
應故以言乎其思則有慮理之所由以揆者也
===
盖吾以一身當乎酬酢之變因其所感而應之
則事物異其制變化異其宜研窮之道有不容
於齊其用者矣用之異此慮之所以分而百也
何也用無定體不能强而一之而亦未嘗不一
也學者知同而一則一之道得矣知殊而百則
貫之道得矣然則天下亦何思而何慮而又何
以憧憧爲哉雖然君子非眞無思也內外兩忘
則無矣無思者致一者也盖有心之思慮不可
有無心之思慮不可無夫子之語爲有心也故

translation_en: …of coming and going, there are paths: these are the routes by which principle operates. When I stand amid the exchanges of life and respond to whatever affects me, affairs and things differ in form, and transformations differ in their manifestations. The standards of what ought to be done cannot be confined to a single direction. This difference in direction is why the paths divide and diverge. Why is this so? Substance has no fixed function: its functions cannot be forced into sameness, yet they have never lacked an underlying sameness. As for what is pursued to its ultimate point, this is called the end attained; what brings it to that ultimate point is simply principle. Principle is the complete virtue of the mind. The judgments governing all affairs and things reach their ultimate standard here; thus their end is one. Yet what is one is the substance of the mind, while what must be put into practice is its response to affairs. Thus, when speaking of its thinking, there are deliberations: these are the means by which principle makes its assessments. When I confront the changes arising amid life's exchanges and respond to whatever affects me, affairs and things differ in their arrangements, and transformations differ in what is appropriate to them. The ways of investigating them fully cannot be made uniform in their application. This difference in application is why deliberations branch out and become a hundredfold. Why is this so? Function has no fixed substance: its manifestations cannot be forced into unity, yet they have never lacked an underlying unity. When learners understand sameness and unity, they grasp the way of the one; when they understand diversity and multiplicity, they grasp the way that threads through them all. What thinking and deliberation, then, does the world require? And what need is there for restless, anxious thought? Nevertheless, the gentleman is not truly without thought. When both the inner and the outer are forgotten, such thought disappears. To be without thought is to attain unity. Deliberation driven by deliberate intent must not be present; deliberation free of deliberate intent must not be absent. The Master's words address deliberate intent; therefore…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
十二人之後立此考績黜陟之法蓋以亮天功
者百官也賢否進退之機夷夏觀瞻所係可不
愼與是故時至三載績用多矣不有以屢省之
則失之玩也可乎于是有考績之法因其敷奏
之言而明試之也即其職分之常而綜核之也
則公道明而人樂于趨事矣人至三考賢否定
矣不有以振厲之則失之濫也可乎于是有黜
陟之法進之而不貳必賢者也退之而不疑必
不肖者也則法度立而人知所畏慕矣夫上有
===
定法則下有定守所操者約而所制者不其廣
耶將見或內或外庶績難乎其熙也今也名實
核而上下信庶明有勵翼之風用舍公而遠近
服庶績著其凝之美禮樂其修明也政教其弘
敷也寧復有倖位而廢事者乎乍臣乍叛三苗
難乎其治也今也紀綱振而朝廷尊既孚其來
格之心內順治而外威嚴自神其區別之化善
者擇而留焉惡者竄而去焉寧復有昏迷而弗
即工者乎由是觀之有功不賞有罪不罰雖堯

punctuated: 十二人之後，立此考績黜陟之法。蓋以亮天功者，百官也；賢否進退之機，夷夏觀瞻所係，可不愼與？是故時至三載，績用多矣，不有以屢省之，則失之玩也，可乎？于是有考績之法，因其敷奏之言而明試之也，即其職分之常而綜核之也，則公道明而人樂于趨事矣。人至三考，賢否定矣，不有以振厲之，則失之濫也，可乎？于是有黜陟之法，進之而不貳，必賢者也；退之而不疑，必不肖者也。則法度立而人知所畏慕矣。夫上有定法，則下有定守，所操者約，而所制者不其廣耶？將見或內或外，庶績難乎其熙也。今也名實核而上下信，庶明有勵翼之風；用舍公而遠近服，庶績著其凝之美。禮樂其修明也，政教其弘敷也，寧復有倖位而廢事者乎？乍臣乍叛，三苗難乎其治也。今也紀綱振而朝廷尊，既孚其來格之心；內順治而外威嚴，自神其區別之化。善者擇而留焉，惡者竄而去焉，寧復有昏迷而弗即工者乎？由是觀之，有功不賞，有罪不罰，雖堯
translation_en:
…after appointing the twelve men, he established this system of evaluating achievements and dismissing or promoting officials. For it is the hundred officials who assist in accomplishing Heaven’s work. Decisions about advancing or dismissing the worthy and unworthy command the attention of both the non-Chinese peoples and the Chinese: could one fail to exercise care? Thus, when three years have elapsed, achievements and services have accumulated. Without repeated scrutiny, matters would lapse into neglect. Could this be acceptable? Hence the system of evaluating achievements: officials are clearly tested against the statements in their reports, and comprehensively assessed against the regular duties of their offices. Impartial standards are thereby made clear, and people gladly attend to their work. Once an official has undergone three evaluations, his worthiness or unworthiness is established. Without measures to spur officials on, indiscriminate retention would result. Could this be acceptable? Hence the system of dismissal and promotion: those advanced without hesitation must be worthy; those dismissed without doubt must be unworthy. Laws and standards are thereby established, and people know what to fear and what to aspire to. When those above have settled rules, those below have settled obligations. Though the principles wielded are simple, is not their reach extensive?
Whether within or beyond the central administration, it might seem difficult to make all undertakings flourish. Now, however, stated performance is checked against actual achievement, and superiors and subordinates trust one another; the many discerning officials display a spirit of diligent assistance. Employment and dismissal are impartial, and those far and near submit; all undertakings display the excellence of firmly established accomplishment. Ritual and music are cultivated and clarified; government and moral instruction are widely extended. Could there still be anyone who obtains office through undeserved favor and neglects his duties? Alternately submitting and rebelling, the Sanmiao were difficult to govern. Now, however, discipline is strengthened and the court commands respect, securing their sincere intention to come and submit. Order prevails within, while authority inspires awe beyond; the transforming influence that distinguishes among them works with marvelous efficacy. The good are selected and retained; the wicked are banished and removed. Could there still be anyone who remains benighted and refuses to attend to his duties? Viewed in this light, if merit goes unrewarded and wrongdoing unpunished, even Yao…

translation_en:
…would certainly be unable to govern All Under Heaven; how much less could those who fall short of Tang and Yu dispense with law? Nevertheless, Tang and Yu did not rely exclusively on law. Observe how Gao Yao, presenting his counsels to Yu, said: “It lies in knowing men and bringing peace to the people.” Yu accordingly held: “If one can be discerning and benevolent, why need one banish the Miao?” Thus we know that the ancient sage kings governed their officials and controlled the peoples beyond their borders through virtue rather than intimidation: once internal affairs were well ordered, external threats were naturally repelled. Later generations failed to strive to bring peace to the people, instead exhausting their armies in distant lands; they failed to strive to know men, instead restraining their subordinates through punishments and the scrutiny of titles and performance. This went beyond clarity into excessive scrutiny, attending closely to external affairs while neglecting internal ones. How could such rule be discussed alongside that of Tang and Yu?

“When an enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, the peoples of the four quarters all come as guests. Without distinction between far and near, all present the products of their regions: clothing, food, utensils, and useful articles. The king then distributes these to states whose rulers bear other surnames, manifesting his virtue so that they do not abandon their service. He distributes precious jade to the states of his paternal uncles, thereby expressing familial affection. People do not treat the objects lightly; they cherish in them the virtue they embody.”

Zhou Rudou

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: “Concise wording that fully conveys the meaning: this composition achieves it. Its author may indeed be said to know how to write.”

text:
考試官左中允李批〔詳整〕
考試官左庶子童批〔明贍〕
古之聖王有謹德以來其遠者有布德以懷其
近者夫來遠人懷諸侯非德不可也有天下者
可不知所慎乎昔召公因西土貢獒作書以訓
武王首及于此蓋謂人主好尚出於一念者甚
微而關於天下者甚大是故古先哲王念慮皆
理也得諸天者不誘於物欲之私舉動皆天也
感於外者惟制以禮義之正初非遠有所慕也
===
然德盛而光則化溥而遠將見東夷西戎焉南
蠻北狄焉地雖異域而類則人也仰中國之有
聖咸重譯而來賔出土壤之所宜合遠近而畢
至列廷實以輸誠者惟服食而已器用而已敢
有以異物而瀆者乎夫殊方而至者物也而所
以致之者德也明王乃昭德所致示方物于異
姓之邦用堅事上之心頒寶玉于同宗之國益
篤尊親之典蓋不私其所有也然德以物而將
則物以德而貴將見疎而諸侯焉親而伯叔焉

考試官左庶子童批〔明贍〕。
古之聖王，有謹德以來其遠者，有布德以懷其近者。夫來遠人，懷諸侯，非德不可也。有天下者，可不知所慎乎？昔召公因西土貢獒，作書以訓武王，首及于此。蓋謂人主好尚，出於一念者甚微，而關於天下者甚大。是故古先哲王，念慮皆理也，得諸天者不誘於物欲之私；舉動皆天也，感於外者惟制以禮義之正。初非遠有所慕也，然德盛而光，則化溥而遠。將見東夷西戎焉，南蠻北狄焉，地雖異域，而類則人也。仰中國之有聖，咸重譯而來賔。出土壤之所宜，合遠近而畢至，列廷實以輸誠者，惟服食而已，器用而已，敢有以異物而瀆者乎？夫殊方而至者，物也；而所以致之者，德也。明王乃昭德所致，示方物于異姓之邦，用堅事上之心；頒寶玉于同宗之國，益篤尊親之典。蓋不私其所有也。然德以物而將，則物以德而貴。將見疎而諸侯焉，親而伯叔焉，
translation_en:
Examiner Li, Left Rectifier of the Heir Apparent, comments: 〔Thorough and orderly.〕
Examiner Tong, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: 〔Clear and ample.〕
Among the sage kings of antiquity, there were those who attended carefully to virtue to draw distant peoples to them, and those who spread virtue to cherish those nearby. To attract distant peoples and cherish the regional lords requires virtue. Can one who possesses All-under-Heaven fail to know what he must attend to carefully? Formerly, when the western lands presented a mastiff as tribute, the Duke of Shao composed a document to admonish King Wu, addressing this matter at its outset. His meaning was that a ruler’s tastes and preferences, arising from a single thought, are exceedingly slight in their beginnings, yet exceedingly great in their consequences for All-under-Heaven. Thus, for the wise kings of antiquity, every thought accorded with principle: what they received from Heaven was not seduced by selfish material desires. Their every action accorded with Heaven: in responding to external things, they governed themselves solely by the rectitude of ritual propriety and righteousness. It was never their original purpose to seek anything in distant lands. Yet when virtue flourishes and shines forth, its transforming influence spreads broadly and reaches far. Then one will see the Yi of the east, the Rong of the west, the Man of the south, and the Di of the north—though their lands lie in different regions, they are all human beings. Looking up to the sage in the Central Kingdom, they all come to pay homage through successive interpreters. Bringing the fitting products of their soil, those from far and near arrive together. What they set out as offerings in the court to convey their sincerity consists only of clothing and food, utensils and implements. Would any dare profane the court with exotic curiosities? What arrives from distant regions is material goods; what brings them there is virtue. The enlightened king therefore makes manifest what virtue has brought about: he displays regional products to states ruled by other surnames, thereby strengthening their resolve to serve their superior; he distributes precious jade to states of his own lineage, further deepening the observances that honor kin. He does not keep what he possesses for himself. Yet when virtue is conveyed through objects, those objects become precious through virtue. Then one will see, among the more distant relations, the regional lords, and among close kin, the elder and younger paternal uncles…

帝德之臨荷寵渥而自慶儼然近天子之光相

人雖殊分，而情則同也。拜殊恩而起敬，隱然若帝德之臨；荷寵渥而自慶，儼然近天子之光相。珍藏而世守者，非榮其賜也，觀其德也，豈有以常物而視者乎？吁！明王慎德，而其效如此。今旅獒之貢，則與方物異，而不可頒於遠近諸侯也明矣。為武王者，可不知所戒哉？大抵物產出於四夷者，非常貢也。當克商之初，而旅貢適來，雖武王威德所加，有以致之，安知非窺伺計邪？故召公反覆惓惓於德之一語，蓋德則來，不德則去。不獨夷狄然也，而諸侯亦視之為輕重。故後世寶照乘之珠、連城之璧，適足以啟諸侯侵陵之患，而狼鹿之獲者，反以納犬戎之侮。噫！然後知召公之訓非闊論也。

translation_en:
…Though their stations differ, their feelings are the same. Receiving extraordinary favor, they are moved to reverence, as though the emperor’s virtue were invisibly present before them; bearing his generous bounty, they rejoice, as though standing close to the Son of Heaven’s radiant countenance. They treasure these gifts and preserve them through the generations, not to glory in the bestowal, but to behold his virtue. How could they regard them as ordinary objects? Ah! Such are the effects when an enlightened king attends carefully to virtue. Now the mastiff presented as tribute by Lü differs from the products offered by the various regions: clearly it cannot be distributed among the feudal lords near and far. Could King Wu fail to understand the warning he should take from this?

Generally, products from the barbarians of the four quarters are not regular tribute. Just after the conquest of Shang, tribute from Lü happened to arrive. Although King Wu’s far-reaching might and virtue had brought it about, how could one know that it was not a scheme to spy out an opportunity? Thus the Duke of Shao repeatedly and earnestly dwelt upon the single word “virtue.” With virtue, they come; without virtue, they depart. This is true not only of the barbarians: the feudal lords, too, assess a ruler’s standing accordingly. Hence, in later ages, treasuring pearls bright enough to illuminate carriages and jade discs worth a chain of cities served only to invite encroachment by the feudal lords; and obtaining wolves and deer [?] instead brought humiliation at the hands of the Quanrong. Alas! Only then does one understand that the Duke of Shao’s admonition was no impractical discourse.

Book of Odes

…very broad in scope. You have expounded it thoroughly and fully, yet your language is never stiff or labored. Reading it leaves one refreshed.
Associate Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: Duke Wu’s purpose in admonishing himself lies in comprehensive deliberation and well-ordered preparation. Ranging beyond the immediate topic, this composition develops that purpose unhurriedly, through turns and repeated consideration, exhausting its meaning. Here indeed is someone with whom one can discuss the Book of Odes.
Associate Examiner Huang, Professor, comments: On topics from the Greater Odes, writers are often constrained by such terms as inner and outer, distant and near, great and small, and constant and changing; the results seem exceedingly convoluted. Only this essay is balanced, straightforward, and elegant.
Examiner Li, Left Companion, comments: The writing leaves a lingering savor.
Examiner Tong, Left Mentor, comments: Meticulous and closely reasoned.
The worthy lord’s self-admonition consists in the comprehensiveness of his deliberation and the orderliness of his preparations. In the way of rulership, vigilance is precious. The lord of Wei’s deliberation and preparations left no detail unaddressed. Could he have achieved this without being worthy? Duke Wu composed the ode “Admonition” (Yi) to admonish himself. Its meaning is that indulgence in excessive pleasure might bring the calamity of shared ruin. How, then, should he govern himself? His virtue must be cultivated, yet many have failed through neglect. Thus, in his daily activity and repose, he must rise early and retire late, with no lapse morning or evening; in the courtyards and approaches, he must sprinkle and sweep, overlooking nothing even in his immediate surroundings. Then cultivation within the palace’s innermost precincts will be complete, and its extension to the great court can be inferred. Why is this? Ruler and people move and respond to one another. In every movement, the ruler provides a manifest example; in his place of honor, he provides a model of conduct. If the actions of the one above should at times go astray, then…

載觀，憂勤惕勵，治之本也。自古人君由乎此，則雖多難必興焉；忽乎此，則雖無虞必替焉。是以聖帝明王率先乎敬，所以事其心而成治化也。武公抑畏而至於此，其知敬乎？其知心之學乎？其知治之道乎？觀其愧屋漏、畏鬼神，則雖帝王之功，何加焉？此所以為睿聖也。嗟夫！武公固國君
translation_en:
…those who observe him will have no means of being transformed. Thus, in extending cultivation from oneself to one’s household, how could one permit neglect and fail to give it attention? Government must be established, yet many fail through laxity. Thus one must put chariots and horses in order, ensuring that they are both well prepared and well matched; one must inspect bows, arrows, and weapons of war, ensuring that they are both sturdy and uniform. Then preparations for military affairs will be complete, and one can understand how this extends to civil government. Why is this? Security and danger depend upon one another, each latent within the other. The strength of the uncivilized regions bears upon the critical circumstances of warfare; the weighty concerns of the frontiers bear upon the strength of the state. If our government has no means of restraining them, their unchecked aggression will find an opportunity to exploit. [Two illegible characters: ?] From the household to the state, how could one again permit laxity and fail to make provision? To attend closely to [illegible text: ?] without neglecting what lies outside, to plan for great matters without neglecting small ones, to make one’s deliberations comprehensive in [five illegible characters: ?], and to maintain order in both ordinary and changing circumstances: then all that the ruler’s Way requires will be fully accomplished, and even Heaven’s disfavor may be reversed. What could surpass this as an instance of the saying, ‘Grand counsels establish the mandate; far-reaching plans are announced in due season’?

Considering further, anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline are the foundation of government. Since antiquity, rulers who have followed this course have invariably flourished, even amid many difficulties; those who have neglected it have invariably declined, even when free from troubles. Thus sage emperors and enlightened kings have taken the lead in reverent attentiveness: through it they tend their minds and accomplish transformative government. Duke Wu carried restraint and apprehension to this degree. Did he not understand reverent attentiveness? Did he not understand the learning of the mind? Did he not understand the Way of governing? Consider his sense of shame even in the secluded corner of his chamber, and his awe before ghosts and spirits: how could even the achievements of emperors and kings surpass these? This is why he is deemed sagacious and sage. Ah! Duke Wu was indeed the ruler of a state…

Surely its author has studied this Classic deeply and gained insight into it!

The zither in the Pure Temple, with its red silk strings and widely spaced sound holes, has one voice leading and three responding in song. This composition approaches that quality.

…honoring one’s parents is the utmost expression of filial piety; posthumously conferring royal status upon them is the utmost expression of honoring them. Moreover, King Wen and Tai Si laid the foundations for the eight-hundred-year dynastic fortune of the Ji house of Zhou, so it was fitting that they should enjoy these offerings. Yet seeking peace was King Wen’s intention, and serving his sovereign was King Wen’s virtue. King Wu succeeded him: his harmonizing and punitive campaigns, his achievements in establishing enlightened order, and his governance through generous rewards all took King Wen as their model. Thus Confucius regarded him as universally filial, saying: “He excelled at carrying forward others’ intentions and continuing their undertakings.” Once this is understood, the virtue of the former kings cannot be confined to their receiving sacrificial recompense; nor can the filial piety of the sage consist merely in conferring exalted titles upon his ancestors!

Spring and Autumn Annals

They failed to understand that the Sage was not reproaching Duke Huan for lowering his dignity to serve Lu. He was simply saying that this was not the best strategy for resisting the barbarians and was inherently no cause for boasting. This essay grasps the meaning truly and precisely; its writing is concise and rigorous. It can serve as a model for those seeking mastery of the Classics.”

punctuated: 之役，齊以燕故，軍獲而旋，遺俘於魯。《春秋》書「來獻」以抑之。然則《六月》之奏公、《泮水》之獻囚，皆非歟？嗚呼！不矜之訓，吾徵諸禹之謨焉；遏劉之功，吾徵諸武之頌焉。先王之於夷也，負固而不服，則樹德以綏之；序成而不至，則命將以征之。及其班師振旅，必告之天子，以警於夷，是以有獻捷之禮。桓之於戎也，果能招徠遠人，以彰文德之修乎？果能對揚王庭，以效敵愾之誠乎？皆未之聞也。而乃以越境闢地之俘，躬遺於過都歷國之日，豈以是尊魯哉？蓋恣其戎心，而誇荒漠遼逖之功；逞其霸圖，而肆汰侈虛喝之計爾。聖人以為近政優于遠略，文德神于武功。是舉也，既失懷柔之策，實急功利之心。矜能恃勝，自爽夫道義之閑；而競力尚謀，適以滋夫厲之階也巳。故抑之而書「來獻」，所以示禦夷之道也，所以杜啓釁徼功者之萌也。抑是時也，純門入，楚成橫，而何急乎戎？噫！此桓之隱也。楚患未巳，則諸侯弗寧。伐戎之餘威，其懾服之基歟？蓋不待召

…in that campaign, Qi took the field on Yan’s behalf, returned with captives, and presented them to Lu. The Spring and Autumn Annals records “came to present” in order to check this presumption. Were, then, the reporting of achievements [?] in “The Sixth Month” and the presentation of prisoners in “The Waters of the Pan” both wrong? Alas! For the admonition against boasting, I find testimony in the Counsels of Yu; for the achievement of stopping slaughter, I find testimony in the hymn “Martial Might.” When dealing with the non-Chinese peoples, if they relied on their strongholds and refused submission, the former kings cultivated virtue to pacify them. If, once order had been established, they failed to come to court, the kings commanded generals to campaign against them. When the armies returned and their ranks were put in order, they invariably reported to the Son of Heaven, to serve as a warning to those peoples. Hence the rite of presenting the fruits of victory.

In his dealings with the Rong, did Duke Huan truly attract people from afar, thereby demonstrating his cultivation of civil virtue? Did he truly acknowledge and extol the king’s commands at the royal court, thereby showing his sincerity in opposing those who provoked the king’s anger? Nothing of either kind has been heard. Instead, while passing through capitals and traversing states, he personally presented captives taken in crossing borders and opening up territory. Could this have been intended to honor Lu? He was merely indulging his warlike disposition and boasting of achievements in remote wildernesses, pursuing his designs for hegemony and giving free rein to extravagant, empty intimidation.

The Sage considered good government close at hand superior to far-reaching military strategy, and civil virtue more wondrous in its efficacy than martial achievement. This undertaking failed as a policy of conciliation and indeed revealed a heart impatient for achievement and advantage. Boasting of his abilities and relying on victory, he himself transgressed the bounds of moral principle; by competing in force and esteeming stratagems, he merely multiplied the steps leading to calamity. Thus the Sage checked his presumption by writing “came to present”: this showed the proper way to deal with non-Chinese peoples and forestalled the first stirrings of those who would provoke hostilities to seek distinction.

Yet at this time Chunmen had been entered and Chu had grown overbearing [?]; why, then, was action against the Rong so urgent? Ah! Here lay Duke Huan’s concealed purpose. Yet authors who explore so fully why the sovereign’s station is exalted and his responsibilities weighty, and exercise such judgment in doing so, are exceedingly rare. This is enough to reveal your loyal devotion. Selected for inclusion.
Comment by Examiner Li, Left Mentor: Able to elucidate the meaning of the commentary.
Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Inceptor: Has a pivotal argument.
In setting forth the sovereign’s exalted titles, the Spring and Autumn Annals sometimes seeks to exalt his station and sometimes to emphasize his responsibilities. Here, its use of the designations “Heavenly King” and “Son of Heaven” expresses the wish that the great ruler fully fulfill the Way proper to him. The king who formerly hunted at Heyang was King Xiang of Zhou. Why is he called “Heavenly King”? The gentleman says: “In the ‘Summary of the Rules of Propriety’ we see the meaning of ‘Heavenly King.’” The Heavenly King is one who rules on Heaven’s behalf and presides over the feudal lords. I see him facing south to govern, reigning over the five ranks of nobility; assuming Heaven’s charge, he comes forth to command the myriad states. Those who serve as his screens and supports all attend his court; small and large jade spheres serve as his pendant ornaments. His station is indeed exalted. Ah! But can this be an empty distinction? Surely he must hold the authority over rites, music, and punitive expeditions, thereby rectifying and enforcing the standards governing the feudal lords. At court audiences, he must carefully observe the rules for dismissal and promotion…

惟德百辟其刑之其臨諸侯之要乎命魯成者

典焉；巡狩也，嚴慶讓之法焉。夫然後羣公列辟莫不震疊，而無愧乎天下之大分矣。《詩》曰：「不顯惟德，百辟其刑之。」其臨諸侯之要乎！命魯成者，周簡也。稱天子者何？君子曰：「於《說命》見天子之義焉。」天子者，繼天爲子，以君夫天下者也。吾見誕膺眷顧，而父母乎天地；上承付託，而臣妾乎華夷。一日二日，有萬機也；匹夫匹婦，皆巳責也。其任重矣！噫，而可徒哉？殆必盡財成輔相之道，以左右乎斯民。作之君也，隆安養之制焉；作之師也，盡教化之道焉。夫然後普天率土莫不尊親，而無忝乎天下之大任矣。《書》曰：「一人元良，萬邦以貞。」其君天下之要乎！由是觀之，臨諸侯者，言乎其法也，法主乎義；君天下者，言乎其恩也，恩主乎仁。雖然，義偏矣，則必過剛，剛則怨，秦其以之；仁偏矣，則必過柔，柔則玩，周其以之。《洪範傳》：「沉潛剛克，高明柔克。」《雝》之詩：「宣哲維人，文武維后。」此帝王之全德也。大君其尚念哉！

禮記
translation_en:
…the regulations governing demotion and promotion; when making inspection tours, he must strictly apply the rules for rewards and reprimands. Only then will all the dukes and assembled lords stand in awed submission, and he will be worthy of his exalted position in the hierarchy of all under Heaven. The Book of Odes says: “How illustrious is his virtue! The hundred lords take it as their model.” Is this not the essential principle of presiding over the regional lords?

It was King Jian of Zhou who conferred a royal charge upon Duke Cheng of Lu. Why is he called the Son of Heaven? The gentleman says: “In the ‘Charge to Yue’ we see the meaning of ‘Son of Heaven.’” The Son of Heaven succeeds Heaven as its son and rules all under Heaven. I see him abundantly receiving Heaven’s favor, treating Heaven and Earth as his parents; receiving his trust from above, and making subjects of the Chinese and the peoples beyond. In a single day or two, there are myriad affairs to attend to; every ordinary man and woman is his own responsibility [?]. His charge is weighty indeed! Ah, can it be merely an empty title? Surely he must fully carry out the work of regulating and assisting the operations of Heaven and Earth, thereby supporting the people. As their ruler, he must strengthen the institutions that secure their peace and sustenance; as their teacher, he must fully carry out moral instruction. Only then will everyone beneath Heaven and throughout the land revere and cherish him, and he will not disgrace his great charge over all under Heaven. The Book of Documents says: “When the one man is supremely good, the myriad states are thereby set right.” Is this not the essential principle of ruling all under Heaven?

Viewed in this light, presiding over the regional lords refers to his standards, and standards are grounded in righteousness; ruling all under Heaven refers to his beneficence, and beneficence is grounded in benevolence. Nevertheless, if righteousness becomes one-sided, it must become excessively rigid; rigidity breeds resentment—Qin exemplified this. If benevolence becomes one-sided, it must become excessively yielding; yielding breeds disrespect—Zhou exemplified this. The Commentary on the Great Plan says: “The retiring and reserved are governed through firmness; the lofty and brilliant are governed through gentleness.” The ode ‘Yong’ says: “Discerning and wise are his men; accomplished in civil and martial virtues is their sovereign.” This is the complete virtue of emperors and kings. May the great ruler give it thought!

Book of Rites
