先王因賦以行禮，而必酌諸地與年也。甚矣，行禮不可無經常之法也！先王因國賦，而以地為之準，年為之差焉，可謂適經權之宜矣。記禮器者意謂：國之所先者禮，禮之所貴者中。先王之合天設地也，而豈徒哉？彼禮必資於財，財必約於數，一或無經，不濫則陋矣。故必舉其定國之賦，量入為出，而所以交乎幽明者，於是乎取焉。要其惟正之供，因財制用，而所以際乎上下者，於是乎取焉。稅於民者有可守之法，而不屈於用之不貲；施於國者有可久之規，而不患乎事
translation_en:
…Thus they must take the established fiscal amounts of the state as the fundamental standard for ritual. The broad ordering of ritual accords with the extent of the territory; its simplicity or lavishness accords with whether the year’s harvest is poor or abundant.

Wang Shi’an

Comment by Associate Examiner Sheng, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): The topic emphasizes that the former kings based their establishment of ritual on fiscal resources and tax revenues, thereby fixing the rules, ensuring the people’s sufficiency, and sustaining moral instruction. Most writers discuss only the management of wealth, which is quite contrary to the original purport. This essay develops almost exhaustively the mutual dependence of fiscal resources and ritual, grasping deeply the meaning of ritual.
Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Rigorous and orderly.
Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction of the Heir Apparent: Expansive and rich.

The former kings relied on tax revenues to carry out ritual, necessarily taking account of the territory and the harvest. How essential it is that the performance of ritual have constant, established rules! The former kings relied on the state’s tax revenues, taking the territory as their standard and the harvest as the basis for variations. They may indeed be said to have suitably reconciled constant principles with adaptation to circumstances. The author of “Ritual Vessels” means that ritual takes precedence in governing a state, and that what matters most in ritual is due measure. Could the former kings’ accordance with Heaven and their ordering of Earth have been without purpose? Ritual necessarily depends on wealth, and wealth must be regulated by numerical limits. If either lacks a constant standard, the result will be either excess or meagerness. Thus they must take the state’s established tax revenues and measure expenditure against income; from these they draw the means for intercourse with both the unseen and the visible worlds. They reckon the regular contributions properly due and regulate expenditure according to available resources; from these they draw the means for relations between those above and those below. Taxes levied upon the people follow rules that can be maintained, without being exhausted by expenditure beyond reckoning; measures applied within the state follow enduring regulations, without concern that undertakings…

translation_en:
…being difficult to sustain. In this way, the proper method of regulating the state is attained. Yet territories differ in extent and cannot be discussed indiscriminately. Could there be no fixed rule for this? Distinctions of rank and dignity are clarified once the state has been constituted, so that hierarchical relationships and categories remain correct; institutions are established at the outset of demarcating the countryside, so that divisions and allocations accord [?]. Where territory is extensive, its rites are comprehensive; where territory is limited, its regulations are strict. For what human effort accomplishes is established upon the advantages of the land. How could one standard be applied throughout? As for years, some yield more and others less: they cannot all be treated alike. Could there be no fitting accommodation to the times? The varying course of the seasons is examined to establish rules for increasing and reducing expenditure; the circumstances that arise are taken into account to establish methods of adaptation. In plentiful years, provision is correspondingly generous; in years of dearth, it is correspondingly reduced. For what is implemented in human affairs is ordered according to Heaven’s seasons. How could it be governed by one uniform rule? Thus, the fixed rules reveal an understanding of constant principles, while fitting accommodation to the times reveals an understanding of discretionary judgment. Can this be denied to be an excellent method for conducting rites and regulating the state?

I have examined the matter: ritual was nowhere more complete than under the established Zhou order. If ritual vessels, prescribed quantities, named objects, and other articles all had to be embellished to the utmost for beauty’s sake, even exhausting the wealth of all under Heaven would surely prove insufficient. This is why ritual achieves its patterned refinement and why the people gladly follow it. Later generations generally regard embellishing government as a means of making a fine display, and the management of resources as tedious talk. Alas! Ceremonial forms, insignia, objects, and ornamentation are certainly called ritual, but who understands that regulation and restraint are precisely…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
序而序則見於外煥乎文章每溢於動容之表
秩然品節皆潤於生色之形使吾身無可象之
儀則節文不能以自行矣禮果可以襲取也哉
夫惟禮之動於外也則似非由中之念而疑於
强世之爲矣故主宰乎三千三百之文而爲禮
之體者恒在於减若或制之而意有弗紓也若
或抑之而力有弗致也斂氣之屈而退藏於密
盖與隂道之闔者同其功禮之主非减而何惟
樂之動於內也則出於自然之情而爲中心之
===
好矣故綱維乎五聲六律之文而爲樂之體者
恒在於盈彌漫布濩而量無不充也會合冲和
而情無不闡也循氣之伸而充積於中盖與陽
道之闢者同其妙樂之主非盈而何學者誠能
致察于內外之分而不失乎盈减之體則治心
治身之功思過半矣雖然禮樂一道也而其動
其主若不同焉何哉盖自天地之高下散殊周
流同化而禮樂之屈伸已有不同者矣此禮所
以能修外而樂所以能修內也至其交錯於中

translation_en:
…order, and order manifests itself outwardly. Its brilliant patterns ever overflow into one’s bearing and movements; its orderly gradations and restraints lend lustre to one’s visible appearance. If our persons lacked a deportment worthy of emulation, the measured forms of ritual could not put themselves into practice. Can ritual really be acquired merely by copying?

Precisely because ritual operates outwardly, it seems not to arise from thoughts within, and may be suspected of being an attempt to coerce the world [?]. Thus, what governs its three thousand and three hundred forms and constitutes the substance of ritual invariably lies in diminution. It is as though something restrains one, leaving one’s intentions not fully expressed, or checks one, leaving one’s strength not fully exerted. Gathering in the contracting vital energy and withdrawing into concealment, it shares the efficacy of the closing movement of yin. What, then, could the governing principle of ritual be but diminution?

Precisely because music operates inwardly, it issues from spontaneous feelings and becomes a delight in the heart. Thus, what orders the patterns of the five notes and six pitch standards and constitutes the substance of music invariably lies in fullness. Spreading everywhere, it fills one’s capacity completely; gathering in balanced harmony, it leaves no feeling unexpressed. Following the expansion of vital energy and accumulating within, it shares the subtle efficacy of the opening movement of yang. What, then, could the governing principle of music be but fullness?

If learners can truly scrutinize the distinction between the inner and the outer, without losing hold of the substance of fullness and diminution, they will have understood more than half of the work of ordering the mind and regulating the person. Yet ritual and music constitute a single Way. Why, then, do their operations and governing principles seem to differ? In the height of Heaven and the lowness of Earth, in their dispersion and differentiation, their circulation and shared transformations, the contraction and expansion embodied in ritual and music already differ. This is why ritual can cultivate the outer and music can cultivate the inner. As for their interweaving within…

The sage takes no deliberate action, yet all under Heaven is well governed: this, too, is simply a matter of recovering his original equilibrium.
Equilibrium is the substance of the Way and the virtue of human nature. Before anything stirs it, it is spontaneously in perfect balance; it is that through which harmony is attained. Everyone possesses this nature, yet not everyone maintains equilibrium, because people incline toward their feelings. The sage fully realizes his nature and recovers his original equilibrium. Thus, in stillness, no principle is lacking; when stirred, there is no incipient impulse to which he fails to respond. He preserves the spiritual efficacy of all under Heaven, yet no one can discern its signs; he knows the transformations of all under Heaven, yet no one can see their traces. Thus, the sage governs all under Heaven simply through earnest reverence. Earnest reverence means taking no deliberate action. Yet through it the nature of human beings can be fully realized, the nature of things can be fully realized, the transforming and nourishing processes can be assisted, and one can participate alongside Heaven and Earth. This is the highest achievement of fully realizing one’s nature. Alas! Who but one possessed of the utmost sincerity under Heaven could participate in this?

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
兩儀由之而立焉三辰由之而位焉五氣由之
而布焉四時由之而行焉萬物由之而成焉莫
非太極之所爲也故其顯諸仁也則乾至大也
坤至廣也其藏諸用也則乾確然易而已坤隤
然簡而已聖人者成天地之能者也聖人之中
聖人之太極也中也者天命之性也道之體也
無所於喜而喜之理具焉者也無所於怒而怒
之理具焉者也無所於哀樂而哀樂之理具焉
者也無聲之可聞無臭之可睹也故聖人之心
===
即天之心天之心一聖人之心亦一一者恭而
已恭故靜虚故動直靜虚則能性性而感之體
具矣體也者中也天下之大本也動直則能物
物而寂之用行矣用也者和也天下之達道也
故感於喜之理達之於天下而無不喜也感於
怒之理達之於天下而無不怒也感於哀樂之
理達之於天下而無不哀且樂也故動而無不
敬言而無不信及其至也不動而敬不言而信
矣賞而無不勸罰而無不威及其至也不賞而

All are the workings of the Supreme Ultimate. Thus, when it manifests itself in benevolence, Qian is supremely great and Kun supremely broad; when it conceals itself in functioning, Qian is simply firm and easy, and Kun simply yielding and simple. The sage fulfills the capacities of Heaven and Earth. The sage’s equilibrium is his Supreme Ultimate. Equilibrium is the nature conferred by Heaven and the substance of the Way. Before there is any occasion for joy, the principle of joy is fully present; before there is any occasion for anger, the principle of anger is fully present; before there is any occasion for sorrow or pleasure, their principles are fully present. There is no sound to be heard and no odor to be seen [?]. Thus the sage’s heart is Heaven’s heart. Heaven’s heart is one, and the sage’s heart is likewise one. This oneness is nothing more than reverence. Through reverence he is still and empty, and hence upright in action. Being still and empty, he can fully realize his nature as such, and the substance underlying responsiveness is complete. This substance is equilibrium, the great foundation of all under Heaven. Being upright in action, he can treat things according to what they are, and the functioning of stillness is put into practice. This functioning is harmony, the universally operative Way of all under Heaven. Thus, responding to the principle of joy, he extends it throughout the world, and none fail to rejoice; responding to the principle of anger, he extends it throughout the world, and none fail to feel anger; responding to the principles of sorrow and pleasure, he extends them throughout the world, and none fail to feel sorrow and pleasure. text:
不罰而威矣故性性者致中者也所以存神
也物物者致和者也所以過化也蓋至是而吾
之心正天地之心亦正矣吾之氣順天地之氣
亦順矣以日月則協度也以風雨則應時也以
寒燠則奠序也以庶草則蕃廡也以鳥獸魚鼈
則咸若也故天地無心而成化聖人有心而無
為聖人之於天下垂衣裳而已矣正南面而已
矣故其易如乾其簡如坤周子曰聖人定之以
仁義中正而主靜主靜者篤恭者也復其未發

…without punishing, he inspires awe. Thus, fully realizing one’s nature means bringing equilibrium to its utmost; through this one preserves the numinous. Dealing with things according to their nature means bringing harmony to its utmost; through this one transforms others wherever one passes. Indeed, at this point, when my heart is rectified, the heart of Heaven and Earth is also rectified; when my vital energy flows harmoniously, the vital energy of Heaven and Earth also flows harmoniously. The sun and moon accord with their appointed courses; wind and rain arrive in season; cold and warmth maintain their proper sequence; all plants flourish; and birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all thrive in accordance with their nature. Here the achievement of attaining utmost sincerity and fully realizing one’s nature reaches its culmination.
I have often wondered at those who, ignorant of substance, regard profound reverence as nothingness, and those who, engrossed in function, regard profound reverence as something existent. Thus purity, quietude, and extinction approach substance, but do not constitute substance; expedient schemes and the pursuit of achievement and profit approach function, but do not constitute function. Those ignorant of substance perceive nonaction but fail to perceive action, and so cannot bring equilibrium to its utmost. Those engrossed in function perceive action but fail to perceive nonaction, and so cannot bring harmony to its utmost. 德則知仁勇焉其功則博學審問謹思明辨篤
行焉其端則尊德性道問學焉其要則明善誠
身焉其極則至誠無息純一不已焉舉聖人之
德而無不協於天命之中用之本也自夫用而
觀之其經則修身也親親也尊賢也敬大臣也
體羣臣也子庶民也來百工也懷諸侯也柔遠

禮制度考文也其効則位天地育萬物也舉天

…its virtues are wisdom, humaneness, and courage; its work consists in learning broadly, questioning closely, reflecting carefully, discriminating clearly, and practicing earnestly. Its points of departure are honoring one's moral nature and pursuing inquiry and learning; its essentials are understanding goodness and making oneself sincere; its culmination is utmost sincerity without cessation, pure unity without end. All the sage's virtues accord with the centrality of Heaven's mandate: this is the foundation of function. Viewed from the standpoint of function, its guiding principles are cultivating oneself, cherishing one's kin, honoring the worthy, respecting the great ministers, showing consideration for the assembled officials, treating the common people as one's children, attracting the various artisans, cherishing the feudal lords, and conciliating people from afar. Its enumerated observances are the three hundred ceremonial rites and the three thousand rules of deportment. Its weighty responsibilities are deliberating on rites, establishing institutions and measures, and examining written forms. Its effects are to establish Heaven and Earth in their proper places and nurture the myriad things. All the ways of the world converge upon the sage's centrality: this is the extension of substance. At this point, the nature conferred by Heaven's mandate is fully realized, the Way of following that nature is practiced, and the teaching that cultivates the Way is established.

Thus, the Mean proceeds from Heaven's mandate and spreads into human affairs: one root becomes myriad diverse manifestations. It proceeds from human affairs and returns to Heaven's mandate: myriad diverse manifestations become one root. The sage is one whose learning has reached this single root. Thus, the ease of Qian consists simply in vigor; the simplicity of Kun consists simply in compliance; and the sage's nonaction consists simply in earnest reverence. Hence it is said: “In breadth and depth, it matches Earth; in height and brightness, it matches Heaven; enduring long, it is without bounds. punctuated: 鴻儀肇舉，睹縟典於乾行；鳳藻均頒，荷湛恩於晉錫。榮施近列，道冠前謨。臣某等誠懽誠抃，稽首頓首。竊惟省方觀民，先王所以設教；博施備物，聖人所以事親。虞四嶽之周巡，輯圭璧於歲覲；漢原廟之特建，奉衣冠於月遊。蓋神靈體魄之崇，豈豐於昵顧？兵衞徵求之寡，匪厲乎民？歷選秘圖，率虧彝典。穆遊萬里，興白雲黃竹之謠；秦錮三泉，侈銀海金鳧之制。迨甘泉汾陰之祀，暨景靈鴻慶之修，簫鼓奏於洪河，簨簴陳於別寢，情鍾湯沐，義謬遊歌。詎知仁孝之謨，復見聖明之世！豫順以動，本教愛而因親；師出而臧，爰布德以展義。茲蓋伏遇皇帝陛下，道隆三重，倫敘九疇。
translation_en:
…As the grand ceremony was first performed, we beheld its elaborate rites in Your Majesty’s progress; as your splendid composition was distributed to all, we received your profound favor in this gracious bestowal. Honor reaches the ranks of your close attendants; your Way surpasses the exemplary plans of former ages. We, your servants, are truly joyful and truly exultant; we bow our heads to the ground and kowtow.

We humbly reflect that touring the regions and observing the people were the means by which the former kings established their teaching; extending bounty widely and providing all requisite things were the means by which the sage served his parents. The ruler of Yu made a circuit of the Four Sacred Peaks, gathering the jade tablets and discs at the audiences of the year. The Han specially established an additional ancestral temple, reverently conveying the deceased emperor’s robes and cap on monthly outings. Yet does honoring the ancestral spirits and bodily remains gain anything from partial attachment? Were the supposedly modest demands for military escorts and requisitions not burdensome to the people [?]? Surveying the treasured historical records, we find repeated departures from the enduring rites. King Mu journeyed ten thousand li, giving rise to the songs of White Clouds and Yellow Bamboo; Qin sealed his tomb beneath the three subterranean springs, indulging in lavish constructions of silver seas and golden ducks. Then came the sacrifices at Ganquan and Fenyin, and the construction of Jingling and Hongqing: flutes and drums resounded beside the great Yellow River, and frames for suspended instruments stood in separate ancestral chambers. Affection centered upon the ancestral estates, but the principle was distorted into excursions and songs.

Who could have known that the exemplary designs of benevolence and filial devotion would appear again in an age of sagely enlightenment! Acting in joyful accord, you ground the teaching of love in affection for parents; sending forth the host to good purpose, you spread virtue and display righteousness. This is because we have humbly encountered Your Majesty the Emperor, whose Way exalts the three weighty duties, and whose ordering of human relationships accords with the Nine Categories…

translation_en:
…Like Yao, naturally at ease and truly reverent; like Shun, ever circumspect and reverently fulfilling his duties. You serve Heaven as father and Earth as mother, bringing equilibrium and harmony to their fullest realization. You honor the virtuous as ancestral exemplars and those of merit as founding ancestors, fully observing familial relationships and ritual institutions. Just as sacrifices were first instituted in the Hall of Light, the maternal carriage suddenly ascended afar—the imperial mother passed away.
Holding filial piety foremost in government, you weighed whether the burial chambers should be separate or joined. Considering timeliness paramount in ritual, you gathered the differing and concurring opinions of the multitude. You investigated and deliberated, consulting those at court and those outside it; insisting on sincerity and trustworthiness, you did so twice and thrice. Thus you undertook the labor of planning and inspection [?], with no fixed arrangement for the imperial tour of inspection [?], extending sacrificial announcements to all…

translation_en:
…the imperial ancestors, while sacrifices offered from afar extended in due order to all the spirits. You rode in the five ceremonial carriages and unfurled the nine banners, surrounded by a thousand chariots and followed by ten thousand mounted men. The great potter’s wheel of Heaven spread its vital breath: birds and beasts were content, and plants and trees revived. The colorful ceremonial guard advanced amid springtime; clouds glowed, and mountains and rivers shone. Your imperial procession approached beneath the Floriate Canopy, its attendant carriages linked in succession beneath the Hooked Array. Princes of the imperial clan came reverently to court, and officials of every office assembled with measured steps. Along three thousand li of imperial highway, all supplies came from the imperial provisioning offices. Though the Palace Guard numbered a hundred thousand, the markets in the towns below remained undisturbed. Despite setting out early, you grew ever more reverent; dressed before dawn, you forgot your weariness.
Arriving in the season of spring rain and dew, you reached the pines and catalpas of your sagely deceased father’s burial ground. You beheld the luxuriant growth at Chunde and stood awaiting the spirit’s presence at Ling’en [?]. You assembled all to deliberate together, selected an auspicious day, and completed the undertaking. You personally determined the burial site for ten thousand years, securing everlasting repose for the spirits of the two imperial parents. We beheld your imperial footsteps in the former palace and felt the significance of the flowing rainbow at Huazhu, the legendary birthplace of a sage ruler. Between the Jiang and Han rivers, poems were presented and collected so that local customs might be observed. In the countryside around Dongting, you erected an altar, burned sacrificial offerings, and arrayed the musicians. You summoned elderly men into your presence and proclaimed your instructions; rejoicing stirred…

translation_en:
…along the thoroughfares of Yao. You broadly issued imperial pronouncements remitting land taxes, your benevolence matching the Zhou distribution of grain. Composing rhapsodies beside the Xiang River, you gathered the fragrance of the orchids of the Li and the angelica of the Yuan; leaving verses at the bend of the Yellow River, you revealed the mysteries of the Tortoise Writing and the Horse Diagram. By the time your jade-belled imperial carriage turned homeward, your celestial compositions had been gathered into a full volume, setting forth illustrious counsels for this dynasty to posterity and far surpassing the precedents of a hundred kings.

We, your servants, were undeservedly privileged by our offices to accompany your progress, yet feel ashamed that we merely hurried along in attendance; serving in the ranks of officials, we contributed nothing to guarding the capital in your absence. We look up in admiration at the brilliance of your sagely writings and receive your imperial gift of these volumes bound in pale blue and yellow silk. We shall wrap them in many layers for safekeeping: they surpass the compositions on passing through Pei and crossing the Fen. Bowing twice, we read them: they record your achievement in ordering Heaven and Earth. We shall transmit them to our descendants, esteeming them more highly than precious jade discs.

We humbly wish that, as you offer the seasonal sacrifices in the nine ancestral temples, you may strive still further for the benevolence of guiding your successors [?]; and that, as you rule with robes hanging down for a thousand springs, you may deepen still further the filial devotion expressed in “zhi ren” [?]. May radiant Heaven respond, so that your ancestors rest ever more peacefully and your descendants flourish ever more abundantly; may your imperial reign endure without end, so that the people preserve harmony and…

translation_en:
…and Heaven secures stability. We, your servants, looking up to Heaven and reverently admiring Your Majesty, cannot contain our joy and profound gratitude. We respectfully submit this memorial of thanks for Your Majesty’s hearing.
Third Session: Five Policy Questions.
First Question.
Zhou Guoqing.
Comment by Associate Examiner Hong, Instructor: The Way of government was originally one; only in later ages did it become divided, and the various accounts of legitimate succession each occasioned debate. You have adjudicated these matters through the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Book of Documents, tracing their thread across thousands of years and reaching firm conclusions. As for the legitimacy with which our imperial ancestor and our reigning emperor acquired the succession, causing the Way of government to become one again and to flourish uniquely beyond all past and present precedent, you have also discerned and expounded it with reverence. Might you be one who has gained something from the transforming influence of the Way of government and been stirred to action by it?
Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: Our imperial ancestor fully established institutions and fulfilled human relationships; our reigning emperor has excelled in carrying on his predecessor’s work and realizing his intentions. This is truly what is meant by fully discharging…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
君師之責而遠紹數千年帝王之統者子能仰窺而揄揚之足占素學且中間
二統相傳之叙考訂精當殆未可以文士目也
考試官左中允李批我
聖祖德符堯舜功高湯武至我
皇上敬一察倫重光而廓大之真可以度越千古遠俟百聖而不惑也子能鋪
張揚厲且曲盡治道相傳之統可以徵
聖化作人之功矣佳士佳士
考試官左庶子童批治道二統宇宙間大論議
子能條答辭嚴義正直欲與古聖賢增翊衛之功裒然佳
===
士也至我
皇祖功德遠紹唐虞
皇上纘承憲章超軼百代尤能仰測於萬一子其涵濡有得者耶
治統正而帝王之政行矣道統正而帝王
之教明矣由政而言謂之君是故曆數存
焉由教而言謂之師是故心法存焉三代
而上政教出於一有其統而亡其名三代
而下政教出於二而正統之名始立正統
者所以建萬世之極而嚴萬世之防者也

punctuated:
君師之責，而遠紹數千年帝王之統者。子能仰窺而揄揚之，足占素學。且中間二統相傳之叙，考訂精當，殆未可以文士目也。

考試官左中允李批：我聖祖德符堯舜，功高湯武。至我皇上，敬一察倫，重光而廓大之，真可以度越千古，遠俟百聖而不惑也。子能鋪張揚厲，且曲盡治道相傳之統，可以徵聖化作人之功矣。佳士！佳士！

考試官左庶子童批：治道二統，宇宙間大論議。子能條答，辭嚴義正，直欲與古聖賢增翊衛之功，裒然佳士也。至我皇祖功德遠紹唐虞，皇上纘承憲章，超軼百代，尤能仰測於萬一。子其涵濡有得者耶？

治統正而帝王之政行矣，道統正而帝王之教明矣。由政而言謂之君，是故曆數存焉；由教而言謂之師，是故心法存焉。三代而上，政教出於一，有其統而亡其名；三代而下，政教出於二，而正統之名始立。正統者，所以建萬世之極而嚴萬世之防者也。
translation_en:
…the responsibilities of ruler and teacher, and continuing the succession of emperors and kings stretching back several thousand years. Your ability reverently to discern and extol this is sufficient evidence of your accumulated learning. Moreover, your account of the transmission of the two successions is precise and sound in its investigation and judgments. You can hardly be regarded merely as a literary man.

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Our sagely ancestor’s virtue matched that of Yao and Shun, and his achievements surpassed those of Tang and Wu. Our present Emperor reverently maintains unity and scrutinizes human relationships, renewing that glory and enlarging it. Truly, he can surpass all antiquity and await sages a hundred generations hence without misgiving. You have expounded and celebrated this magnificently, while fully elucidating the transmission of the successions of governance and the Way. This attests to the achievement of the sagely transforming influence in nurturing men of talent. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Vice Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent: The two successions of governance and the Way constitute a great subject of debate within the universe. You have answered point by point, with disciplined language and correct principles, aspiring directly to augment the work of the ancient sages and worthies in supporting and defending them. You are an outstanding scholar indeed. Concerning our imperial ancestor, whose achievements and virtue continued the distant legacy of Tang and Yu, and our Emperor, who carries on that inheritance and follows its exemplary institutions, surpassing a hundred generations, you have been especially able reverently to fathom some small portion of their greatness. Surely you have gained something from being steeped in their influence?

When the succession of governance is correct, the government of emperors and kings is carried out; when the succession of the Way is correct, the teaching of emperors and kings is made clear. In terms of government, one is called a ruler; hence the succession mandated by Heaven resides therein. In terms of teaching, one is called a teacher; hence the method of the mind resides therein. During the Three Dynasties and earlier, government and teaching issued from a single source: their succession existed, but its name did not. After the Three Dynasties, government and teaching issued from two sources, and only then was the designation ‘legitimate succession’ established. Legitimate succession is the means of establishing the supreme standard for all ages and strictly maintaining the boundaries for all ages.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
故治之統有正有閏而變例不與焉道之
統有正有羽翼而異端不與焉二者立而
陵節犯分者不敢偪衼說横議者不敢肆
矣昔者三皇五帝三王之相承也凡以開
物而成務也故其治顥顥乎爾熈熈乎爾
二典三謨之相傳也凡以繼天而立極也
故其道平平乎爾蕩蕩乎爾自周之東王
綱解紐黍離降爲國風孔子以天縱之聖
不得其位廼取六經而刪述之政教之責
===
始移於下孔子既歿霸術日隆異端日熾
孟子辭而闢之盖廓如也自是以降治道
湮蝕淪胥於亡而正統之說不得不立然
二者之辨愚必以孔子焉質治統質諸春
秋道統質諸書孔子之作春秋也周雖弱
必尊之桓文雖強必抑之吳楚雖大必外
之所以明正統也周之後取天下而不失
其正者吾得漢唐宋焉漢取其誅無道秦
也唐取其平隋亂也宋取其混一五季也

始移於下孔子既歿霸術日隆異端日熾
孟子辭而闢之蓋廓如也自是以降治道
湮蝕淪胥於亡而正統之說不得不立然
二者之辨愚必以孔子為質治統質諸春
秋道統質諸書孔子之作春秋也周雖弱

之所以明正統也周之後取天下而不失
其正者吾得漢唐宋焉漢取其誅無道秦
也唐取其平隋亂也宋取其混一五季也
punctuated: 故治之統有正有閏，而變例不與焉；道之統有正有羽翼，而異端不與焉。二者立，而陵節犯分者不敢偪，衼說横議者不敢肆矣。昔者三皇五帝三王之相承也，凡以開物而成務也，故其治顥顥乎爾，熈熈乎爾。二典三謨之相傳也，凡以繼天而立極也，故其道平平乎爾，蕩蕩乎爾。自周之東，王綱解紐，《黍離》降爲國風。孔子以天縱之聖，不得其位，廼取六經而刪述之，政教之責始移於下。孔子既歿，霸術日隆，異端日熾，孟子辭而闢之，盖廓如也。自是以降，治道湮蝕，淪胥於亡，而正統之說不得不立。然二者之辨，愚必以孔子焉質：治統質諸《春秋》，道統質諸《書》。孔子之作《春秋》也，周雖弱，必尊之；桓文雖強，必抑之；吳楚雖大，必外之，所以明正統也。周之後，取天下而不失其正者，吾得漢唐宋焉。漢取其誅無道秦也，唐取其平隋亂也，宋取其混一五季也。
translation_en:
Thus, the succession of political rule includes both legitimate and intercalary lines, but anomalous cases have no place in it; the transmission of the Way includes both its principal line and those who assist it, but heterodox teachings have no place in it. Once these two distinctions are established, those who overstep their rank and transgress their allotted station dare not encroach, and those who advance aberrant doctrines [?] and reckless arguments dare not act without restraint.

In antiquity, the succession of the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, and Three Kings served throughout to unfold the potential of things and accomplish human affairs. Hence their government was luminous and harmonious. The transmission of the Two Canons and Three Counsels served throughout to carry forward Heaven’s work and establish the supreme standard. Hence their Way was equitable and all-embracing. After the Zhou moved east, the bonds of royal authority came undone, and “The Millet Hangs Low” was relegated to the Airs of the States. Confucius, though a sage endowed by Heaven, did not attain the appropriate position. He therefore took the Six Classics and edited and expounded them. Responsibility for government and instruction thus began to pass to those below. After Confucius died, the arts of hegemony grew daily more powerful, and heterodox teachings daily more rampant. Mencius refuted them through argument, clearing them away. Thereafter, the way of government was obscured and eroded, and all sank together toward ruin; the doctrine of legitimate succession therefore had to be established.

Yet, in distinguishing these two successions, I, in my humble judgment, must turn to Confucius for verification: political succession is to be tested against the Spring and Autumn Annals, and the transmission of the Way against the Book of Documents. In composing the Spring and Autumn Annals, Confucius invariably honored the Zhou, although it was weak; invariably restrained Dukes Huan and Wen, although they were powerful; and invariably treated Wu and Chu as outsiders, although they were great states. This was how he made legitimate succession clear. Among those who took possession of All under Heaven after the Zhou without forfeiting legitimacy, I find the Han, Tang, and Song. I accept the Han because it punished the tyrannical Qin; the Tang because it quelled the disorder of the Sui; and the Song because it unified the realm divided under the Five Dynasties.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
附之正統爲其足以修政而立敎也朱子
作綱目黜曹魏而進昭烈蓋以漢賊不兩
立而帝室之胄固炎祚之所屬也得尊王
之義矣然以秦晉隋列之周漢唐之間夫
謂秦晉隋之有天下可也謂其爲正統不
可也何也秦暴也晉隋篡也秦之不可以
繼周猶魏之不可以繼漢也昭堅之與操
其惡等爾乃以之列於正統豈非徒據其
有天下之跡而未探其取天下之心耶歐
===
陽子曰正者正天下之不正也統者合天
下之不一也蓋有統而不正未有正而不
可以統者也司馬氏曰不能一統者有其
名而無其實者也夫治之道亦先正其名
而已名苟正則實雖偏安不害其爲統名
苟非正則實雖全盛猶弗統也且帝王之
興必有强有力者起而併之以爲一代之
驅除故秦併六國而漢興隋併六朝而唐
興周幾併五代而宋興然則秦漢之間也

驅除故秦併六國而漢興隋併六朝而唐
興周幾併五代而宋興然則秦漢之閏也
punctuated: 附之正統，爲其足以修政而立敎也。朱子作《綱目》，黜曹魏而進昭烈，蓋以漢賊不兩立，而帝室之胄固炎祚之所屬也，得尊王之義矣。然以秦、晉、隋列之周、漢、唐之間，夫謂秦、晉、隋之有天下可也，謂其爲正統不可也。何也？秦暴也，晉、隋篡也。秦之不可以繼周，猶魏之不可以繼漢也。昭、堅之與操，其惡等爾，乃以之列於正統，豈非徒據其有天下之跡，而未探其取天下之心耶？歐陽子曰：「正者，正天下之不正也；統者，合天下之不一也。」蓋有統而不正，未有正而不可以統者也。司馬氏曰：「不能一統者，有其名而無其實者也。」夫治之道，亦先正其名而已。名苟正，則實雖偏安，不害其爲統；名苟非正，則實雖全盛，猶弗統也。且帝王之興，必有强有力者起而併之，以爲一代之驅除。故秦併六國而漢興，隋併六朝而唐興，周幾併五代而宋興。然則秦漢之間也，
translation_en:
…They are included in the legitimate succession because they were capable of putting government in order and establishing moral instruction. Master Zhu, in composing the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror (Gangmu), demoted Cao Wei and elevated Emperor Zhaolie [Liu Bei]. He did so because the Han and its usurpers could not both stand, and a descendant of the imperial house was indeed the rightful heir to the Han imperial line. In this he grasped the principle of honoring the rightful sovereign. Yet he placed Qin, Jin, and Sui among Zhou, Han, and Tang. To say that Qin, Jin, and Sui possessed All-under-Heaven is permissible; to say that they belonged to the legitimate succession is not. Why? Qin was tyrannical, while Jin and Sui usurped power. Qin could no more succeed Zhou than Wei could succeed Han. The wickedness of [Sima] Zhao and [Yang] Jian equaled that of [Cao] Cao. To rank them nevertheless within the legitimate succession—is this not merely to rely upon the outward fact that they possessed All-under-Heaven, without examining the intentions with which they acquired it?

Master Ouyang said: “Legitimacy means rectifying what is not right in All-under-Heaven; unity means bringing together what is divided in All-under-Heaven.” There can thus be unity without legitimacy, but there has never been legitimacy incapable of providing a basis for unity. Master Sima said: “Those unable to bring about unity have the name but lack the substance.” Yet the way of governing consists first in rectifying the name. If the name is rightful, then even if a regime in fact holds only a portion of the realm, this does not prevent it from carrying on the succession. If the name is not rightful, then even if its power is at its height throughout the realm, it still does not carry on the succession.

Moreover, whenever an imperial dynasty arises, some strong and powerful figure must first arise and annex the competing states, clearing the way for that dynasty. Thus Qin annexed the Six States, and Han arose; Sui annexed the Six Dynasties, and Tang arose; Zhou nearly completed the unification of the Five Dynasties, and Song arose. Thus Qin was an interval before Han [?] …

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
隋唐之閏也周宋之閏也或者又以東晋
之紹典午後唐之祖神堯皆欲進之於統
夫琅邪牛金之種也司馬氏且見黜矣克
用沙陀之種也吾見其尤非類矣甚至作
通鑑者帝魏而寇蜀帝朱梁而寇河東作
元經者帝北魏而黜江左君子不能無憾
焉則超漢唐宋以續帝王之曆數者寧無
屬哉孔子之序書也堯傳之舜舜傳之禹
禹傳之湯湯傳之文武周公繼周公而集
===
羣聖者孔子也繼孔子而閑先聖者孟子
也孟子而後傳道而不失其正者吾得濂
洛關閩之學焉周子之圖書也二程子之
踐履也張子之精思也朱子之大成也列
之正統爲其足以立教而裨政也宋史作
道學傳取康節南軒而舍象山蓋以内聖
外王之學義利之辨於道有功而高明簡
徑之見其流不能無弊也傳心之法蓋得
之矣然胡康侯呂伯恭蔡季通眞希元魏

之矣然胡康侯呂伯恭蔡季通眞希元魏
punctuated: 隋唐之閏也，周宋之閏也。或者又以東晋之紹典午、後唐之祖神堯，皆欲進之於統。夫琅邪，牛金之種也，司馬氏且見黜矣；克用，沙陀之種也，吾見其尤非類矣。甚至作《通鑑》者帝魏而寇蜀，帝朱梁而寇河東；作《元經》者帝北魏而黜江左，君子不能無憾焉。則超漢唐宋以續帝王之曆數者，寧無屬哉？孔子之序《書》也，堯傳之舜，舜傳之禹，禹傳之湯，湯傳之文武周公。繼周公而集羣聖者，孔子也；繼孔子而閑先聖者，孟子也。孟子而後，傳道而不失其正者，吾得濂洛關閩之學焉。周子之圖書也，二程子之踐履也，張子之精思也，朱子之大成也，列之正統，爲其足以立教而裨政也。《宋史》作《道學傳》，取康節、南軒而舍象山，蓋以内聖外王之學、義利之辨於道有功，而高明簡徑之見，其流不能無弊也。傳心之法，蓋得之矣。然胡康侯、呂伯恭、蔡季通、眞希元、魏
translation_en:
…an intercalary interval between Sui and Tang, and an intercalary interval between Zhou and Song. Some, moreover, wish to admit Eastern Jin into the legitimate succession because it continued the Sima line, and Later Tang because it claimed Shenyao as its ancestor. Yet the Prince of Langye was descended from Niu Jin, so even the Sima house must be excluded; Keyong was of Shatuo stock, and I find him still less of our kind. Indeed, the author of the Comprehensive Mirror treats Wei as emperors and Shu as bandits, and Zhu Liang as emperors and Hedong as bandits; the author of the Classic of Origins treats Northern Wei as emperors and excludes Jiangzuo. Gentlemen cannot but regret this. Surely, then, there must be someone to whom belongs the continuation of the imperial succession, surpassing Han, Tang, and Song?

When Confucius arranged the Book of Documents, Yao transmitted the succession to Shun, Shun to Yu, Yu to Tang, and Tang to Kings Wen and Wu and the Duke of Zhou. Confucius succeeded the Duke of Zhou and brought together the achievements of all the sages; Mencius succeeded Confucius and defended the earlier sages. After Mencius, I find those who transmitted the Way without losing its correctness in the learning of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min. Master Zhou’s diagrams and writings, the two Masters Cheng’s practical conduct, Master Zhang’s profound reflection, and Master Zhu’s great synthesis warrant their inclusion in the orthodox succession, for they suffice to establish teaching and aid government.

In compiling its Biographies of Masters of the Learning of the Way, the History of the Song included Kangjie and Nanxuan but omitted Xiangshan. This was presumably because the learning of inner sagehood and outer kingship, and the distinction between righteousness and profit, contributed to the Way, whereas lofty and lucid views offering a short path could not be free of harmful consequences in their subsequent development. In this, it seems to have grasped the method of transmitting the mind. Yet Hu Kanghou, Lü Bogong, Cai Jitong, Zhen Xiyuan, and Wei…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
華父咸無取焉夫謂五子之不得為正統
可也謂其不當在本傳不可也何也文定
之卓立得伊洛之秘成公之博文節之精
於紫陽有資益焉而文忠之直文靖之堅
又皆明正學於厲禁之後比之游楊黃李
其賢均也乃以之列於儒林豈非有見於
其論撰無見於其造詣耶程子曰道不行
百世無善治學不傳千載無真儒未有道
而非儒亦未有儒而不本於道者也朱子
===
曰道之託於人者有絕有續故其行於世
者有明有晦夫道之傳亦存乎其人而已
苟續而明也不敢以其輩出而略之也苟
絕而晦也不敢以其僅見而取之也且聖
賢之作必有聲應氣求者出而助之以為
吾道之羽翼故堯舜之興而有臯夔禹湯
之興而有益稷伊尹文武之興而有周召
顏曾思孟羽翼乎孔子者也胡呂而下羽
翼乎四子者也或者於漢取廣川於隋取

而非儒亦未有儒而不本於道者也宋子

苟續而明也不敢以其輩出而略之也苟

吾道之羽翼故堯舜之興而有臯夔禹湯
之興而有益稷伊尹文武之興而有周召
顔曾思孟羽翼乎孔子者也胡呂而下羽
翼乎四子者也或者於漢取廣川於隋取
punctuated:
華父咸無取焉。夫謂五子之不得為正統，可也；謂其不當在本傳，不可也。何也？文定之卓立，得伊洛之秘；成公之博、文節之精，於紫陽有資益焉。而文忠之直、文靖之堅，又皆明正學於厲禁之後。比之游、楊、黃、李，其賢均也。乃以之列於儒林，豈非有見於其論撰，無見於其造詣耶？程子曰：「道不行，百世無善治；學不傳，千載無真儒。」未有道而非儒，亦未有儒而不本於道者也。朱子曰：「道之託於人者有絕有續，故其行於世者有明有晦。」夫道之傳，亦存乎其人而已。苟續而明也，不敢以其輩出而略之也；苟絕而晦也，不敢以其僅見而取之也。

且聖賢之作，必有聲應氣求者出而助之，以為吾道之羽翼。故堯舜之興而有臯夔，禹湯之興而有益稷伊尹，文武之興而有周召。顏曾思孟，羽翼乎孔子者也；胡呂而下，羽翼乎四子者也。或者於漢取廣川，於隋取
translation_en:
…Huafu—all were excluded. To say that these five masters could not belong to the orthodox succession is acceptable; to say that they ought not to appear in this biography section is not. Why? Wending’s outstanding independence attained the profound teachings of the Yi–Luo tradition; Chenggong’s breadth of learning and Wenjie’s precision benefited Ziyang. Moreover, Wenzhong’s uprightness and Wenjing’s steadfastness both brought orthodox learning to light after the severe prohibitions. Compared with You, Yang, Huang, and Li, they were equal in worthiness. To place them instead in the Biographies of Confucian Scholars—does this not recognize their writings while failing to recognize their attainments? Master Cheng said: “When the Way is not practiced, a hundred generations lack good government; when learning is not transmitted, a thousand years lack true Confucians.” There has never been a bearer of the Way who was not a Confucian, nor a Confucian who was not rooted in the Way. Master Zhu said: “The Way, as entrusted to human beings, has interruptions and continuities; hence its practice in the world has periods of illumination and obscurity.” The transmission of the Way rests simply with the individuals concerned. If they continue it and make it clear, we dare not omit them because they appear in great numbers; if they interrupt it and obscure it, we dare not include them because they are rarely encountered.

Furthermore, whenever sages and worthies arise, others whose voices respond to theirs and whose vital energies seek theirs must emerge to assist them, serving as wings to our Way. Thus, when Yao and Shun arose, there were Gao and Kui; when Yu and Tang arose, there were Yi, Ji, and Yi Yin; when Wen and Wu arose, there were the Dukes of Zhou and Shao. Yan, Zeng, Si, and Meng were wings to Confucius; Hu, Lü, and those after them were wings to the four masters. Some select Guangchuan from the Han, and from the Sui select…

王韓皆衛道者也然其學也吾見亦駁矣
至於勝國二子皆信道者也然其事元也
君子至今有遺論焉則由魯鄒以繼帝王
之心法者寧無屬哉夫治統之正者以其
本於道也道統之正者以其適於治也得
之不以其道而又足以害治推之不達於
治而又足以害道君子必絕之故吕雉之
於漢武曌之於唐以婦乗夫者也劉石符

…Hefen; for the Tang, they select Changli; and for the Yuan, Luzhai and Caolu. Dong, Wang, and Han all defended the Way, yet I find their learning also to be impure. As for the two masters of the preceding dynasty, both believed in the Way; nevertheless, gentlemen to this day continue to criticize their service to the Yuan. Can there really be no one belonging to the succession that, through the sages of Lu and Zou, carries on the sovereigns’ essential teaching of the mind?
The succession of governance is legitimate because it is rooted in the Way; the transmission of the Way is legitimate because it is suited to governance. If someone acquires power contrary to the Way and thereby endangers governance, or expounds the Way without making it applicable to governance and thereby endangers the Way, the gentleman must exclude him. Thus Lü Zhi in the Han and Wu Zhao in the Tang were women who overrode men. The Liu, Shi, Fu, Yao, Murong, and Helian houses in relation to the Jin were the outcasts [?] of the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, and Qiang; the Liao, Jin, and Yuan in relation to the Song represented the intrusion of the Qidan, Nüzhi, and Menggu. All were cases of outsiders bringing disorder to the Chinese realm, departures from the proper succession of governance. The Spring and Autumn Annals brings order to an age of disorder and restores what is correct: anyone is entitled to condemn them.
As for the constriction of learning by textual glosses in the Han and its submergence in literary composition in the Tang, these constitute distorted learning. The emptiness and nonbeing of Laozi, the quiescence and extinction of Buddhism, and the hundred schools and their many arts obstructing benevolence and righteousness constitute heterodox teachings. These are what the Book of Documents calls ‘malicious doctrines and destructive conduct’; anyone is entitled to attack them. Thus what the succession of governance excludes is female rulers, usurping ministers, and foreign peoples; what the transmission of the Way excludes is emptiness and nonbeing, quiescence and extinction, and techniques and numerological arts…

translation_en:
…Thus the proper positions of yin and yang are rectified, the distinction between ruler and minister is clarified, and the boundaries protecting Huaxia are strictly maintained; government thereby operates. The subtle distinctions between the heterodox and the orthodox are discerned, judgments concerning their differences and similarities are settled, and the incipient signs of order and disorder are distinguished; moral instruction thereby becomes clear. Yet governance and the Way originate in Heaven, while their flourishing or decline depends upon the times. Thus the Book of Documents ends with King Ping, indicating the extinction of the traces of true kingship; the Spring and Autumn Annals begins with King Ping, indicating the rise of hegemonic ambitions. Here lies the turning point in the rise and decline of governance and the Way. Kangjie [Shao Yong] said that the Three Sovereigns were like spring, the Five Emperors like summer, the Three Kings like autumn, and the Five Hegemons like winter. Caolu [Wu Cheng] said that Confucius represented origination, Yan Hui and Zeng Shen flourishing, Zisi benefit, and Mencius constancy. They surely perceived something of this.
Never was the severance of the two lines of transmission more severe than under the Yuan. Our imperial ancestor drove out the dogs and sheep to restore the territory of the emperors and kings, and swept away the rank stench to restore their caps and robes. He rectified the Three Bonds after they had fallen into ruin and established the Nine Laws after they had been corrupted. In the legitimacy of his acquisition of All under Heaven, compared with Tang he had no cause for moral shame; compared with King Wu, he was perfect in goodness. I have ventured to examine this: his divine counsels and sagely virtue, his broad principles and detailed provisions, cannot be exhaustively recounted. …and the establishment of statutes and ordinances: these are the great achievements in governance. For officials and commoners there are pronouncements; for schools, inscribed stelae; to guide the world, instructions; and to teach the people, posted proclamations. These are the great achievements in moral instruction. Thus the tradition of the Way of governance, once obscured, became bright again; once severed, it was renewed. In these achievements there is something surpassing even Yao and Shun. The course of the age opened anew, and human culture was awakened once more. Was this not the springtime of the Three Sovereigns, the inception celebrated by Confucius?
Our sage sovereign received Heaven’s mandate and succeeded to the throne of his imperial ancestor. He rectified the rites for the various sacrifices, clarified the Way of the enduring human relationships, gave weight to sericulture and mulberry cultivation, and held the authority to punish and reward. For maintaining reverent single-mindedness, there is an Instruction; for the Five Admonitions, there are annotations. Over twenty years, governance has been put in order and moral instruction established: the duties of ruler and teacher have truly both been fulfilled to the utmost. Previously, he established the Temple of Emperors and Kings in the capital, where sacrifices are invariably offered each year, showing his understanding of the succession of rightful governance. …the sages of the past and continuing the work of the imperial ancestor: these achievements may indeed be called magnificent. Is this not the season when spring advances into summer, when origination advances into flourishing? Yet I have heard that the Way is the foundation of government. The Way of the Book of Documents lies in centrality; the Way of the Spring and Autumn Annals lies in rectitude. Refinement and single-mindedness are the means of holding fast to the mean; appointing the virtuous and punishing the guilty are the means of abiding in rectitude. Here precisely lie the essential teaching for transmitting the mind through countless ages and the foundation of Heaven’s allotted succession. With the humble sincerity of one offering celery or the warmth of the sun, I wish to submit this through you, honored officials.

The foundation of the state lies in the heir apparent. The methods by which the wise kings of antiquity assisted and nurtured their heirs are abundantly documented. His Majesty has now first established the household of the heir apparent and carefully selected its staff. His care in making a proper beginning and preserving the greatness of the dynasty, thereby securing boundless blessings, is seen but once in a thousand years. This policy essay weighs ancient and present practices and fully extols these magnificent achievements. 以有齒冑之禮其職固典樂之所專后夔
之所司也且周官師氏教國子以三德三
punctuated:
上身教之功，而望以后夔、周召之助。子之見，非書生也。

考試官左庶子童批：輔儲之道，於今爲切。職守、人品，則所當豫講者。是策敷對詳明，而周官教冑之意，尤爲得之。末復有意於周召之業，知非凡近士也。

教本之地，翊贊之官，審諭之才，不可以不慎也。古之明王率重乎此，而後世職之脩廢、人之得失，恒弗齊焉。何者？制度略而體統昧，習華寵而忽事守也。是故其職明，其業可得而修矣；其人賢，其職可得而盡矣。

執事策士，以宮臣爲問，愚以是知非出位之思也。昔者周公之輔成王，其歷年久，而勞勳甚眾也。至其建官分職，自朝廷以及比閭，纖悉畢具，而元子不爲置官，雖有六傅，不爲置屬，又何簡也？《記》曰：「虞夏商周，有師保，有疑丞，設四輔及三公，不必備，唯其人。」蓋古者天子之元子、眾子皆入太學，是以有齒胄之禮。其職固典樂之所專，后夔之所司也。且《周官》師氏教國子以三德、三

…the efficacy of His Majesty’s teaching by personal example, and hopes for assistance such as that provided by Hou Kui and the Dukes of Zhou and Shao. Your insight is no mere bookish scholar’s.

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Secretariat Supervisor: The way to assist the heir apparent is a pressing concern today. Official duties and personal character are matters that ought to be discussed beforehand. This policy essay presents its response clearly and thoroughly, and particularly well grasps the intent of educating noble scions in the Offices of Zhou. Its conclusion also aspires to the achievements of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao: this shows that its author is no ordinary, shallow scholar.

The position at the foundation of moral instruction, the officials charged with assisting it, and the talent required for discerning instruction must all be treated with care. The enlightened kings of antiquity generally attached great importance to these matters. In later ages, however, the performance or neglect of duties and the success or failure of personnel selection were persistently uneven. Why was this? Institutions were sketchy and the structure of authority unclear; men grew accustomed to splendor and favor and neglected their responsibilities. Thus, when duties are clearly defined, the work can be properly carried out; when the men are worthy, their duties can be fully discharged.

You gentlemen, in examining scholars through policy questions, have asked about the officials of the heir apparent’s palace. From this I understand that such reflections do not exceed the bounds of one’s station. In former times, the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng for many years and rendered very many distinguished services. When he established offices and apportioned duties, every detail was provided for, from the court down to the neighborhood units. Yet he established no separate offices for the eldest son; even though there were six tutors, he appointed no subordinate staff for them. Why, then, such simplicity? The Record of Rites says: “Under Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou, there were preceptors and protectors, advisers and assistants. The Four Aides and the Three Dukes were established, but their posts did not have to be fully staffed: what mattered was finding the right men.” In antiquity, the Son of Heaven’s eldest son and his other sons all entered the Imperial University. Hence there was a rite by which noble scions took their places according to age. This responsibility belonged specifically to the Director of Music: it was the charge of Hou Kui. Moreover, in the Offices of Zhou, the Preceptor instructs the sons of the state in the three virtues and the three…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
行即教以事而喻諸德者也保氏養國子
以六藝六儀即慎其身以輔翼之而歸諸
道者也故師保謂之三公充其數則有傳
疑丞謂之四輔充其數則有輔弼至於庶
子之官職諸侯卿大夫士之庶子之倅國
有大事則率國子而致於太子惟所用之
是周之教太子其與胄子國子一也故官
簡而禮尊制詳而情洽其曰將以君我而
與我齒讓何也則虞廷典樂之意猶有存
===
者矣秦漢而下勢日遠而情日間故官不
得不備而先王之法於是乎弛遂使養老
乞言承師問道之禮卒不可復見也其後
陵夷雖官屬之建亦或闕略惟唐六典倣
周官之意而立之儲賓宮采其制稍備職
守之專差可考見故以道德輔教凡動靜
起居皆可以法此其屬三師之職也奉太
子以觀三師之道德此其屬三少之職也
侍從規諫而先後焉此其屬賓客之職也

punctuated: 行，即教以事而喻諸德者也。保氏養國子以六藝、六儀，即慎其身以輔翼之而歸諸道者也。故師保謂之三公，充其數則有傳；疑丞謂之四輔，充其數則有輔弼。至於庶子之官，職諸侯卿大夫士之庶子之倅。國有大事，則率國子而致於太子，惟所用之。是周之教太子，其與胄子、國子一也。故官簡而禮尊，制詳而情洽。其曰：「將以君我，而與我齒讓，何也？」則虞廷典樂之意猶有存者矣。秦漢而下，勢日遠而情日間，故官不得不備，而先王之法於是乎弛，遂使養老乞言、承師問道之禮卒不可復見也。其後陵夷，雖官屬之建亦或闕略。惟《唐六典》倣《周官》之意而立之，儲賓宮采，其制稍備，職守之專差可考見。故以道德輔教，凡動靜起居皆可以法，此其屬三師之職也；奉太子以觀三師之道德，此其屬三少之職也；侍從規諫而先後焉，此其屬賓客之職也。
translation_en:
…forms of conduct: this means teaching through practical affairs and thereby imparting an understanding of virtue. The Protector nurtured the sons of the state through the Six Arts and Six Ceremonial Forms: this meant conducting himself carefully so as to support and guide them, bringing them to the Way. Thus the Grand Preceptor and Grand Guardian were called the Three Dukes, with the Grand Tutor [?] completing their number; the Adviser and Assistant were called the Four Auxiliaries, with the Supporter and Corrector completing their number. As for the officer responsible for younger sons, he supervised the younger sons of the feudal lords, ministers, grand masters, and servicemen who served as deputies. Whenever the state had a great undertaking, he led the sons of the state to the heir apparent, to be employed as needed. Thus, under the Zhou, the heir apparent received the same education as the sons of noble houses and the sons of the state. Accordingly, the offices were few, yet ritual was honored; the arrangements were detailed, yet relations were harmonious. The saying, “He is to rule over us, yet he yields precedence to us according to age—why is this?” shows that something of the intent behind the Director of Music at the court of Shun still survived.

From the Qin and Han onward, differences in status increasingly separated people, and their feelings grew increasingly estranged. Thus a full complement of offices became indispensable, while the methods of the former kings fell into disuse. Consequently, the rites of nourishing the aged and soliciting their counsel, and of attending upon teachers and inquiring about the Way, ultimately ceased to be seen. Thereafter, as institutions declined, even the establishment of subordinate offices was sometimes incomplete. Only the Six Statutes of the Tang, modeled on the intent of the Offices of Zhou, established these arrangements. In its provision for the heir apparent’s guests and palace officers [?], its system was fairly complete, and the distinct responsibilities of its offices can be ascertained to some extent. Thus, assisting in instruction through the Way and virtue, with every movement and stillness, rising and retiring, serving as a model: this was assigned to the Three Preceptors. Attending upon the heir apparent so that he might observe the Way and virtue of the Three Preceptors: this was assigned to the Three Junior Preceptors. Accompanying him, admonishing and remonstrating with him, and attending before and behind him: this was assigned to the Advisers.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
統其綱紀而修其職務此其屬詹事之職
也贊相駁正而獻納此其屬庶子之職而
中允副之者也諭以道德隨事規諷此其
屬諭德之職也陳古以箴此其屬贊善之
職也彈劾糾舉規諫駁正此其屬司直司
議之職而司議即今之司諫也掌圖書備
供進此其屬洗馬之職也校理刊正此其
屬校書正字之職也宮臣之制庶幾備矣
朱子所為善之者也至於其人則宿德隆
===
望鴻名嘉績炳然方冊盖可考焉於周則
明堂之位曰篤信而好學多聞而道順者
是周公也誠立而敢斷輔善而相義者是
太公也廉潔而切直匡過而諫邪者是召
公也博聞彊記捷給而善對者是史佚也
於漢則四皓之羽翼也張良之忠義也叔
孫通之禮儀也疏廣之勇决也石奮之恭
謹也王商之肅敬也鮑勛之清白也桓榮
之經術也於唐則長孫無忌房玄齡之勛

謹也王商之肅敬也鮑勛之清白也桓榮
之經術也於唐則長孫無忌房玄齡之勛
punctuated:
統其綱紀而修其職務，此其屬詹事之職也；贊相駁正而獻納，此其屬庶子之職，而中允副之者也；諭以道德，隨事規諷，此其屬諭德之職也；陳古以箴，此其屬贊善之職也；彈劾糾舉，規諫駁正，此其屬司直司議之職，而司議即今之司諫也；掌圖書，備供進，此其屬洗馬之職也；校理刊正，此其屬校書正字之職也。宮臣之制庶幾備矣，朱子所為善之者也。
至於其人，則宿德隆望，鴻名嘉績，炳然方冊，盖可考焉。於周，則明堂之位曰：「篤信而好學，多聞而道順者，是周公也；誠立而敢斷，輔善而相義者，是太公也；廉潔而切直，匡過而諫邪者，是召公也；博聞彊記，捷給而善對者，是史佚也。」於漢，則四皓之羽翼也，張良之忠義也，叔孫通之禮儀也，疏廣之勇决也，石奮之恭謹也，王商之肅敬也，鮑勛之清白也，桓榮之經術也。於唐，則長孫無忌房玄齡之勛
translation_en:
…To oversee its order and discipline and attend to its duties belonged to the Household Administrator (zhanshi). To assist, correct errors, and present advice belonged to the Secretariat Supervisors (shuzi), with the Palace Secretaries (zhongyun) as their deputies. To instruct through moral principle and virtue, offering admonition as circumstances arose, belonged to the Admonishers (yude). To invoke antiquity as a warning belonged to the Counselors (zanshan). To impeach and expose misconduct, remonstrate, and correct errors belonged to the Directors of Rectitude (sizhi) and Remonstrance Advisors (siyi); the latter correspond to today’s Remonstrators (sijian). To keep books and documents ready for presentation belonged to the Librarians (xima). To collate and correct texts belonged to the Collators (jiaoshu) and Proofreaders (zhengzi). The organization of the heir apparent’s officials was thus nearly complete. This was what Master Zhu approved.
As for the men themselves, their longstanding virtue, lofty reputations, great renown, and admirable achievements shine forth in the written records and can indeed be examined. For the Zhou, the account of positions in the Hall of Enlightenment states: “Firm in faith and devoted to learning, widely informed and compliant with the Way—such was Zhou Gong. Sincere and steadfast, daring in decision, supporting goodness and assisting righteousness—such was Tai Gong. Incorruptible and uncompromisingly forthright, correcting faults and remonstrating against wrongdoing—such was Shao Gong. Broadly learned and strong in memory, quick of speech and adept in reply—such was Shi Yi.” For the Han, there were the protective support of the Four Hoary Elders, Zhang Liang’s loyalty and righteousness, Shusun Tong’s command of ritual, Shu Guang’s courage and resolve, Shi Fen’s deference and circumspection, Wang Shang’s solemn reverence, Bao Xun’s unsullied integrity, and Huan Rong’s learning in the Classics. For the Tang, there were the meritorious achievements of Zhangsun Wuji and Fang Xuanling…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
德也李綱之慷慨也于志寧之規益也張
說褚無量之啓迪也吕元英之讜直也李
敬元之高峻也於宋則王陶韓維之厚德
也晏殊之謹密也魯宗道之忠實也朱震
范沖之極選也劉焞之問學也李彥穎之
操履也楊萬里之剛正也黃裳之端純也
婁機之正論也斯皆甲觀端府之英翼德
諭教之最著者也是故思其職則三師八
舍莫非弼亮者矣思其人則九德六行莫
===
非儀刑者矣故成王之未涖阼太公爲太
師常立于左周公爲太傅常立于前召公
爲太保常立於右史佚爲少師常立於後
故成王中立而寡於過周之所以長有道
也此其職之修而其人之聖且賢者也漢
興稍用秦制置詹事中庶子之官然多以
他官監護疏廣以爲示狹非所以廣太子
者也唐制雖備中多虛曠甚者疎賤之三
師保傅之官非眊聵不任事即休兵罷帥

也此其職之修而其人之聖且賢者也漢

師保傅之官非眊瞶不任事即休兵罷帥
punctuated:
德也，李綱之慷慨也，于志寧之規益也，張說、褚無量之啓迪也，吕元英之讜直也，李敬元之高峻也。於宋則王陶、韓維之厚德也，晏殊之謹密也，魯宗道之忠實也，朱震、范沖之極選也，劉焞之問學也，李彥穎之操履也，楊萬里之剛正也，黃裳之端純也，婁機之正論也。斯皆甲觀端府之英，翼德諭教之最著者也。是故思其職，則三師八舍莫非弼亮者矣；思其人，則九德六行莫非儀刑者矣。
故成王之未涖阼，太公爲太師，常立于左；周公爲太傅，常立于前；召公爲太保，常立於右；史佚爲少師，常立於後。故成王中立而寡於過。周之所以長，有道也。此其職之修，而其人之聖且賢者也。
漢興，稍用秦制，置詹事、中庶子之官，然多以他官監護。疏廣以爲示狹，非所以廣太子者也。唐制雖備，中多虛曠，甚者疎賤之。三師保傅之官，非眊聵不任事，即休兵罷帥
translation_en:
…and virtue; Li Gang’s high-minded resolve; Yu Zhining’s beneficial admonitions; Zhang Yue’s and Chu Wuliang’s enlightening instruction; Lü Yuanying’s forthrightness; and Li Jingyuan’s lofty integrity. Under the Song there were Wang Tao’s and Han Wei’s abundant virtue; Yan Shu’s circumspection and discretion; Lu Zongdao’s loyalty and sincerity; Zhu Zhen and Fan Chong, men of the choicest calibre; Liu Tun’s learning and inquiry; Li Yanying’s moral conduct; Yang Wanli’s firmness and uprightness; Huang Shang’s rectitude and purity; and Lou Ji’s sound counsel. These were all outstanding men of the heir apparent’s household, most distinguished in fostering virtue and providing instruction. Thus, considering their offices, the Three Preceptors and the eight attendants were all helpers and guides; considering the men themselves, all exemplified the nine virtues and six forms of conduct.
Before King Cheng ascended the throne, the Grand Duke served as Grand Preceptor and always stood on his left; the Duke of Zhou served as Grand Mentor and always stood before him; the Duke of Shao served as Grand Guardian and always stood on his right; and Shi Yi served as Junior Preceptor and always stood behind him. Thus King Cheng stood in their midst and seldom erred. There was a sound principle behind the Zhou dynasty’s longevity. Here were offices whose duties were fulfilled, and men who were sages and worthies.
When the Han arose, it adopted parts of the Qin system, establishing the offices of Household Administrator and Middle Companion to the Heir Apparent, yet often assigned officials holding other posts to supervise and protect him. Shu Guang considered this a display of narrowness, no way to broaden the heir apparent’s outlook. Although the Tang system was comprehensive, many of its offices remained vacant; worse still, they were treated with neglect and contempt. The offices of the Three Preceptors, guardians, and mentors were occupied either by men too dim-sighted and deaf to conduct affairs or by commanders relieved of military service and dismissed from command…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者處焉故其始也馬周以位高恨不得爲
司議郎其末也賓諭贊議之秩以爲疎冗
散賤縉紳至耻之如元稹所云可慨也宋
制尤簡陋春坊僅用武弁之小才其次纔
講讀數員而贊善大夫諸官又爲散階而
非實職神宗以六典改官制而不備如此
朱子有深慨焉若夫秦始使趙高以刑名
傅胡亥故今日即位而明日射人漢文使
鼂錯以術數教景帝因致七國之變梁徐
庾諸人競爲浮豔之詞號曰宮體而無益
臺城之禍至如隋之唐敬則請奏琵琶唐
之唐儉趙元鼎操刀膾腥則自比於割烹
優伶之事尚望其弼諧明德繩糾愆過哉
故知職之修廢人之得失其繫甚重也昔
者趙王欲傅周紹而紹辭曰立傅之道六
智慮不躁達於變身行寬惠達於禮威嚴
不足以易於位重利不足以變其心恭於
教而不快和於下而不危而臣無一焉以

朱子有深慨焉若夫秦始使趙高以刑名
傅胡亥故今日即位而明日射人漢文使
鼂錯以術數教景帝因致七國之變梁徐
===
庾諸人競爲浮豔之詞號曰宮體而無益
臺城之禍至如隋之唐敬則請奏琵琶唐
之唐儉趙元昕操刀膾腥則自比於割烹
優伶之事尚望其弼諧明德繩糾愆過哉
故知職之修廢人之得失其繫甚重也昔
者趙王欲傅周紹而紹辭曰立傅之道六
智慮不躁達於變身行寬惠達於禮威嚴
不足以易於位重利不足以變其心恭於
教而不快和於下而不危而臣無一焉以
punctuated:
者處焉。故其始也，馬周以位高恨不得爲司議郎；其末也，賓諭贊議之秩，以爲疎冗散賤，縉紳至耻之，如元稹所云，可慨也。宋制尤簡陋，春坊僅用武弁之小才，其次纔講讀數員，而贊善大夫諸官又爲散階，而非實職。神宗以六典改官制，而不備如此，朱子有深慨焉。
若夫秦始使趙高以刑名傅胡亥，故今日即位而明日射人；漢文使鼂錯以術數教景帝，因致七國之變；梁徐庾諸人競爲浮豔之詞，號曰宮體，而無益臺城之禍。至如隋之唐敬則請奏琵琶，唐之唐儉、趙元鼎操刀膾腥，則自比於割烹優伶之事，尚望其弼諧明德、繩糾愆過哉？故知職之修廢、人之得失，其繫甚重也。
昔者趙王欲傅周紹，而紹辭曰：「立傅之道六：智慮不躁，達於變；身行寬惠，達於禮；威嚴不足以易於位；重利不足以變其心；恭於教而不快；和於下而不危。而臣無一焉。」以
translation_en:
…held these positions. Thus, in the early Tang, Ma Zhou regretted that his rank was too high for him to become a Remonstrance Secretary. By its end, the posts of Guest Adviser, Admonisher, Companion, and Remonstrance Secretary were regarded as superfluous, idle, and lowly appointments; officials even felt ashamed to hold them, as Yuan Zhen remarked. This is lamentable. The Song arrangements were still more rudimentary. The Spring Offices of the heir apparent employed only military officers of modest ability, with merely a few lecturers and readers below them. Posts such as Grand Master as Companion were moreover honorary ranks rather than substantive offices. Emperor Shenzong reformed the official system according to the Six Statutes, yet it remained incomplete to this extent. Master Zhu deeply lamented this.
As for the First Emperor of Qin, he had Zhao Gao tutor Hu Hai in punishments and administrative accountability; consequently, Hu Hai took the throne one day and shot people the next. Emperor Wen of Han had Chao Cuo teach Emperor Jing techniques of statecraft, which brought about the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms. Under the Liang, the Xu and Yu writers competed in composing frivolous, ornate verse, calling it “palace style,” but this did nothing to avert the disaster at Taicheng. As for Tang Jingze of the Sui requesting to play the pipa, or Tang Jian and Zhao Yuanding of the Tang wielding knives to slice raw meat, they reduced themselves to the work of cooks and entertainers. Could one still expect them to assist in cultivating illustrious virtue and to correct faults and transgressions? We can therefore see that whether these offices are properly maintained or allowed to lapse, and whether suitable or unsuitable men fill them, has consequences of the utmost gravity.
Formerly, the king of Zhao wished to appoint Zhou Shao as tutor, but Shao declined, saying: “There are six principles governing the appointment of a tutor: his judgment must be free from rashness, and he must understand changing circumstances; his conduct must be generous and benevolent, and he must understand ritual propriety; intimidating authority must not suffice to make him abandon his position; great profit must not suffice to change his heart; he must be conscientious in teaching without impatience [?]; and he must be harmonious toward those below without causing danger [?]. Yet your servant possesses none of these qualities.” Given …

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
趙之小紹之陋皆不足道然可謂知本矣
唐元稹之為教本書也而曰目不得閱淫
豔妖誘之色耳不得聞優笑陵亂之聲口
不得習操斷擊搏之書居不得近容陰順
邪之黨游不得恣追禽戮獸之樂翫不得
愛遐異僻絕之珍稹文士也非有道德之
實然亦可謂知要矣故立傅教本之道不
止於此而此其略也盖能選傅斯得人矣
能得人斯盡職矣故道之敦厚以體仁道
===
之剛毅以立義道之辭讓以隆禮道之辨
別以明智道之果確以守信道之嚴畏以
篤忠道之親愛以致孝道之經緯以昭文
道之戡定以修武道之彊健以務勤道之
撙節以崇儉道之恭敬以盡誠此教本之
道也故得一周公則無剪桐之戲矣得一
太公則鮑魚不登於俎矣故曰練左右急
也我
太祖宫臣之建稍倣六典詹事坊局先後創置

也我
太祖官臣之建稍倣六典詹事坊局先後創置
punctuated:
趙之小，紹之陋，皆不足道，然可謂知本矣。唐元稹之為《教本書》也，而曰：「目不得閱淫豔妖誘之色，耳不得聞優笑陵亂之聲，口不得習操斷擊搏之書，居不得近容陰順邪之黨，游不得恣追禽戮獸之樂，翫不得愛遐異僻絕之珍。」稹，文士也，非有道德之實，然亦可謂知要矣。故立傅教本之道，不止於此，而此其略也。盖能選傅，斯得人矣；能得人，斯盡職矣。故道之敦厚以體仁，道之剛毅以立義，道之辭讓以隆禮，道之辨別以明智，道之果確以守信，道之嚴畏以篤忠，道之親愛以致孝，道之經緯以昭文，道之戡定以修武，道之彊健以務勤，道之撙節以崇儉，道之恭敬以盡誠，此教本之道也。故得一周公，則無剪桐之戲矣；得一太公，則鮑魚不登於俎矣。故曰：「練左右，急也。」
我太祖宫臣之建，稍倣六典，詹事坊局，先後創置。
translation_en:
…Zhao was a small state, and Shao a man of limited attainments; neither merits much discussion. Yet he may be said to have understood the foundation. When Yuan Zhen of the Tang wrote his Letter on the Foundations of Education, he said: “The eyes must not behold lascivious beauty or seductive sights; the ears must not hear the sounds of entertainers’ jests or disorderly clamor; the mouth must not rehearse writings on wielding power, making decisions, striking, and fighting [?]; one’s dwelling must not be near factions that harbor hidden schemes and comply with evil [?]; in excursions one must not indulge in the pleasures of pursuing birds and slaughtering beasts; in amusements one must not cherish rarities from distant and secluded places.” Zhen was a literary man, without substantial attainment in the Way and virtue, yet he too may be said to have understood the essentials. Thus, the principles of appointing tutors and establishing the foundations of education extend beyond these points, but these are their broad outlines. If one can select tutors properly, one will obtain the right men; if one obtains the right men, they will fully discharge their duties.
Thus, guide him toward generosity and sincerity, so that he embodies benevolence; toward firmness and resolution, so that he establishes righteousness; toward deference and yielding, so that he exalts ritual propriety; toward discrimination, so that he makes wisdom clear; toward decisiveness and certainty, so that he preserves trustworthiness; toward solemnity and reverence, so that he deepens loyalty; toward affection, so that he fulfills filial devotion; toward ordering and organizing, so that he manifests civil accomplishment; toward pacification, so that he cultivates martial accomplishment; toward strength and vigor, so that he applies himself diligently; toward restraint, so that he honors frugality; and toward respectfulness, so that he fully realizes sincerity. These are the principles underlying education. Thus, obtain a Duke of Zhou, and there will be no jest involving a cut paulownia leaf; obtain a Taigong, and salted fish will not be set upon the sacrificial stand. Hence the saying: “Carefully selecting those who attend him is urgent.”
When our Taizu established the offices of the palace staff, he modeled them to some extent on the Six Institutes, successively creating the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent and its secretariats and bureaus.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其在
朝廷詹事則六卿也坊局則侍從也司直清
紀司諫則諫垣也法制備矣而又
鑒前代之失每以近臣兼領并攝姦萌釁端無
由而起
聖謨神識萬世無弊者也廼者
皇上蚤建
東朝茂簡寮寀天下訢訢罔不歡戴
養蒙順巽以
===
身為教
父師之道蓋交盡焉然
龍姿鳳表日就岐嶷則講學輔德深培遠溉
且有日矣舜命夔曰直而温寬而栗剛而
無虐簡而無傲此德性之學也弼亮之職
莫要於此矣周公之無逸太公之敬義召
公之顧畏皆古聖人也儀刑之道宜莫先
焉漢唐宋諸君子不足期也名卿碩弼濟
濟在列愚非賈生也何足以知之

濟在列愚非賈生也何足以知之
punctuated:
其在朝廷，詹事則六卿也，坊局則侍從也，司直、清紀、司諫則諫垣也。法制備矣，而又鑒前代之失，每以近臣兼領并攝，姦萌釁端無由而起。聖謨神識，萬世無弊者也。
廼者皇上蚤建東朝，茂簡寮寀，天下訢訢，罔不歡戴。養蒙順巽，以身為教，父師之道蓋交盡焉。然龍姿鳳表，日就岐嶷，則講學輔德，深培遠溉，且有日矣。舜命夔曰：「直而温，寬而栗，剛而無虐，簡而無傲。」此德性之學也，弼亮之職莫要於此矣。周公之無逸，太公之敬義，召公之顧畏，皆古聖人也，儀刑之道宜莫先焉。漢唐宋諸君子不足期也。名卿碩弼，濟濟在列。愚非賈生也，何足以知之？
translation_en:
…In terms of their counterparts at the imperial court, the Household Administrator corresponds to the Six Ministers; the palace secretariats and bureaus correspond to the attendant officials; and the Rectifiers, Disciplinary Officers, and Remonstrators correspond to the remonstrance establishment. The institutional arrangements were complete. Moreover, taking warning from the failings of earlier dynasties, he regularly had close ministers concurrently direct and oversee these offices, leaving no opening for the seeds of treachery or causes of disorder to arise. Such sagely planning and divine discernment would remain free of harmful consequences for ten thousand generations.
Recently, Your Majesty established the heir apparent’s court at an early date and carefully selected its officials. All under Heaven rejoiced, and none failed to acclaim and support him. In nurturing the untutored prince with gentle guidance and teaching through personal example, you have fully fulfilled the duties of both father and teacher. Yet as his dragon-like bearing and phoenix-like appearance daily mature into exceptional intelligence, there will still be many days ahead for expounding learning and fostering virtue, cultivating deeply and irrigating far into the future. Shun instructed Kui: “Be upright yet mild, broad-minded yet stern, firm without cruelty, and straightforward without arrogance.” This is the learning that cultivates moral character; nothing is more essential to the duties of those who assist and guide the prince. The Duke of Zhou’s avoidance of ease, the Grand Duke’s reverence and righteousness, and the Duke of Shao’s vigilance and awe—all were ancient sages, and nothing should take precedence over following their example. The gentlemen of the Han, Tang, and Song are insufficient as the standard to aspire to. Renowned ministers and great counsellors stand in abundant ranks. I, in my ignorance, am no Jia Sheng: how could I presume to understand these matters?

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第三問
田應弼
同考試官教諭董批史之難其來乆矣中
膠者不偏則陋曲綴者不繆則浮故一関之市必立之平
旁言博藝匪聖曷折是策獨能淹貫數十家之言而該理
千百載之事取義於春秋考度於周禮精微不爽隱顯旁
通其有志於用世之學者而非可以經生目子矣
考試官左中允李批史非積學之士不能觀其
會通此篇上下古今援引斷證歷歷明盡子非博學而詳
===
說者邪
考試官左庶子童批夾漈之書其志甚偉而學
甚博大也經生率未易言子獨取數千年之法之事而商
榷焉其斯有志於會通者乎
文獻者述作之大者也會通者學術之大
者也夫因革存乎法而損益施焉理亂存
乎事而勸戒昭焉二者必資乎文獻文或
懼其繁而亂獻或懼其背而馳故必會紀
載之異同而爲之刪述通世次之上下而

translation_en:
Third Policy Question
Tian Yingbi

Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Instructor: The difficulty of writing history is longstanding. Those whose minds are rigidly fixed [?] are either biased or narrow; those who piece accounts together tortuously are either mistaken or superficial. Thus, even a market at a single barrier [?] must establish a standard of fairness. With diverse pronouncements and extensive learning, who but a sage can adjudicate? This policy essay alone comprehensively integrates the statements of several dozen schools and brings order to the events of hundreds and thousands of years. It draws its principles from the Spring and Autumn Annals and tests its standards against the Rites of Zhou. It is exact in subtle matters and connects the hidden with the manifest. You aspire to learning that can serve the world; you cannot be regarded merely as a student of the Classics.

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Only a scholar of accumulated learning can discern the interconnected whole of history. This essay ranges through ancient and recent times; its citations, judgments, and supporting evidence are clear and exhaustive in every particular. Are you not one who learns broadly and expounds in detail?

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Mentor to the Heir Apparent: The work of Jiaji shows a magnificent ambition and exceptionally broad learning. Ordinary students of the Classics generally find it difficult to discuss. You alone have taken up the institutions and events of several thousand years and critically examined them. Surely you aspire to comprehensive understanding?

Documentary and scholarly testimony is fundamental to historical composition; comprehensive understanding is fundamental to scholarship. Continuity and change reside in institutions, to which reductions and additions are applied; order and disorder reside in events, through which encouragements and warnings are made evident. Both necessarily depend on documentary and scholarly testimony. With documents, one may fear excessive profusion and confusion; with scholarly testimony, one may fear divergence and contradiction. title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
爲之編摩使法本於道而詳略具事原於
法而得失形然後往者可傳焉來者可徵
焉故文獻者天下之大述作也會通者天
下之大學術也孔子曰文獻不足故也又
曰觀其會通以行其典禮聖人之志豈不
可見哉請因明問而訂之昔軒轅受命倉
頡沮誦實居史職而文籍生焉三墳五典
八索九丘邈乎不可知已周官太史小史
內史外史皆掌書志而右史記言左史記
===
動則有專職出於言者法也出於動者事
也二者其職盖相通也故韓宣觀書而嘉
周禮在魯季札觀樂而歷嘆帝王之德豈
非文獻猶有存者哉孔子曰我欲觀夏道
是故之杞而不足徵也吾得夏時焉我欲
觀殷道是故之宋而不足徵也吾得坤乾
焉盖思有以會通之也於是定禮樂刪詩
書賛周易修春秋總二帝三王之法而會
於一人貫唐虞三代之事而通於一家然

焉蓋思有以會通之也於是定禮樂刪詩

…and compile and arrange them, so that institutions are grounded in the Way and presented in both outline and detail, while events are traced to institutions and their successes and failures made manifest. Only then can the past be transmitted and those who come later find evidence to consult. Thus, documentary and learned testimony constitutes the world's great undertaking of historical composition; comprehensive synthesis constitutes the world's great scholarly endeavor. Confucius said, “It is because documentary and learned testimony is insufficient.” He also said, “Observe their convergences and connections, in order to carry out their established rites.” Can we not see the sage's intention here? Allow me to examine this in response to your illuminating question.

In antiquity, when Xuanyuan received the mandate, Cang Jie and Ju Song held the offices of scribes, and written records came into being. The Three Tombs, Five Canons, Eight Cords, and Nine Mounds are so remote that their contents can no longer be known. Among the Zhou officials, the Grand Scribe, Minor Scribe, Interior Scribe, and Exterior Scribe all had charge of written records. The Scribe of the Right recorded words, and the Scribe of the Left recorded deeds: each had a specialized duty. What issued in words was institutions; what issued in deeds was events. The duties of these two offices were therefore interconnected. Thus Han Xuan, on viewing the records, praised the preservation of Zhou ritual in Lu; and Ji Zha, on viewing musical performances, successively acclaimed the virtues of the emperors and kings. Was this not because documentary and learned testimony still survived?

Confucius said, “I wished to observe the Way of Xia, and therefore went to Qi, but there was insufficient evidence. I obtained the Seasons of Xia there. I wished to observe the Way of Yin, and therefore went to Song, but there was insufficient evidence. I obtained the Kun-Qian there.” He was evidently seeking a means of bringing these materials into a comprehensive synthesis. Accordingly, he established rites and music, edited the Odes and Documents, elucidated the Changes of Zhou, and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals. He gathered the institutions of the Two Emperors and Three Kings together in one person, and connected the events of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties within a single scholarly tradition. Thus…

…[Illegible] the writings of past and present, and fully explored the transformations of past and present; the [illegible] of all ages would draw their evidence from this. Subsequently, Qin burned the Odes and Documents and buried Confucian scholars alive; the textual and learned tradition survived by only a thread. When the Han arose, it gradually restored and collected this legacy. What elderly scholars and women transmitted, and what emerged from ruined walls and damaged tombs, barely remained in circulation after the ravages of flames and cruel punishments. Sima Qian thereupon looked back to the intentions of Zhongni (Confucius). He brought together the accounts in the Odes, Documents, Zuo Commentary, Discourses of the States, Genealogical Records (Shiben), Strategies of the Warring States, and Annals of Chu and Han, encompassing the eras of the Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun, the Three Dynasties, the Seven States, Qin, and Han. He composed the Records of the Grand Historian, comprising twenty Basic Annals [?], ten Tables, eight Treatises, thirty Hereditary Houses, and seventy Biographies. Discriminating without being ornate, plain without being vulgar, his writing was straightforward and his account of events soundly grounded. He neither bestowed unfounded praise nor concealed wrongdoing. His work, too, was a faithful record of the textual and learned tradition from antiquity onward.
Ban Gu’s History of the Han followed Qian’s precedents throughout. Neither extravagant nor eccentric, neither unduly disparaging nor unduly exalting, it was ample without being cluttered, detailed yet well ordered. Its author could be ranked next to the Grand Historian. Yet Su Xun, in praising Qian and Gu, said: “Implicit yet revealing, straightforward yet generous, concise yet clear, subtle yet incisive.” Gu, in criticizing Qian, said: “He gives precedence to the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi over the Six Classics, relegates scholars who remain out of office while advancing unscrupulous men of power, and esteems power and profit while treating low station and poverty as shameful.” Fu Xuan, in criticizing Gu, said: “He glosses over his ruler’s faults and disparages loyal ministers, prizes currying favor and disdains upright integrity, and attends carefully to literary expression while slighting the facts.” Although their merits and shortcomings are evident on both sides, Qian was indeed Gu’s model. 復會通故一帝而數紀一人而數傳天文
出於璿璣方域定於禹貢五行本於洪範
而每代作志郡邑各為區別禮樂自為更
張此表志之未同者也居攝不附於漢平

東南謂北為索虜北謂南為島夷尊中興

收以爾朱可方伊霍房彥謙以玄齡而擅

世踵之，人出新論，家立異見，紛紜錯雜，無復會通。故一帝而數紀，一人而數傳。天文出於《璿璣》，方域定於《禹貢》，五行本於《洪範》，而每代作志，郡邑各為區別，禮樂自為更張，此表志之未同者也。居攝不附於漢平，孺子下列於新莽；抑聖公於傳內，登文叔於紀首；帝曹魏而寇蜀漢，帝朱梁而寇河東；南謂北為索虜，北謂南為島夷；尊中興則黜永元，顯義寧則隱大業，錄光宅則略嗣聖，此本紀之未同者也。班固深排賈誼，范曄虛美隗囂，陳壽謂諸葛不逮管蕭，魏收以爾朱可方伊霍；房彥謙以玄齡而擅名，虞荔、虞寄以世南而立傳。甚者，晉史黨司馬氏，而魏之王凌、諸葛誕、毌丘儉遂為叛臣；齊史黨蕭氏，而宋之袁粲、劉秉、沈攸之遂為逆賊。此列傳之未同者也。
王通氏曰：「遷固而下，帝王之道暗而不明，天人之意否而不交，制理者叅而不一，陳事者亂
translation_en:
…successive generations followed this practice. Each person advanced new arguments, and each school established divergent views, producing a confused jumble with no further comprehensive integration. Thus a single emperor appears in several sets of annals, and a single person in several biographies. Astronomy derives from the Jade Armillary Sphere (Xuanji) [?], territorial divisions are established in the Tribute of Yu (Yu gong), and the Five Phases are grounded in the Great Plan (Hong fan). Yet each dynasty compiled its own treatises, distinguished commanderies and counties differently, and made its own changes to rites and music. These are the inconsistencies in the tables and treatises. The Jushe regency period is not appended to Emperor Ping of Han; the child ruler Ruzi is instead placed under Wang Mang of Xin. Shenggong is relegated to a biography, while Wenshu is elevated to the head of the annals. Cao Wei is accorded imperial legitimacy while Shu Han is treated as a bandit regime; Zhu Liang is accorded imperial legitimacy while Hedong is treated as a bandit regime. The south calls the northerners “queue-wearing barbarians,” while the north calls the southerners “island barbarians.” To honor the Zhongxing reign is to demote Yongyuan; to give prominence to Yining is to obscure Daye; to record Guangzhai is to slight Sisheng. These are the inconsistencies in the basic annals. Ban Gu harshly disparaged Jia Yi; Fan Ye praised Wei Xiao without foundation. Chen Shou held that Zhuge Liang fell short of Guan Zhong and Xiao He; Wei Shou considered Erzhu Rong comparable to Yi Yin and Huo Guang. Fang Yanqian attained renown because of Fang Xuanling, while Yu Li and Yu Ji received biographies because of Yu Shinan. Worse still, the history of Jin favored the Sima house, and so Wang Ling, Zhuge Dan, and Guanqiu Jian of Wei became rebellious ministers; the history of Qi favored the Xiao house, and so Yuan Can, Liu Bing, and Shen Youzhi of Song became traitorous rebels. These are the inconsistencies in the collected biographies.
Master Wang Tong said: “From Sima Qian and Ban Gu onward, the Way of emperors and kings has been obscured rather than illuminated, and the intentions of Heaven and humanity have been blocked from communicating with one another. Those who set forth principles of governance are divided rather than united; those who recount events are confused …
