唐杜佑作《通典》，自上古以終天寶，盖以《政典》爲未盡，而叅益《新禮》，統二百卷。說者謂其綱領宏大，考訂該洽。然節目未備，而備者頗欠精當。至若馬總之《通曆》、宋白之《續通典》，大抵皆經制之書也。元馬端臨乃廣佑之九門，曰天文，曰地理，曰禮樂，曰兵刑，曰財用，曰職官，曰學校，曰封建，曰戶口，爲二十
translation_en:
…and lack coherent order. Works such as these may reasonably be called lacking in substantiation. Wu Jun of the Liang compiled the General History (Tongshi), extending from the very beginning of time to the end of the Qi dynasty. He principally followed the Records of the Grand Historian, supplementing it with the annals and biographies of the two Han dynasties, in a total of 620 juan. Commentators said that it connected earlier and later ages throughout and that its parts shared a common spirit. Yet its biographies remained unfinished, and what had been completed was subsequently destroyed by fire. As for Song Xiang’s Comprehensive Chronological Register (Tongpu) and Zhang Heng’s Comprehensive Record (Tongzai), these were, by and large, works arranged by year. Sima Guang then drew upon the sixteen histories—those of the Zhou, Qin, Han, Six Dynasties, Sui, Tang, and Five Dynasties—and gathered the order and disorder of more than 1,300 years into a single work, entitled the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian). Its good examples could serve as models, and its bad examples as warnings. Emperor Shenzong wrote in his preface at the time: “Comprehensive yet grasping the essentials, concise yet encompassing events in full: a gathering of exemplary precedents, a vast repository of written records.” Is this not a work that draws upon historical events to bring them together into a coherent whole?

Du You of the Tang compiled the Comprehensive Institutions (Tongdian), extending from high antiquity to the end of the Tianbao era. Considering the Compendium of Government (Zhengdian) incomplete, he supplemented it with material from the New Rites (Xinli), producing a total of 200 juan. Commentators said that its overall framework was expansive and its critical examination comprehensive. Yet its detailed provisions were incomplete, and those that were included often lacked precision and sound judgment. As for Ma Zong’s Comprehensive Chronology (Tongli) and Song Bai’s Continuation of the Comprehensive Institutions (Xu Tongdian), these were, by and large, works on governmental institutions. Ma Duanlin of the Yuan then expanded Du You’s nine categories—astronomy, geography, rites and music, military affairs and punishments, finance, official posts, schools, enfeoffment, and households and population—into twenty…

text:
四目粹爲一書號曰通考本之經史而可
據會之典禮而可行當時儒臣稱之曰纂
集今古殫盡精力濟世之儒有用之學此
非取諸其法而會通之者乎夫修史之難
無出於志故范曄無表而陳壽李延壽無
志溫公馬氏其學術非不能叅稽互考以
擅一代之述作盖溫公之鑑有意於本朝
之弊而馬氏之考亦所以備溫公之遺也
若宋鄭樵通志取上下數千百年之事與
===
法而並錄之盖有志於會通者其所撰二
十略自謂前十五略出其胸臆不涉諸儒
論議後五略雖本前人之典亦非諸史之
文自任盖不淺矣然今觀之器服失之疎
藝文失之贅校讐金石博物之技也昆虫
草木稗官之說也不可以言立法本紀世
家荒誕並述列傳載記繁蕪未刋不可以
言紀事且佑生唐貞元間通典所載止於
天寶樵乃全用佑文自宋以前闕而不續

四目，粹爲一書，號曰《通考》。本之經史而可據，會之典禮而可行。當時儒臣稱之曰：「纂集今古，殫盡精力，濟世之儒，有用之學。」此非取諸其法而會通之者乎？夫修史之難，無出於志，故范曄無表，而陳壽、李延壽無志。溫公、馬氏，其學術非不能叅稽互考，以擅一代之述作。盖溫公之《鑑》有意於本朝之弊，而馬氏之《考》亦所以備溫公之遺也。
若宋鄭樵《通志》，取上下數千百年之事與法而並錄之，盖有志於會通者。其所撰二十略，自謂前十五略出其胸臆，不涉諸儒論議；後五略雖本前人之典，亦非諸史之文，自任盖不淺矣。然今觀之，器服失之疎，藝文失之贅；校讐、金石，博物之技也；昆虫、草木，稗官之說也，不可以言立法。本紀、世家，荒誕並述；列傳、載記，繁蕪未刋，不可以言紀事。且佑生唐貞元間，《通典》所載止於天寶，樵乃全用佑文，自宋以前闕而不續，
translation_en:
…[twenty-]four categories, distilling them into a single work entitled Comprehensive Examination (Tongkao). Grounded in the classics and histories, it offers reliable evidence; bringing together institutional precedents and ritual rules, it offers guidance that can be put into practice. Confucian officials of the time praised it, saying: “Compiling past and present, exhausting his intellectual energies: a scholar who aids the world, a learning of practical use.” Is this not an instance of drawing upon institutions and comprehensively integrating them? In compiling history, nothing is more difficult than the treatises. Thus Fan Ye included no tables, while Chen Shou and Li Yanshou included no treatises. It was not that the learning of Duke Wen (Sima Guang) and Master Ma (Ma Duanlin) left them incapable of comparing sources and checking them against one another to produce works preeminent in their age. Rather, Duke Wen’s Mirror was directed at the failings of his own dynasty, while Master Ma’s Examination also served to supply what Duke Wen had omitted.
As for the Comprehensive Treatises (Tongzhi) of Zheng Qiao of the Song, it records together the events and institutions of thousands of years: its author clearly aspired to comprehensive integration. Of the twenty summaries he composed, he himself said that the first fifteen arose from his own thinking and did not draw upon the discussions of other scholars; although the last five were based on earlier authorities’ institutional records, they too were not texts taken from the histories. His estimation of his own achievement was certainly considerable. Yet, viewed now, the treatment of utensils and dress is too sketchy, and that of writings too prolix. Textual collation and the study of bronze and stone inscriptions are techniques of antiquarian learning; accounts of insects and plants belong to the lore of minor unofficial writers. These cannot be called the establishment of institutional principles. In the basic annals and hereditary houses, fantastic tales are recounted indiscriminately; in the biographies and records of regional regimes, prolix and extraneous material remains unpruned. These cannot be called the proper recording of events. Moreover, Du You lived during the Tang’s Zhenyuan era, yet the Comprehensive Institutions (Tongdian) records matters only down to the Tianbao era. Zheng Qiao nevertheless adopted Du You’s text wholesale, leaving a gap in the period before the Song without supplying a continuation…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
謂非諸史之文不可也樵譏遷采摭未備
又譏固專事剽竊至其所自爲書不免蹈
之述作豈易言哉夫百川異趨而不歸於
海則汎濫之流也萬國殊軌而不通於華
則壅塞之途也世儒博稽載籍習誦古今
而無以會通之亦豈折衷之論適用之道
哉學者於通鑑究其事而折以孔子之春
秋則理亂明而勸戒可昭矣於通考酌其
法而證以周官之六典則因革當而損益
===
可施矣其於通志事苟未公以是而斷之
法苟未明以是而核之芟其蕪而補其闕
刋其誤而正其訛以弘天下之學術以備
天下之述作以成天下之治道如濟險之
舟而不眩於衆流也如指南之車而不迷
於多岐也則經世之具通儒之業庶幾盡
矣雖然帝王之所同者心也所不同者跡
也跡固以文獻而存心則無俟於會通而
得故傳心之要千聖相授守一道其事其

translation_en:
…it cannot be claimed that these are not passages from the various histories. Zheng Qiao criticized Sima Qian for collecting material incompletely, and also criticized Ban Gu for doing nothing but plagiarizing; yet in the book he himself composed, he could not avoid falling into the same faults. How could historical composition be spoken of lightly! If the hundred rivers take different courses but do not reach the sea, they become overflowing streams; if the myriad states follow different routes but have no passage to the Chinese heartland, their roads are blocked. Scholars broadly investigate written records and become practiced in reciting accounts of past and present; yet if they have no means of comprehending and integrating them, how can theirs be balanced judgments or practically useful methods?
Scholars should investigate the events in the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian) and judge them against Confucius’s Spring and Autumn Annals. Then the causes of order and disorder will become clear, and encouragements and warnings can be made manifest. They should weigh the institutions in the Comprehensive Examination (Tongkao) and verify them against the six canons of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan). Then decisions about retaining or changing institutions will be appropriate, and additions and reductions can be put into effect. As for the Comprehensive Treatises (Tongzhi), where its accounts of events lack impartiality, they should judge them by these standards; where its treatment of institutions lacks clarity, they should examine it by these standards. They should prune its overgrowth and fill its omissions, expunge its errors and correct its inaccuracies, thereby broadening scholarship throughout the realm, bringing historical composition to completeness, and perfecting the way of government. Like a boat crossing dangerous waters without being bewildered by the many currents, or a south-pointing carriage that does not lose its way among many branching roads, they would then come close to fully realizing the means of ordering the world and the work of a comprehensively learned scholar.
Nevertheless, what emperors and kings share is their mind; what differs is the traces of their actions. Those traces are indeed preserved through documentary and learned testimony, but their mind can be apprehended without awaiting such comprehensive integration. Thus the essential teaching in transmitting the mind has been handed down from sage to sage, all adhering to one Way. As for their affairs and their…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
法則時之隆汙人之存亡繫焉孔子曰殷
因於夏禮所損益可知也周因於殷禮所
損益可知也其或繼周者雖百世可知也
然則所因者心也所損益者跡也而勸戒
之實亦不外是矣故事本於法法本於道
道本於心此又會通之要也敢以是復
第四問
劉一麟
同考試官教諭林批三代以下人物如數
子者亦難矣惜塲中作者往往掇拾舊聞可否由人瑕瑜
失實令人厭觀惟此作直遡其心源要其始末權其重輕
出獨見會公理破陳詞立新案一字一句有不容移易者
數子可作當為之俯首矣偉哉文乎
同考試官教諭湯批評品人物正欲觀士
子之學識也塲中作者聞見不真類造迂說以厚誣古人
者多矣子能原其時勢所遇証以先正格論而復叅以己
意俾古人心事庶暴白於天下公恕之心諒不失為君子
其視過為矯激者不侔矣宜錄以為尚論古人者式

法，則時之隆汙、人之存亡繫焉。孔子曰：「殷因於夏禮，所損益可知也；周因於殷禮，所損益可知也。其或繼周者，雖百世，可知也。」然則所因者心也，所損益者跡也，而勸戒之實亦不外是矣。故事本於法，法本於道，道本於心，此又會通之要也。敢以是復。

第四問
劉一麟

同考試官教諭林批：三代以下，人物如數子者亦難矣。惜塲中作者往往掇拾舊聞，可否由人，瑕瑜失實，令人厭觀。惟此作直遡其心源，要其始末，權其重輕，出獨見，會公理，破陳詞，立新案，一字一句有不容移易者。數子可作，當為之俯首矣。偉哉，文乎！

同考試官教諭湯批：評品人物，正欲觀士子之學識也。塲中作者聞見不真，類造迂說，以厚誣古人者多矣。子能原其時勢所遇，証以先正格論，而復叅以己意，俾古人心事庶暴白於天下。公恕之心，諒不失為君子。其視過為矯激者不侔矣。宜錄以為尚論古人者式。
translation_en:
…methods, however, are bound up with the flourishing or decline of the age and the survival or loss of the people concerned. Confucius said: “The Yin followed the rites of the Xia; what they subtracted and added can be known. The Zhou followed the rites of the Yin; what they subtracted and added can be known. Should anyone succeed the Zhou, even a hundred generations hence, this can be known.” Thus, what is inherited is the heart; what is subtracted or added is its outward expression. The substance of encouragement and admonition likewise lies within this. Affairs are therefore rooted in methods, methods in the Way, and the Way in the heart. This, too, is essential to comprehensive understanding. I venture to offer this in reply.

Fourth Question
Liu Yilin

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: Since the Three Dynasties, men like these have been rare indeed. Regrettably, writers in the examination hall often merely glean familiar accounts, letting others determine their judgments of approval or disapproval. Their assessments of faults and virtues depart from the truth, making them tiresome to read. This essay alone traces these men’s intentions directly to their source, grasps their conduct from beginning to end, and weighs the relative importance of their actions. It offers independent insights that accord with impartial principles, overturns stale formulations, and establishes fresh judgments. There are words and sentences here that admit of no alteration. Could these men rise again, they would surely bow their heads before it. What a magnificent essay!

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: In asking candidates to appraise historical figures, our precise intention is to observe their learning and discernment. Many writers in the examination hall lack sound knowledge and concoct far-fetched arguments that gravely misrepresent the ancients. You can examine the circumstances of the times they encountered, substantiate your assessment with the authoritative judgments of earlier worthies, and then bring your own understanding to bear, so that the intentions of the ancients may at last be made clear to the world. With such an impartial and sympathetic heart, you surely merit the name of gentleman. Your work differs from that of those who go to excessive lengths in provocative judgments. It should be recorded as a model for those who aspire to discuss the ancients.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:

折衷衆論而意見和平不為過激詭隨之談子之所蘊從
可知也取之
考試官左庶子童批漢代人品如數子者其彰
明較著者也然評隲不一子能歷探其心公而恕覈而嚴
可與尚論古人矣
君子尚論古人當觀其建立之大節而不
可膠于是非之陳迹何則士君子効用明
時未嘗不欲策勳於當時流風於後世而
===
時之所遇有順逆勢之所遭有難易不能
盡如吾意者亦盡其在我而已至於是非
成敗非所計也苟千載而下不究其心而
據其迹不度其時而審其勢則古人之心
事荒矣夫豈尚論之公哉請因明問所及
而陳之漢之張良始終為韓篤春秋復讎
之義功成而退如鴻冥鳳舉三代而下出
處可觀未易得也故伊川南軒皆以為有
儒者氣象而唐子西以為從黃老中來愚

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Mentor: The intentions and deeds of the ancients must not be treated lightly. This essay weighs the various judgments against one another, and its views are balanced and temperate. It indulges neither in excessive denunciation nor in unprincipled agreement. From this one can discern the learning and judgment you possess. Accept it.

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Supervisor of Instruction: Among men of the Han dynasty, the character of these several figures is particularly well known. Yet assessments differ. You have explored their intentions one by one, with fairness and sympathetic understanding, exacting scrutiny and rigor. You may indeed join in judging the ancients.

When a gentleman discusses the ancients, he should consider the great principles they upheld in their achievements, rather than cling to the surviving traces of their rights and wrongs. Why is this? When gentlemen render service in an enlightened age, they invariably wish to establish meritorious achievements in their own time and leave an enduring influence upon later generations. Yet the times they encounter may be favorable or adverse, and the circumstances they face may be difficult or easy. When things cannot all accord with their wishes, they can only fulfill what lies within their own power. As for judgments of right and wrong, success and failure, these are not what they calculate. If, a thousand years later, we rely on the traces of their actions without investigating their intentions, and assess their circumstances without considering their times, then the intentions and deeds of the ancients will be obscured. How could this constitute fairness in judging them? Allow me to set forth my views on the matters raised in your illuminating question.

Zhang Liang of the Han dynasty remained devoted to the state of Han throughout, steadfastly upholding the duty of vengeance taught in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Once his achievement was complete, he withdrew, like a wild goose disappearing into the heights or a phoenix soaring aloft. Since the Three Dynasties, it has been difficult to find anyone whose conduct in entering service and withdrawing from it so merits admiration. Thus Yichuan and Nanxuan both considered him to possess the bearing of a Confucian scholar, whereas Tang Zixi thought that it derived from the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi. I, in my humble view…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以爲未盡然也彼博浪一椎奮不顧身夫
豈黃老之所能爲乎紫陽朱子謂其事多
陰謀非養虎遺患之言秦將賈人之賂耶
夫幾會之來間不容髮否則天下之事去
矣何以成佐漢之功故邵子曰智哉留侯
善藏其用可以釋陰謀之說矣諸葛孔明
三顧而起得撥亂反正之義至于鞠躬盡
瘁死而後已三代而下出處明白未之有
也故朱黼稱其爲王者之佐伊尹之儔也
===
而輔廣謂其嘗學申韓彼出師二表正大
光明又豈申韓之所能到耶朱子謂其學
不純正非取劉璋一事乎或以爲先主之
意耳否則干戈之擾久矣何以成討賊之
勢故程子曰取其志在興復漢室則正也
可以原孔明之心矣賈誼慮諸侯之疆以
爲失今不治必爲痼疾文帝惑絳灌之譖
而謫誼長沙鼂錯建削吳之策以爲削亟
禍小削遲禍大景帝聽袁盎之計而斬錯

translation_en:
…I consider this not entirely so. With that single hammer blow at Bolang, he acted boldly without regard for his own life. Could such a deed have come from the teachings of Huang-Lao? Master Zhu of Ziyang said that Zhang Liang’s undertakings often involved covert plotting. Was he not referring to the warning about rearing a tiger and leaving future trouble, and the bribery of the Qin general, a merchant [?]? When an opportunity arrives, there is not a hair’s breadth to spare; otherwise, the chance to settle the affairs of the realm is lost. How else could he have accomplished his service in assisting the Han? Thus Master Shao said: “Wise indeed was the Marquis of Liu, adept at concealing the exercise of his abilities.” This can answer the charge of covert plotting.

Zhuge Kongming rose to serve after three visits, acting in accordance with the principle of bringing order out of chaos and restoring rightful rule. He bent himself to his task, exhausting his strength and stopping only at death. Since the Three Dynasties, no one’s conduct in entering service or remaining in retirement had been so irreproachable. Thus Zhu Fu called him an assistant to a true king and a peer of Yi Yin. Yet Fu Guang said that he had studied Shen Buhai and Han Fei. His two Memorials on Dispatching the Army are upright and open-hearted: how could Shen Buhai and Han Fei have attained such a standard? When Master Zhu said that his learning was not wholly orthodox, was he not referring to the single affair of seizing Liu Zhang’s territory? Some consider this merely the intention of the Former Sovereign, Liu Bei. Otherwise, the turmoil of warfare would have continued for a long time: how could he have established a position from which to punish the rebels? Thus Master Cheng said: “If we consider his intention to revive and restore the house of Han, then it was upright.” This allows us to understand Kongming’s heart sympathetically.

Jia Yi worried about the territorial power of the princes, believing that if the opportunity to deal with it were missed, it would inevitably become a chronic affliction. Emperor Wen was misled by the slanders of Jiang and Guan and banished Jia Yi to Changsha. Chao Cuo proposed a policy of reducing Wu’s territory, believing that prompt reduction would bring a lesser calamity, while delayed reduction would bring a greater one. Emperor Jing accepted Yuan Ang’s plan and executed Chao Cuo…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
東市史氏類不足于二子者其以是與嗚
呼是以成敗論也使誼之策行於文帝豈
有後日七國之禍錯之策行于景帝必無
倉皇周章之悔殺謀臣以悅仇人杜忠臣
之口爲後世戒盖文帝鎮靜之過景帝輕
率之失使二子之策不售於二子也奚尤
衞青七擊匈奴益封三子即其微賤之跡
無以肺腑之親似若憑藉光寵因人以成
功名者及觀辭周覇之請不擅殺裨將於
境外以存人臣之義謝蘇建招賢之說但
知奉法不敢僭人主之柄此非過人之識
乎書曰臣無有作福作威青實有之青亦
豪傑也哉騎奴側陋之常耳豈足以病青
乎青以布衣草莽之微驟致大將軍尊重
之位其不滿於人意者有由然也東方朔
持論不根玩世諧俗似若隨世浮沉容悅
事主者及觀諫武帝之微行諫上林之不
可起指董偃之罪當誅本朝守道持正之

功名者及觀辭周霸之請不擅殺裨將於

之位其不滿於人意者有由然也東方朔

可起指董偃之罪當誅本朔守道持正之
punctuated:
東市。史氏類不足于二子者，其以是與？嗚呼！是以成敗論也。使誼之策行於文帝，豈有後日七國之禍？錯之策行于景帝，必無倉皇周章之悔。殺謀臣以悅仇人，杜忠臣之口，爲後世戒。盖文帝鎮靜之過，景帝輕率之失，使二子之策不售，於二子也奚尤？
衞青七擊匈奴，益封三子。即其微賤之跡，無以肺腑之親，似若憑藉光寵、因人以成功名者。及觀辭周覇之請，不擅殺裨將於境外，以存人臣之義；謝蘇建招賢之說，但知奉法，不敢僭人主之柄，此非過人之識乎？《書》曰：「臣無有作福作威。」青實有之。青亦豪傑也哉！騎奴，側陋之常耳，豈足以病青乎？青以布衣草莽之微，驟致大將軍尊重之位，其不滿於人意者，有由然也。
東方朔持論不根，玩世諧俗，似若隨世浮沉、容悅事主者。及觀諫武帝之微行，諫上林之不可起，指董偃之罪當誅，本朝守道持正之
translation_en:
…at the Eastern Market. Historians generally seem to regard these two men as wanting: is this the reason? Alas! This is to judge by success and failure. Had Jia Yi’s proposals been implemented under Emperor Wen, how could the subsequent calamity of the Seven States have occurred? Had Chao Cuo’s proposals been implemented under Emperor Jing, there would surely have been no cause to regret the ensuing panic and confusion. Killing a minister who offers counsel to please one’s enemies and silencing loyal ministers should serve as a warning to later generations. It was Emperor Wen’s excessive attachment to calm and Emperor Jing’s error of rashness that prevented the two men’s proposals from being put into effect. What blame, then, attaches to the two men?

Wei Qing attacked the Xiongnu seven times, and his three sons were additionally granted enfeoffments. Considering his humble origins and his close kinship with the emperor [?], he seems to have relied upon imperial favor and achieved fame and merit through others. Yet consider how he declined Zhou Ba’s request, refusing to execute a subordinate general on his own authority beyond the frontier, thereby preserving the proper duty of a subject; and how he rejected Su Jian’s suggestion that he recruit worthy men, knowing only to uphold the law and not daring to usurp the ruler’s prerogatives. Was this not discernment surpassing that of others? The Book of Documents says: “A minister must not confer blessings or wield awe.” Qing truly possessed this restraint. Qing, too, was an outstanding man! Having been a mounted attendant and slave was merely an ordinary circumstance of obscure birth: how could it suffice to discredit Qing? From the humble condition of a commoner outside official life, Qing rose abruptly to the honored position of General-in-Chief. There was thus a reason why some people were dissatisfied with him.

Dongfang Shuo advanced arguments without firm foundations, made light of the world, and accommodated its customs with humor. He seems to have drifted with the times and served his ruler by ingratiating himself. Yet consider his remonstrances against Emperor Wu’s incognito excursions, his insistence that Shanglin Park must not be established, his declaration that Dong Yan’s offenses warranted execution, and his admonition concerning upholding the Way and maintaining rectitude at court…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
諭漢廷尊禮公卿皆噤聲莫敢言者而朔
也乃能奮然辟戟以爭不可其所以犯顏
動主雖古忠直無以過也而史謂俳優畜
之無乃太甚矣乎想其調笑公卿陵轢將
相朔之不理于口也或有以取之耳龔勝
薛方辭辟徵不就逢萌梅福棄妻子而隱
此何時也為楊雄者既不能去及莽之篡
漢又拜為大夫且作為文章稱頌逆賊之
功德是誠何心哉雄之出處去就如此而
===
史謂恬于勢利者果如是乎大易有進退
存亡之義太玄可以準耶論語有守死善
道之言法言可以擬耶彼所謂文章者真
足以覆醬瓿耳漢祚既衰佐曹操以起兵
及事就功畢斥董昭之諂佞彧也豈無扶
漢之心哉故先辭三公至于十數後議九
錫繼之以死是以蘇子稱之非無見也夫
死生之際亦大且難矣杜牧謂其盜虛名
于漢代不亦過乎至於勸操以取兗州則

錫繼之以死是以蘇子稱之非無見也夫

punctuated:
諭。漢廷尊禮公卿，皆噤聲莫敢言者，而朔也乃能奮然辟戟，以爭不可。其所以犯顏動主，雖古忠直無以過也，而史謂俳優畜之，無乃太甚矣乎？想其調笑公卿，陵轢將相，朔之不理于口也，或有以取之耳。
龔勝、薛方辭辟徵不就，逢萌、梅福棄妻子而隱，此何時也？為楊雄者，既不能去，及莽之篡漢，又拜為大夫，且作為文章，稱頌逆賊之功德，是誠何心哉？雄之出處去就如此，而史謂恬于勢利者，果如是乎？《大易》有進退存亡之義，《太玄》可以準耶？《論語》有守死善道之言，《法言》可以擬耶？彼所謂文章者，真足以覆醬瓿耳！
漢祚既衰，佐曹操以起兵，及事就功畢，斥董昭之諂佞，彧也豈無扶漢之心哉？故先辭三公至于十數，後議九錫，繼之以死，是以蘇子稱之，非無見也。夫死生之際，亦大且難矣。杜牧謂其盜虛名于漢代，不亦過乎？至於勸操以取兗州，則
translation_en:
…admonitions. At the Han court, where dukes and ministers were treated with reverence, all kept silent and none dared speak; yet Dongfang Shuo could rise resolutely, push aside the halberds [?], and insist that this must not be done. In braving his ruler’s displeasure and moving him to reconsider, even the loyal and upright men of antiquity could not surpass him. Yet the historian says that he was kept as an entertainer. Is this not going too far? Presumably, by mocking dukes and ministers and riding roughshod over generals and chief ministers, Shuo’s unrestrained speech [?] may have brought this treatment upon himself.
Gong Sheng and Xue Fang declined official invitations and imperial summonses and would not take office; Feng Meng and Mei Fu abandoned their wives and children and went into seclusion. What a time this was! Yang Xiong, however, could not bring himself to leave; and when Wang Mang usurped the Han, he moreover accepted appointment as a Grand Master and composed writings praising the achievements and virtue of that rebel. What could his intentions really have been? Such were Xiong’s choices about serving or retiring, leaving or remaining; yet the historian describes him as indifferent to power and profit. Was he truly so? The great Book of Changes contains principles concerning advance and retreat, preservation and destruction: can the Supreme Mystery measure up to it? The Analects speaks of holding fast unto death and perfecting the Way: can the Model Sayings compare with it? His so-called writings are indeed fit only to cover a sauce jar!
When the fortunes of the Han had declined, Xun Yu assisted Cao Cao in raising troops; once their undertaking had succeeded and their work was accomplished, he denounced Dong Zhao’s sycophancy. Could Yu have lacked the desire to uphold the Han? Thus he first declined appointment among the Three Dukes more than ten times; later, when the conferral of the Nine Bestowals was discussed, he followed this with his death. Master Su’s praise of him was therefore not without insight. The choice between life and death is indeed momentous and difficult. Was not Du Mu excessive in saying that he stole an empty reputation under the Han? As for his urging Cao Cao to seize Yanzhou, then…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
比之高光官渡不令還許則比之楚漢縱
使盡出其口亦相時論勢取其相似云爾
而况飾於史氏之文乎觀操至長安不問
計於彧而問計于昭可以明彧之心事矣
善乎文中子有言荀氏有二仁而司馬温
公之論則以彧之仁居管仲之先彧不利
于佐命元勳而利于殺身以邀名豈人情
乎則庶幾乎公論矣嗚呼名義者天下古
今之所畏史官者萬世是非之權衡循其
===
名而不察其實則失其真泥其是非成敗
之迹而不本於吾心之獨見則古人之心
事終不暴白於後世也是故論其人不察
其心可乎張良身雖在漢而心則在韓也
當秦楚雲擾之時非高帝之資不足以報
韓之讎其他何暇計乎孔明之志則急於
復漢當羣雄鼎沸之日時至不取而人必
取之矣故論二子者當取其大節而小疵
可畧者也誼之謀于未形而錯則謀於將

比之高光官渡不令還許則比之楚漢緃
使盡出其口亦相時論勢取其相似云爾
而況飾於史氏之文乎觀操至長安不問
計於彧而問計于昭可以明彧之心事矣
善乎文中子有言荀氏有二仁而司馬温
公之論則以彧之仁居管仲之先彧不利

乎則庶幾乎公論矣嗚呼名義者天下古
今之所畏史官者萬世是非之權衡循其
===
名而不察其實則失其真泥其是非成敗
之迹而不本於吾心之獨見則古人之心
事終不暴白於後世也是故論其人不察
其心可乎張良身雖在漢而心則在韓也

韓之讎其他何暇計乎孔明之志則急於
復漢當羣雄鼎沸之日時至不取而人必
取之矣故論二子者當取其大節而小疵
可略者也誼之謀于未形而錯則謀於將
punctuated:
比之高光，官渡不令還許，則比之楚漢。縱使盡出其口，亦相時論勢，取其相似云爾，而况飾於史氏之文乎？觀操至長安，不問計於彧，而問計于昭，可以明彧之心事矣。善乎，文中子有言：「荀氏有二仁。」而司馬温公之論，則以彧之仁居管仲之先。彧不利于佐命元勳，而利于殺身以邀名，豈人情乎？則庶幾乎公論矣。
嗚呼！名義者，天下古今之所畏；史官者，萬世是非之權衡。循其名而不察其實，則失其真；泥其是非成敗之迹，而不本於吾心之獨見，則古人之心事終不暴白於後世也。是故論其人，不察其心，可乎？張良身雖在漢，而心則在韓也。當秦楚雲擾之時，非高帝之資，不足以報韓之讎，其他何暇計乎？孔明之志，則急於復漢。當羣雄鼎沸之日，時至不取，而人必取之矣。故論二子者，當取其大節，而小疵可畧者也。誼之謀于未形，而錯則謀於將
translation_en:
…he compared him to Gaozu and Guangwu; when, at Guandu, he urged him not to return to Xu, he compared the situation to the struggle between Chu and Han. Even if all these words came from his own mouth, he was merely assessing the circumstances and discussing the balance of power, drawing on points of resemblance. How much more allowance must be made for embellishment by the historian’s pen! Consider how Cao Cao, upon reaching Chang’an, sought counsel not from Xun Yu but from Dong Zhao: this makes Xun Yu’s intentions clear. Well did Wenzhongzi say, “The Xun family had two benevolent men.” In his assessment, Sima Guang, Duke of Wen, ranked Xun Yu above Guan Zhong in benevolence. Would it accord with human nature for Xun Yu to see no advantage in becoming a founding meritorious servant of a new dynasty, yet see advantage in sacrificing his life to win a reputation? This assessment comes close to an impartial judgment.
Alas! Reputation and moral obligation command respect throughout the world, past and present; historians hold the scales by which right and wrong are weighed for all ages. To follow a person’s reputation without examining the reality is to lose the truth. To cling to the outward traces of right and wrong, success and failure, without grounding one’s judgment in the independent insight of one’s own heart is to leave the intentions of the ancients forever unrevealed to posterity. Thus, can we judge a person without examining his heart? Though Zhang Liang served the Han dynasty, his heart remained with the state of Han. Amid the turmoil of Qin and Chu, only Emperor Gaozu’s abilities could enable him to avenge the state of Han. What leisure did he have to consider anything else? Kongming’s ambition, meanwhile, was urgently directed toward restoring the Han dynasty. When rival heroes were seething in contention, if he failed to seize an opportunity when it arose, someone else would surely seize it. Thus, those who judge these two men should recognize their integrity in great matters; their minor faults may be passed over. Jia Yi laid his plans before trouble had taken shape, whereas Chao Cuo planned when it was about to…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
著史氏之文不歸咎於絳灌袁盎之傾險
而歸於二子之擅亂夫豈是非之公乎將
使後賢雖有憂君謀國之情忠誠正直之
節亦沉吟觀望於後世也觀衞青之識度
而騎奴之跡未必然也即東方朔之直諫
而俳優之譏不足信也取文學者而略雄
失身之非泥言語者而沒彧殺身之義操
也漢之逆賊固不足齒然終其身而不敢
偃然於南面者則彧之死未必不有以愧
===
===
其良心也唐之王魏視文若之風下矣而
後世猶有取焉執事謂漢世人物猶爲近
古不其然乎雖然士以名節自立固係於
所養之純而勳業相成則係于所遇之主
惟聖賢之才見道分明自然安於所遇而
得禮義之正至於英雄豪傑生不逢時而
志不遇主非天資近道才識過人鮮有不
失其正者向使子房孔明遇湯武之君則
功烈所就非伊呂之儔耶惜乎良之輔者

著。史氏之文，不歸咎於絳灌袁盎之傾險，而歸於二子之擅亂，夫豈是非之公乎？將使後賢雖有憂君謀國之情、忠誠正直之節，亦沉吟觀望於後世也。觀衞青之識度，而騎奴之跡未必然也；即東方朔之直諫，而俳優之譏不足信也。取文學者而略雄失身之非，泥言語者而沒彧殺身之義。操也，漢之逆賊，固不足齒；然終其身而不敢偃然於南面者，則彧之死未必不有以愧其良心也。唐之王魏，視文若之風下矣，而後世猶有取焉。執事謂漢世人物猶爲近古，不其然乎？

雖然，士以名節自立，固係於所養之純，而勳業相成，則係于所遇之主。惟聖賢之才，見道分明，自然安於所遇，而得禮義之正。至於英雄豪傑，生不逢時，而志不遇主，非天資近道、才識過人，鮮有不失其正者。向使子房孔明遇湯武之君，則功烈所就，非伊呂之儔耶？惜乎良之輔者
translation_en:
…became manifest. The historians’ writings lay the blame not on the treacherous machinations of Jiang, Guan, and Yuan Ang, but on the two men for fomenting disorder [?]. Can this be an impartial judgment of right and wrong? It would make worthy men of later generations hesitate and wait upon events, even though they possess concern for their ruler, plans for their state, and loyal, honest, upright principles. Judging by Wei Qing’s discernment and breadth of mind, the account of him as a mounted slave need not be true. Judging by Dongfang Shuo’s forthright remonstrances, the sneer that he was a mere jester deserves no credence. Those who esteem literary accomplishment overlook Yang Xiong’s fault in compromising his integrity; those who cling to words obscure the righteousness of Xun Yu’s sacrifice of his life. Cao Cao was a traitor to the Han and certainly unworthy of mention. Yet he never dared, throughout his life, openly to assume the south-facing position of a sovereign: Xun Yu’s death may well have stirred shame in his conscience. Wang Gui and Wei Zheng of the Tang fell below Wenruo [Xun Yu] in moral bearing, yet later generations still found much to commend in them. You say that the men of the Han were still close to antiquity—is that not so?

Nevertheless, although a scholar’s establishment of his reputation and integrity depends upon the purity of his self-cultivation, the fulfillment of meritorious deeds also depends upon the ruler he encounters. Only those endowed with the capacities of sages and worthies perceive the Way clearly, naturally remain at ease in whatever circumstances they encounter, and attain what is right in ritual propriety and righteousness. As for heroes and outstanding men born at an inopportune time, whose ambitions find no receptive ruler, few avoid departing from what is right unless their natural endowments approach the Way and their abilities and discernment surpass those of others. Had Zifang [Zhang Liang] and Kongming [Zhuge Liang] encountered rulers such as Tang and King Wu, would their achievements not have rivaled those of Yi Yin and Lü Shang? Alas, the ruler whom Liang assisted…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詩書不事之君而亮之逢者炎劉既衰之
運時逆而勢難能從容而中道乎賈誼賢
也而所遇者未遑之君鼂錯忠也而所遇
者深峭之主使二子不得其死豈非命乎
夫何誼也進不能以審勢退不能以處窮
而錯也竟不免於術數則學術不正涵養
未深無足怪者青非喜功之君則終身於
牧豎朔非雄才之主則卒老於金馬門矣
二子顧不謂之遭邪雄之不智見于投閣
===
之時而彧之不明在操弑后之日固可以
飄然而遠遁矣向使二子不生於濁亂之
世則彧不失爲名世之臣而雄之著作卓
然爲有道君子矣孔子曰因不失其親亦
可宗也彧之見未早也又曰危邦不入亂
邦不居而雄實愧之二子所養均未得聞
道也嗟乎彧之有見於死尚不得爲全節
之臣君子有遺憾焉雄之有見於生則不
得爲有道之士矣豈不深可惜乎管見如

translation_en:
…a ruler who paid no heed to the Book of Odes or the Book of Documents, while Zhuge Liang encountered an age when the fortunes of the Liu house of Han, associated with Fire, were already declining. With the times adverse and circumstances difficult, could they act with composure and remain in accord with the Way? Jia Yi was worthy, yet the ruler he encountered had no leisure to attend to his proposals; Chao Cuo was loyal, yet the sovereign he encountered was harsh and severe. That these two men failed to meet a proper end—was this not fate? Yet why was Yi unable, when advancing in office, to judge the circumstances, or, when withdrawing, to bear adversity, while Cuo ultimately remained entangled in manipulative stratagems? Their learning was unsound and their self-cultivation insufficiently deep: there is nothing surprising in this. Had Wei Qing not encountered a ruler eager for achievements, he would have remained a herdsman all his life; had Dongfang Shuo not encountered a sovereign of exceptional ability, he would have grown old at the Gate of the Golden Horse. Can these two nevertheless be said not to have met their opportunity?

Yang Xiong’s lack of wisdom was evident when he threw himself from the pavilion, and Xun Yu’s lack of discernment was evident on the day Cao Cao murdered the empress [?]. They could certainly have withdrawn freely and fled far away. Had these two not been born into an age of corruption and disorder, Yu could still have been a minister renowned in his age, while Xiong, through his writings, could have stood out as a gentleman possessed of the Way. Confucius said, “If those upon whom one relies are fit to be close to, they may also be honored as guides.” Yu’s discernment came too late. He also said, “Do not enter a state in peril; do not dwell in a state in disorder.” Xiong indeed fell shamefully short of this. In their self-cultivation, neither man had attained an understanding of the Way. Alas! Even Yu’s discernment in choosing death did not qualify him as a minister of unblemished integrity; the gentleman finds grounds for regret in him. As for Xiong’s discernment in choosing life, he could not qualify as a man possessed of the Way. Is this not deeply regrettable? Such is my limited view…

…such are my views. I hope that you, honored sir, will favor me with further instruction.

Fifth Policy Question
Zhang Chaogang

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: In discussing the demand for substantive results, you identify the abuses of our time one by one and devise measures to rectify and eliminate them, all of which are demonstrably practicable. Your words thus already have practical utility. It is entirely fitting to select this essay and recommend it.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Instructor: The reason abuses cannot be rectified and scrutinized is confusion over names and realities. This policy essay weighs what should be retained and what reformed, and understands the discretionary judgment needed to adapt to change. The principles of government and the essential concerns of the state all fall within its deliberations. It shows a fine talent for governance [?], not merely literary ability.

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Professor: Names and realities are the distinctions by which governance is judged; the ethos of scholars is the guiding thread of government. The workings of their interconnection seem obscure but are supremely manifest. This policy essay alone investigates the abuses thoroughly and directs attention to those in a position to set an example. Its concerns are profound and its thinking far-reaching: its author is committed to the affairs of the world.

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion of the Heir Apparent: You enumerate the abuses and conclude that scholars’ habits must be corrected. This reveals your ambition to put the world in order. I shall have hopes for you.

Comment by Examiner Tong, Left Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent: Most candidates can discuss names and realities in a policy essay. But only in this essay have I seen clear insight into contemporary abuses and a searching examination of their source. You are surely someone who comprehends the essential concerns of the state.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
積之爲實學其擴之爲實政其馴而致之
爲實功實者名之本也名者實之賓也未
有實積而名不彰者也亦未有無其實而
徒享其名者也不務其實而惟名之計則
將并其名而亡之矣故善爲治者因名以
考實不善爲治者昧實而徇名極治之世
不知有實也而况於名乎極亂之世不知
有名也而况於實乎故治亂之機亦察乎
此而已矣昔者孔子之答子路曰必也正
===
名蓋救時之急務所謂循名而責實者也
其答子貢曰無信不立蓋治世之常道所
謂先實而後名者也唐虞之際道德隆盛
渾淪淳樸故其詩曰不識不知順帝之則
三代以來制度明備忠信誠愨故其詩曰
民之質矣日用飲食然孔子猶曰虞夏之
質不勝其文商周之文不勝其質而其於
周也又欲從先進之禮樂綜名實之意可
知矣後世實常不足始有責實之說名常

積之爲實學，其擴之爲實政，其馴而致之爲實功。實者，名之本也；名者，實之賓也。未有實積而名不彰者也，亦未有無其實而徒享其名者也。不務其實而惟名之計，則將并其名而亡之矣。故善爲治者，因名以考實；不善爲治者，昧實而徇名。極治之世，不知有實也，而况於名乎？極亂之世，不知有名也，而况於實乎？故治亂之機，亦察乎此而已矣。
昔者孔子之答子路曰：「必也正名。」蓋救時之急務，所謂循名而責實者也。其答子貢曰：「無信不立。」蓋治世之常道，所謂先實而後名者也。唐虞之際，道德隆盛，渾淪淳樸，故其詩曰：「不識不知，順帝之則。」三代以來，制度明備，忠信誠愨，故其詩曰：「民之質矣，日用飲食。」然孔子猶曰：「虞夏之質不勝其文，商周之文不勝其質。」而其於周也，又欲從先進之禮樂，綜名實之意可知矣。後世實常不足，始有責實之說；名常
translation_en:
…accumulated, it becomes genuine learning; extended, it becomes genuine government; gradually brought to fruition, it becomes genuine achievement. Substance is the root of name; name is the attendant of substance. Never has substance accumulated without the corresponding reputation becoming manifest, nor has anyone without substance enjoyed the corresponding reputation indefinitely. If one neglects substance and calculates only how to gain a name, one will lose even that name. Thus, those skilled in governing use names to examine substance; those unskilled in governing disregard substance and pursue names. In an age of perfect order, people are unaware even of substance—how much less of names! In an age of utter disorder, people recognize not even names—how much less substance! The workings of order and disorder can therefore be discerned simply by examining this relationship.
Long ago, Confucius answered Zilu: “It must be the rectification of names.” This was an urgent task for rescuing his age: what is called following names and demanding the corresponding substance. In answering Zigong, he said: “Without trust, there is no standing.” This was the enduring way of governing the world: what is called putting substance first and names afterward. In the time of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, the Way and virtue flourished, whole and undivided, simple and unspoiled. Thus the poem says: “Without awareness or knowledge, they follow the sovereign’s pattern.” From the Three Dynasties onward, institutions were clearly defined and fully established, and people were loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and honest. Thus the poem says: “Such is the people’s simplicity: daily they eat and drink.” Yet Confucius still said: “The simplicity of Yu and Xia did not exceed their refinement; the refinement of Shang and Zhou did not exceed their simplicity.” And concerning Zhou, he wished to follow the rites and music of earlier generations. His intention to bring names and substance into accord can thus be understood. title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有餘始有狥名之弊以漢宣之綜核卒為
王成所欺唐德宗剛明而裴延齡敢為誣
罔之說宋神宗勵精有為而呂惠卿鄧綰
以傅新法見任用斯皆徒信其名者也至
於光武中興之主而墾田之詐河南南陽
至不可問如東海王言唐太宗宋仁宗皆
致治盛美而十漸五規之疏魏徵司馬光
蓋責備焉則實之積也雖英君誼辟亦已
難矣
===
明興道化浹洽法禁齊壹移易斯世之耳目
而洒濯斯世之心志是以上下惇信內外
感孚百五十年間時有升降勢有重輕人
有得失事有常變而法之張弛俗之隆污
亦因以異迨我
皇上起而轉移恢弘之天下莫不回心而嚮道
比德而同風如琴瑟之弦更張而可鼓也
蓋又二十年於茲矣然宏綱要領昭如日
星而繁文縟節久而寢失其初者不可謂

…was excessive, and thus arose the abuse of pursuing reputation. Despite Emperor Xuan of Han’s comprehensive scrutiny, he was ultimately deceived by Wang Cheng. Emperor Dezong of Tang was resolute and discerning, yet Pei Yanling dared to advance deceitful claims. Emperor Shenzong of Song devoted himself energetically to government, yet Lü Huiqing and Deng Wan gained appointments through their adherence to the New Policies. These rulers all put their trust merely in reputation. Even under Guangwu, the ruler who restored the dynasty, fraud in the registration of cultivated land in Henan and Nanyang reached the point where investigation was impossible, as the Prince of Donghai said. Emperor Taizong of Tang and Emperor Renzong of Song both achieved splendid government; nevertheless, in their memorials on the Ten Gradual Failings and the Five Admonitions, Wei Zheng and Sima Guang demanded perfection of them. Thus, the accumulation of substantive achievement is difficult even for outstanding rulers and righteous sovereigns.
When the Ming arose, moral transformation permeated the realm, and laws and prohibitions were made uniform. What the people of this age saw and heard was transformed, and their hearts and aspirations were cleansed. Consequently, those above and below cultivated trustworthiness, and those within and beyond the court responded with confidence. Over a hundred and fifty years, circumstances rose and fell, the balance of power shifted, people succeeded and failed, and affairs followed their usual course or underwent change. Accordingly, the enforcement or relaxation of laws and the flourishing or corruption of customs also varied. Then Our Emperor arose to redirect and expand this work. Throughout the realm, all turned their hearts toward the Way, harmonized their virtue, and shared a common moral ethos, just as the strings of zithers, once restrung, can be played anew. It has now been another twenty years. Yet although the great principles and essential guidelines shine as clearly as the sun and stars, the elaborate regulations and detailed observances have, over time, gradually departed from their original form; this cannot be said…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
非奉行之罪也易曰通其變使民不倦神
而化之使民宜之今之謂矣愚請究言之
比者官多數遷罕久任萌覬覦之心巧宦
或展轉以覘除目黠吏或逢迎以希薦剡
銓司别淑慝課殿最於紙筆此不可以覈
幽明也國有常賦而内困於役外困於邊
使取盈焉猶未足也加以天災蠲賦吏限
於額格不下究又從而加朘削焉民柰何
不轉徙以死也風俗日益侈僭貴貲賤名
===
販夫市子至冒學籍此何以示衆庶也邊
圉日弛虜數蹂躪然且張虛捷隱實衊甚
者債帥搋兵符而良將受羈文吏比忽經
略事牽拘所執者舛也民易犯禁聽讞者
任聰明遠嫌疑或觀望焉一有成獄則泥
而不能改頃歲役興日費不貲財力常倍
而期復淹緩私索充而公帑益耗迺者司
農屢告匱矣中外言事多爲首鼠往或過
激而今則過巽此輕獻替而畏忌衆也至

…the fault of those charged with carrying them out. The Book of Changes says: “Adapt to changing circumstances so that the people do not grow weary; transform things with spiritual efficacy so that the people find them fitting.” This speaks to the present situation. Permit me, in my humble judgment, to explain fully.

Recently, officials have frequently been transferred and seldom remained long in office, fostering ambitions for advancement. Scheming officeholders maneuver to obtain advance knowledge of appointment lists, while crafty officials ingratiate themselves in hopes of securing written recommendations. The personnel authorities distinguish the worthy from the wicked and assess the worst and best performers through paperwork; this cannot establish who is benighted and who is enlightened in office. The state has regular taxes, yet within the realm it is strained by labor services, and on its frontiers by defense expenditures. Even when the full amounts are collected, they remain insufficient. Moreover, when natural disasters occasion tax remissions, officials, constrained by their quotas, obstruct relief from reaching those below and then subject them to further exactions. How can the people avoid wandering from their homes and dying?

Customs grow daily more extravagant and transgress distinctions of rank: wealth is esteemed and reputation despised. Peddlers and men of the marketplace even fraudulently enter the student registers. What sort of example does this set for the populace? Frontier defenses grow daily more lax, and the enemy repeatedly tramples our territory. Yet false victories are magnified and actual disgrace concealed [?]. Worse still, commanders who have incurred debts to obtain their posts hold the military tallies, while capable generals are restrained. Civil officials repeatedly neglect strategic planning [?], and affairs become entangled in restrictions: the principles they insist upon are misguided.

The people readily violate prohibitions, while those who hear and adjudicate cases rely on their own cleverness, seek to avoid suspicion, or wait to see which way opinion turns. Once a judgment has been reached, they cling to it and cannot revise it. In recent years, construction projects have proliferated, with immense daily expenses. Expenditure of funds and labor regularly doubles, yet completion is again delayed. Private demands are satisfied while public treasuries are increasingly depleted. Lately, the revenue authorities have repeatedly reported shortages. Those who offer counsel, both at court and in the provinces, mostly vacillate. Formerly they were sometimes excessively vehement; now they are excessively submissive. …As for the soldiers, they draw their grain allowances from the imperial granaries but serve as laborers in private households. Thus the ranks grow emptier by the day, and military affairs become increasingly lax, almost beyond effective performance. All these are cases in which outward form is abundant but substance insufficient. Yet how can the fault lie with the laws? Laws order the world; people uphold the laws; habitual practices, through disregard, bring them into disrepair. I have long deplored the habits of today’s scholar-officials: they take shortcuts for learning and disdain precise institutional particulars; they take flights of fancy for exposition and neglect essential principles; they take following precedent for government and remain ignorant of its foundations; they take technical accomplishments for ability and disparage judgment and breadth of understanding; they take ingratiation for harmony and forget integrity; they take factional solidarity for concord and make light of what is publicly right. Our August Emperor thoroughly understands the essentials of government and clearly perceives the abuses of the age. Resolutely intent upon the institutions of high antiquity, he repeatedly urges in his sacred instructions that outward embellishment be discarded in favor of substance. title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
挈綱濬委而探源誠得通變宜民之道矣
夫張官置吏以為民也輔理承化以事君
也望道思治至勞
宵旰之慮則承式嚮風奮庸熈績豈獨有司者
之事哉愚非通國體識時務者也然竊以
為今之法固森然具也今之天下固帖然
無虞也補敝興滯雖帝王亦所不免要亦
去其所以害治者以反其初而已然則循
名責實固今日之首務也是故重進退拔
淹逸課功能黜貪濁之吏塞僥倖之門此
官人之實也而評品之道舉矣會計必先
蠲貸必信覈登耗之數審盈縮之節此度
支之實也而計理之道舉矣謹庠序以重
名器禁奢僭以正風軌此典禮之實也而
寅清之道舉矣嚴用舍以重帷幄之權信
賞罰以鼓疆場之氣此御將之實也而安
攘之道舉矣持之以平用之以公不拘於
成不詘於勢此讞獄之實也而欽恤之道

是故重進退，拔淹逸，課功能，黜貪濁之吏，塞僥倖之門，此官人之實也，而評品之道舉矣。會計必先，蠲貸必信，覈登耗之數，審盈縮之節，此度支之實也，而計理之道舉矣。謹庠序以重名器，禁奢僭以正風軌，此典禮之實也，而寅清之道舉矣。嚴用舍以重帷幄之權，信賞罰以鼓疆場之氣，此御將之實也，而安攘之道舉矣。持之以平，用之以公，不拘於成，不詘於勢，此讞獄之實也，而欽恤之道

…grasping the guiding cord, dredging the lower reaches and tracing the source: this truly attains the way of adapting to change and benefiting the people. Offices are established and officials appointed for the people; officials assist in governing and carry forward the transforming influence of the ruler in order to serve him. His Majesty’s aspiration toward the Way and concern for good government tax his thoughts from before dawn until late at night. Is following his example, responding to his influence, exerting oneself in service, and bringing achievements to fruition the responsibility of the officials in charge alone? I am not one who comprehends the principles of state or understands the needs of the times. Yet I venture to think that the laws of the present day are already fully arrayed, and that the realm is settled and free from danger. Even sage emperors and kings could not avoid having to repair defects and revive neglected affairs. The essential task is simply to remove what impairs good government and restore its original condition. Thus, holding officeholders accountable for the actual performance of their named duties is indeed today’s foremost task.
Accordingly, taking promotions and dismissals seriously, advancing worthy men who languish unrecognized or live in retirement, assessing ability and achievement, dismissing corrupt officials, and closing the door to advancement through undeserved favor constitute the substance of appointing men to office; thereby the proper way of appraisal is fulfilled. Giving priority to accounting, faithfully carrying out remissions and loans, verifying figures for increases and losses, and scrutinizing the circumstances of surpluses and shortfalls constitute the substance of fiscal administration; thereby the proper way of financial management is fulfilled. Attending carefully to schools so as to uphold the dignity of official ranks and their insignia, and prohibiting extravagance and the usurpation of status so as to rectify customs and standards of conduct, constitute the substance of administering rites; thereby the way of reverence and purity is fulfilled. Exercising strict care in employing or dismissing commanders so as to strengthen the authority of military command, and faithfully administering rewards and punishments so as to rouse morale on the frontiers, constitute the substance of directing generals; thereby the way of securing peace within and repelling threats from without is fulfilled. Maintaining fairness and acting impartially, neither being bound by precedent nor yielding to power, constitute the substance of adjudicating criminal cases; thereby the way of reverent care and compassion…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
舉矣詳多寡之數□□役之次嚴考閱以
絕影射愼磨勘以杜乾沒此董役之實也
而節省之道舉矣至於勤訓練覈游惰實
營伍修器具此統軍之實而武事未有不
精者也持政體察事勢作敢言之氣思補
過之益此進言之實而論劾未有適已者
也夫天下之事主之者君也行而致之民
者臣也君操其約以用天下者也臣任其
繁以為天下用者也故治亂之機常繫士
===
大夫之習然則今日之務必先正乎此而
後天下之治可舉矣是故盡格致之功篤
中庸之行究根極之論獎敦厚之風勵廉
耻之節嚴正直之守凡厥有位莫不舍文
而趨質崇雅而黜浮則所明者實理所存
者實心所修者實德所遵者實道所務者
實學所敷者實政而吏之廉平士之醇謹
民之樸茂政之簡乂俗之忠厚馴而致之
將以超漢唐宋之初治而登唐虞三代之

punctuated:
舉矣。詳多寡之數，□□役之次，嚴考閱以絕影射，愼磨勘以杜乾沒，此董役之實也，而節省之道舉矣。至於勤訓練，覈游惰，實營伍，修器具，此統軍之實，而武事未有不精者也。持政體，察事勢，作敢言之氣，思補過之益，此進言之實，而論劾未有適已者也。
夫天下之事，主之者君也，行而致之民者臣也。君操其約以用天下者也，臣任其繁以為天下用者也。故治亂之機，常繫士大夫之習。然則今日之務，必先正乎此，而後天下之治可舉矣。
是故盡格致之功，篤中庸之行，究根極之論，獎敦厚之風，勵廉耻之節，嚴正直之守。凡厥有位，莫不舍文而趨質，崇雅而黜浮，則所明者實理，所存者實心，所修者實德，所遵者實道，所務者實學，所敷者實政。而吏之廉平，士之醇謹，民之樸茂，政之簡乂，俗之忠厚，馴而致之，將以超漢唐宋之初治，而登唐虞三代之
translation_en:
… is thereby put into effect. Ascertain the numbers involved, whether large or small; [two illegible characters] the sequence of labor service [?]; conduct rigorous inspections to eliminate fraudulent claims of exemption; and carefully scrutinize accounts to prevent embezzlement. These are the substantive duties of supervising labor service, through which economy is achieved. As for diligently conducting military training, investigating idleness, filling the ranks of the encampments and units, and repairing equipment, these are the substantive duties of military command; with these fulfilled, military affairs cannot fail to be proficiently managed. Uphold the principles of government, examine the circumstances of affairs, foster the courage to speak frankly, and consider the benefit of remedying faults. These are the substantive duties of offering counsel; then criticism and impeachment will never merely gratify oneself [?].
In the affairs of the realm, the ruler presides, while his ministers carry them out and bring their effects to the people. The ruler grasps the essentials in order to employ the talents of the realm; ministers undertake the manifold details in order to serve the realm. Thus the pivot between order and disorder always lies in the habits of scholar-officials. The urgent task today, then, must be first to rectify these habits; only afterward can good government be established throughout the realm.
Therefore, fully pursue the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge; earnestly practice the Mean; thoroughly examine discussions of fundamental and ultimate principles; encourage a spirit of sincerity and generosity; cultivate integrity and a sense of shame; and strictly maintain upright conduct. If all who hold office abandon ornament in favor of substance, honor what is refined, and reject frivolity, then what they understand will be genuine principles; what they preserve within will be sincere intentions; what they cultivate will be genuine virtue; what they follow will be the true Way; what they pursue will be substantive learning; and what they implement will be substantive government. Officials will become incorruptible and impartial, scholars sincere and conscientious, and the people simple and generous; government will become uncomplicated and orderly, and customs loyal and kind. These results will be attained gradually, so that we may surpass the good government of the early Han, Tang, and Song and ascend to the … of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties.

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盛豈非愚之所謂實功者哉雖然周之士
上貴之士亦自貴焉秦之士上賤之士亦
自賤焉士自貴故難進士自賤故難退貴
士進則治未有不善者也賤士進則治未
有不惡者也盖君心之重輕士習之厚薄
也士習之厚薄民情之淳澆也董子曰正
心以正朝廷正朝廷以正百官正百官以
正萬民正萬民以正四方此務實之本而
善治之機也芻蕘之見不知有裨執事之
===
獻納否

也士習之厚薄民情之淳澆也董子曰正

正萬民正萬民以正四方此務實之本而
善治之機也愚竊竟之見不知有裨執事之
===
獻納否
punctuated: 盛，豈非愚之所謂實功者哉？雖然，周之士，上貴之，士亦自貴焉；秦之士，上賤之，士亦自賤焉。士自貴，故難進；士自賤，故難退。貴士進，則治未有不善者也；賤士進，則治未有不惡者也。盖君心之重輕，士習之厚薄也；士習之厚薄，民情之淳澆也。董子曰：「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民，正萬民以正四方。」此務實之本，而善治之機也。芻蕘之見，不知有裨執事之獻納否？
translation_en: …flourishing greatness—would this not be what I, in my humble view, call substantive achievement? Nevertheless, the scholars of the Zhou were esteemed by those above them, and esteemed themselves as well; the scholars of the Qin were held cheap by those above them, and held themselves cheap as well. Because scholars esteemed themselves, they were reluctant to enter office; because they held themselves cheap, they were reluctant to withdraw. When scholars who value themselves enter office, government is invariably good; when scholars who hold themselves cheap enter office, government is invariably bad. For the weight or slight regard accorded them in the ruler’s heart determines whether scholarly habits are substantial or shallow; whether scholarly habits are substantial or shallow determines whether the people’s dispositions are sincere or debased. Master Dong said: “Rectify the heart in order to rectify the court; rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people; rectify the myriad people in order to rectify the four quarters.” This is the foundation of pursuing substance and the key to good government. These are the views of a humble gatherer of grass and firewood; I do not know whether they may be of any help in the counsel you respectfully submit to the throne.

順天府鄉試錄後序

嘉靖庚子仲秋，復當順天鄉試之期。臣承敘、臣學詩寔奉上命主試事。既陛辭入院，相與殫厥心力而校之，得士如制，刻其名氏及文之粹者為錄以獻。臣學詩乃颺言于多士曰：「聖天子敬一執中，察倫建極，薄海內外喁喁嚮風，十有九年于茲矣。矧爾多士，皆燕趙之良、四方之英，觀光於國，而其煦濡也尤密以深，孰無帝臣之願乎？夫不有定志，致遠恐泥。
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the middle month of autumn in the gengzi year of Jiajing [1540], the time for the Shuntian Provincial Examination came round once again. Your servants Chengxu and Xueshi duly received the imperial command to preside over the examination. After taking leave of His Majesty and entering the examination compound, we together devoted all our mental and physical energies to evaluating the papers. Having selected candidates in accordance with the regulations, we had their names and the finest of their compositions engraved for printing as a record to present to the throne. Your servant Xueshi then addressed the assembled scholars, saying:

“The sagely Son of Heaven reverently maintains unity of purpose and holds fast to the mean, discerns human relationships and establishes the supreme standard. Throughout the realm, to the seas and beyond, people have eagerly looked toward his transforming influence for nineteen years now. How much more so you scholars, the finest men of Yan and Zhao and the outstanding talents of the four quarters! You behold the glory of the realm, and have received its nurturing influence with particular closeness and depth. Who among you does not aspire to serve as the Emperor’s minister? Without a settled resolve, I fear that you will become mired in your efforts to reach far …

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
志顓而氣鼓舞焉若虞之省括
其不中者少矣
國家稽古定制取士純以經術夫
經道之筌也欲其因文而致諸
道也士之識度涵養匪文弗彰
而亦不盡係于文者存乎其志
也宋周敦頤有言志伊尹之所
===
志學顏子之所學夫學也者學
乎其志也顏淵言於夫子曰願
得明王聖主而輔相之顏之志
猶乎伊也咸有一德尹之學猶
乎顏也是故千駟一介不渝其
素瓢飲屢空不改其樂凡以豫
乎其志也若夫始仕也而志絕

志頵而氣鼓舞焉若虞之省括
其不中者少矣
國家稽古定制取士純以經術夫
經道之筌也欲其因文而致諸
道也士之識度涵養匪文弗彰
而亦不盡係于文者存乎其志
也宋周敦頤有言志伊尹之所
===
志學顔子之所學夫學也者學
乎其志也顔淵言於夫子曰願
得明王聖主而輔相之顔之志
猶乎伊也咸有一德尹之學猶
乎顔也是故千駟一介不渝其
素瓢飲屢空不改其樂凡以豫
乎其志也若夫始仕也而志絶
punctuated:
志顓而氣鼓舞焉，若虞之省括，其不中者少矣。
國家稽古定制，取士純以經術。夫經，道之筌也，欲其因文而致諸道也。士之識度涵養，匪文弗彰，而亦不盡係于文者，存乎其志也。宋周敦頤有言：「志伊尹之所志，學顏子之所學。」夫學也者，學乎其志也。顏淵言於夫子曰：「願得明王聖主而輔相之。」顏之志猶乎伊也。「咸有一德」，尹之學猶乎顏也。是故千駟一介不渝其素，瓢飲屢空不改其樂，凡以豫乎其志也。若夫始仕也而志絕
translation_en:
…With resolve concentrated and spirit stirred, one is like the archer checking the arrow’s nock in the Book of Yu: seldom will one miss the mark.
The state has examined antiquity to establish its institutions and selects men solely through learning in the Classics. The Classics are the means of apprehending the Way: the intention is that, through their texts, men should attain the Way. A scholar’s discernment, breadth of mind, and self-cultivation cannot become manifest without writing; yet what does not depend entirely upon writing lies in his resolve. Zhou Dunyi of the Song said: “Aspire to what Yi Yin aspired to; learn what Master Yan learned.” Learning means learning to emulate their resolve. Yan Yuan said to the Master: “I wish to find an enlightened king, a sage ruler, and assist him.” Yan’s resolve was like Yi Yin’s. “Both possessed a single virtue”: Yi Yin’s learning was like Yan’s. Thus, neither a thousand teams of four horses nor the smallest consideration could alter Yi Yin’s original principles; drinking from a gourd and repeatedly suffering want could not diminish Yan’s joy. All this was because they had established their resolve beforehand [?]. As for one who, upon first entering office, sets his aspirations utterly beyond…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
溫飽窮居也而先天下之憂若
人者雖未必與伊顏並駕而馳
然竟其所樹立亦近于較然不
欺其志者乎爾多士煦濡
聖化素以誦習伊顏為事不可謂無
其志矣茲復以文掇巍科浸嚮
用於
===
明時正試志之初也其或紛華蕩
乎其心而屈伸渝乎其守舉平
生而弁髦之則所謂文者無乃
虛車之飾青紫之媒乎夫惟確
然自信不回于利不疚于義不
怵于勢不波于俗以身世為浮
雲以古今為晝夜矻矻然求所

然竟其所樹立亦近于較然不

聖化素以誦習伊顔爲事不可謂無
其志矣玆復以文擬魏科寖嚮

明時區試志之初也其或紛華蕩
乎其心而區仲渝乎其守舉乎
生而弁髦之則所謂文者無乃
虛車之飾青紫之媒乎夫惟確
然自信不回于利不疚于義不
怵于勢不波于俗以身世爲浮
雲以古今爲晝夜所所然求所
punctuated: 溫飽，窮居也而先天下之憂，若人者雖未必與伊顏並駕而馳，然竟其所樹立，亦近于較然不欺其志者乎？爾多士煦濡聖化，素以誦習伊顏為事，不可謂無其志矣。茲復以文掇巍科，浸嚮用於明時，正試志之初也。其或紛華蕩乎其心，而屈伸渝乎其守，舉平生而弁髦之，則所謂文者，無乃虛車之飾、青紫之媒乎？夫惟確然自信，不回于利，不疚于義，不怵于勢，不波于俗，以身世為浮雲，以古今為晝夜，矻矻然求所
translation_en: …food and clothing; while living in straitened circumstances, they take upon themselves the cares of the realm before others do. Such men may not necessarily keep pace with Yi Yin and Yan Yuan; yet, considering what they ultimately establish, do they not come close to being men who manifestly remain true to their aspirations? You assembled scholars, nurtured by the sage sovereign’s transforming influence, have long devoted yourselves to reciting and studying the teachings and examples of Yi Yin and Yan Yuan. It cannot be said that you lack their aspirations. Now, moreover, through your writing you have attained distinction in the examination and are gradually advancing toward employment in this enlightened age: this is precisely the beginning of the testing of your aspirations. Should worldly splendor unsettle your hearts, and advancement or adversity alter the principles you uphold, so that you discard your lifelong commitments like a ceremonial cap and childhood forelocks, would what you call literary accomplishment amount to no more than ornament on an empty carriage, a means of obtaining the blue and purple insignia of office? Only by trusting firmly in yourselves, neither swerving for profit, nor falling short in righteousness, nor quailing before power, nor drifting with prevailing custom; by regarding your own worldly fortunes as floating clouds, and antiquity and the present as day and night; and by striving tirelessly to seek what is…

title: 嘉靖十九年順天府鄉試錄
text:
謂不朽者而終身從事焉則庶
幾償厥志矣至于遇有利鈍者
命也苟以天下爲憂者皆伊也
以仁爲已任者皆顏也人將指
其錄曰若人也乃出是科矣乎
是
聖天子作人之光主司得士之榮矣
===
若夫蕩且渝焉如前之云則上
負
天子下負所學且以貽主司他日之
羞也臣用是懼所以諭于多士
者不于其藝而先之以志書有
之功崇惟志業廣惟勤爾多士
其尚定厥志哉
alt_text:
謂不朽者而終身從事焉則庶
幾償厥志矣至于遇有利鈍者
命也苟以天下爲憂者皆伊也
以仁爲己任者皆顏也人將指
其錄曰若人也乃出是科矣乎
是
聖天子作人之光主司得士之榮矣
若夫蕩且渝焉如前之云則上
===
負
天子下負所學且以貽主司他日之
羞也〔臣〕〔愿是懼所以諗于多士〕
者不于其實而先之以志書有
之功崇惟志業廣惟勤爾多士
其尚定厥志哉
punctuated:
謂不朽者，而終身從事焉，則庶幾償厥志矣。至于遇有利鈍者，命也。苟以天下爲憂者，皆伊也；以仁爲已任者，皆顏也。人將指其錄曰：「若人也，乃出是科矣乎！」是聖天子作人之光，主司得士之榮矣。

若夫蕩且渝焉，如前之云，則上負天子，下負所學，且以貽主司他日之羞也。臣用是懼，所以諭于多士者，不于其藝，而先之以志。《書》有之：「功崇惟志，業廣惟勤。」爾多士，其尚定厥志哉！
translation_en:
…what is called lasting achievement, and devote their entire lives to it, then they may hope to fulfill their aspirations. As for whether their circumstances prove favorable or adverse, that is fate. If they take the world's troubles as their concern, they are all Yi Yin; if they take benevolence as their own responsibility, they are all Yan Hui. People will point to this examination record and say, “Such men indeed emerged from this examination!” This will bring glory to the sage Son of Heaven for nurturing men of talent, and honor to the presiding examiners for obtaining worthy scholars.

But if their hearts are led astray and their principles change, as described above, they will fail the Son of Heaven above and betray their own learning below, while also bringing shame upon the presiding examiners in days to come. This is what your servant fears. Thus, in admonishing the assembled scholars, I give priority to their resolve rather than their literary skill. The Book of Documents says: “Achievement is exalted through resolve; endeavors are broadened through diligence.” You assembled scholars, may you firmly establish your resolve!
